There was one case of severe temporary facial nerve paralysis but no cases of permanent palsy. All operations were performed using the peripheral approach to the facial nerve and the technique employed is described.
Management on Bell's palsy; Although the prognosis in Bell's palsy is generally good, there is a risk of sequelae in 10 to 15% of cases (incomplete recovery, hemifacial spasms). This warrants emergency medical treatment and repeated neurosensory test with a view to undertaking surgical decompression in severe cases. Conservative treatment consists of combining antiedema agents, vasodilators and vitamins of the B group. After ten days, clinical and electromyographic evaluation should be repeated. The absence of clinical recovery combined with altered or abolished electrical conduction is an indication for surgical decompression of the facial nerve.
Microvascular decompression of the facial nerve for hemifacial spasm: Clinical and electrophysiologic observations; Eight patients with idiopathic hemifacial spasm were studied before and after decompression of the facial nerve. Seven patients had an excellent clinical response to surgery, with total resolution of the spasm. One patient had a complete facial palsy and sensorineural deafness on the involved side after surgery, with recurrence of the spasm 6 months later. In all patients, synkinetic activity was present on the involved side before surgery and disappeared after surgery. These findings suggest that the disorder involves the extra-axial portion of the facial nerve. The findings do not require an etiologic role of vascular compression because the response to surgery could be related either to mild trauma of the nerve during the surgical procedure or to subsequent fibrosis.
Facial palsy. Surgical treatment; In this paper the authors present 15 patients treated for irreversible facial paralysis. After making a study of the different etiological agents which may cause this kind of paralysis and a description of the surgical possibilities that present day surgery offers, the authors analyse the conditions of the criteria used for their treatment, drawing conclusions from the results obtained. They feel that Thompson's muscle grafts should be the treatment of choice for the surgery of the muscle in long standing palsies. Cross facial anastomosis, on the other hand, is the method of choice when the facial musculature is not totally atrophic and still has some degree of functionality.
Occult neoplasms in facial paralysis; A review of 14 cases of occult neoplasms associated with facial paralysis indicated that when the onset was gradual over a period of weeks or months, when all of the scientific and technological investigations, including CT scanning, polytomes, neurosensory and otologic tests, sialography, lacrimation, taste, internal acoustic meatus, evaluation of the deep lobe of the parotid, and clinical examination of the parotid and neck were negative, the tumor was almost always found in association with the main trunk of the extratemporal portion of the parotid gland. Of these neoplasms, 80% were malignant tumors of the parotid gland and 15% were neurilemomas of the main trunk of the facial nerve. The above situation is an indication for human assessment by surgical investigation of the facial nerve, with the first priority being given to the main trunk of the extratemporal portion.
Spontaneous return of facial motion following seventh cranial nerve resection; Four patients who had undergone operative procedures, wherein substantial segments of the VIIth cranial nerve had been resected, experienced some degree of reanimation of the muscles of expression despite the fact that no restitutive measures were employed. The site of insult was in the face in two; the temporal bone in one; and the fourth occurred in the cerebellopontine angle. Teeth-clenching and grimacing were practiced before a mirror by each subject, and one wonders if 're-education' of dormant trigeminal nerve fibers might have facilitated the rehabilitation which was achieved.
Cholesteatoma in the petrous apex; Six patients with extensive cholesteatoma in the petrous pyramid are reported. All patients had a facial palsy of long duration. In five patients with a history of otitis media, radiographic examinations and surgical explorations revealed chronic inflammatory changes in the middle ear, which suggested that the cholesteatoma in the petrous pyramid was associated with a preceding otitis media. Only in one patient, without a past history of otitis media, was the cholesteatoma assumed to be of congenital origin. The cholesteatoma was totally removed in five patients using a translabyrinthine approach and in one by a middle cranial fossa approach. Control of middle ear infection, obliteration of the mastoid petrosal cavity, and facial nerve repair were supplementary but significant surgical problems.
Two cases of the brain metastasis from the cancer of colon. Case reports and literature review; Two unusual cases of brain metastasis from cancer of the colon were reported. A 63 year old female (case 1), who underwent hemicolectomy for carcinoma of the transverse colon about a year ago, was admitted because of progressive unsteady gait, nausea and vomiting. She disclosed marked trunkal ataxia, right limb ataxia, right Horner sign, right facial palsy and bilateral horizontal gaze nystagmus. Computed tomogram revealed a low density area (4x5 cm) in the posterior fossa. Following the infusion of contrast material a scattered enhancement was noted within this low density area. Surgical removal was total and the pathological diagnosis of the tumor was adenocarcinoma, consistent with a primary colon carcinoma. A 52 year old male (case 2) had generalized convulsion and then walked unsteadily. Four months ago, he had low anterior resection of a carcinoma of the sigmoid colon. On examination, he showed mild dysarthria, left facial palsy and left limb ataxia. Computed tomogram revealed a mild increased density (5 cm in size) with surrounding edema in right frontal region. After infusion of contrast material there was marked enhancement of a mass lesion. On neurological examination, pursuit movement was saccadic, especially on the right, optokinetic nystagmus was suppressed on the left side and visual suppression of caloric nystagmus disappeared in both directions. However, after removal of the mass these abnormal findings were all improved. Surgery (subtotal removal) revealed metastatic adenocarcinoma, compatible with a primary carcinoma. We postulated that his ataxia was attributed to frontal ataxia and this was discussed from a neurotological point of view. Carcinoma of the large intestine relatively rarely metastasizes to the brain, possibly because of the filtering effect of the pulmonary and hepatic circulation.
Two cases of bilateral simultaneous facial palsy; Case 1. A 50-year-old woman who had a long-term administration of steroid, presented peripheral facial palsy on both sides at a time interval of six days. Her illness was diagnosed as bilateral Bell's palsy because there was no evidence of systemic diseases. Case 2. A 58-year-old woman with an ovarian tumor and polyneuritis, presented bilateral facial palsy at intervals of two days. CSF tests revealed the existence of Guillain-Barre syndrome. After the gynecological operation facial palsy recovered slowly. In the two cases the recovery was earlier and more complete on the following side than on the preceding side of facial palsy.
Free muscle grafting in facial paralysis; For the dynamic restoration of elevation of the angle of the mouth in facial paralysis six possible variations of free muscle and nerve graft techniques are described. One of the techniques using the previously denervated extensor digitorum brevis muscle with its motor nerve in continuity serving as a cross-face nerve graft, was used in eight patients. The results were disappointing and it is concluded that the method should be abandoned.
Basal cell adenoma of the major salivary glands. Report of a case with facial nerve encroachment; Basal cell adenoma of the parotid gland showed histopathologic evidence of facial nerve encroachment. A review of the pertinent literature and a discussion of current concepts of the histogenesis of the tumor indicate that a spectrum of benign to malignant forms of this unusual tumor may exist. The sparsely reported association of this tumor and its malignant variants to facial nerve pathology is discussed, and recommendations for treatment are made.
Parotid tumours. A 10-year series from the Department of ENT. Oslo city Hospital Ulleval Sykehus; Parotid enlargement is a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge to all physicians. In a study of 193 patients with parotid tumours operated upon in an ENT department, the incidence of complications such as facial paralysis, tumour recurrence and gustatory sweating (Frey syndrome) is reviewed and discussed. The histological specimens collected during the 10-year period have been reevaluated and are listed in accordance with the WHO classification for salivary gland tumours. Biopsy of a parotid tumour should be avoided in view of the risk of local implantation of tumour cells. It is our opinion that the tumour should be removed via a superficial or total parotidectomy even if benign. The operation should be carried out in an ENT-department and by a surgeon well conversant in the anatomy of the facial nerve.
Surgery for Bell's palsy; Electroneuronographic study of the spontaneous course of Bell's palsy shows that chance of a satisfactory spontaneous return of facial function is reduced to 50% when 95% or more maximal degeneration is reached within two weeks of onset. For this reason immediate surgical decompression (including the meatal foramen) was performed on 14 patients with 90% or more degeneration within three weeks of palsy onset. These patients and 13 who refused treatment under similar conditions were reviewed one to three years later by three physicians familiar with facial nerve problems. Results show that to obtain satisfactory (80% to 100%) return of facial movements in all cases of Bell's palsy, surgical decompression should be performed within 24 hours when degeneration reaches 90% to 94% within one to 21 days after onset. By using these guidelines, the number of unnecessary operations will be kept under 16%.
The temporalis myofascial dynamic sling; The temporalis myofascial dynamic sling is a facial rehabilitative technique commonly used to reanimate the paralyzed face. The technique is especially useful after facial muscle atrophy has occurred or neurotization attempts have failed. The temporalis myofascial transfer can rehabilitate both the eye and the corner of the mouth and in contrast to static sling procedures can restore dynamic motor function. By applying the dynamic force of the myofascial pedicle generated by clenching the teeth the motivated patient can produce facial movement. The psychological reward for the patient in this case is significant.
Gold implant to upper eyelid for correction of lagophthalmos; Individually fitted upper eyelid gold implants were placed in 18 patients with lagophthalmos due to facial palsy, with satisfactory results. The advantages, disadvantages, and possible complications are reported.
Facial paralysis of neoplastic origin: Diagnosis and management; The individual with a progressive (weeks to months) facial weakness should be considered to have a tumor involving the facial nerve until proved otherwise. All individuals experiencing a facial paralysis must undergo a thorough neurotologic evaluation to establish the etiology. Bell's palsy is a diagnosis by exclusion. While computerized axial tomography (CAT) scans, polytomography and arteriograms are extremely helpful, these studies very often fail to demonstrate intrinsic tumors involving the facial nerve. For this reason all individuals experiencing a progressive facial paralysis should have an exploration of their facial nerve from the internal auditory canal (IAC) through the stylomastoid foramen into the parotid gland. The purpose of this paper is to present a series of cases of facial paralysis having as their etiology intrinsic or extrinsic neoplasms. Clinical patterns are established, diagnostic protocols formulated and the results of surgical management reviewed.
The use of cromolyn sodium in the prevention of nerve degeneration in Bell's palsy; Clinical use by inhalation of cromolyn sulphate, a mast cell degranulator inhibitor, within 4 days after the onset of Bell's palsy will prevent nerve degeneration and provide complete recovery within a range of 2 wk. The successful administration of the drug supports the authors' experimental concept of Bell's palsy as an immunological disease. The triggering action of the mast cell as a part of IgE antibody cell mediator system is postulated as the key role on controlling the neural edema. In this paper the authors contrast the difference in disease duration time and degree of recovery in a group of patients using high dose prednisone therapy and a group using cromolyn sulphate.
Rhabdomyosarcoma of the middle ear in a child; An embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the middle ear occurring in a child is described. The disease history showed an acute process in the middle ear accompanied by early seventh nerve paralysis. The external auditory canal was filled with a rapidly growing polypoid mass. Surgical treatment was limited and provided adequate biopsy material. Treatment consisted of multiple-drug chemotherapy and radiation therapy followed by maintenance chemotherapy. The facial nerve paralysis resolved and the patient has remained free of disease one year after treatment was started.
Management of cranial nerves I through VII following skull base surgery; Cranial nerve injuries are common with skull base surgery. While injuries to the seventh and tenth cranial nerves can be corrected to satisfactory degrees, rehabilitation of the third, fourth, and sixth nerves is possible to only a limited degree. This study stresses the management of facial paralysis following skull base surgery and is based upon the author's experiences in dealing with 38 patients who suffered such a facial paralysis. The best results of rehabilitative surgical treatment were achieved with techniques that connect the central stump to the peripheral system. The time between nerve injury and repair was the most significant determinant of the success of the surgical procedure: when the nerve was repaired within three months of the injury, the best results were obtained; when the central stump was not available or the injury was more than two years old, repair was not as satisfactory. In the latter case the procedure of choice was the 12th-7th nerve hookup. Indications and results of facial nerve grafting, cross faciofacial nerve hookups, muscle swings, free muscle implantations, and eye reanimation techniques are discussed.
Superficial musculoaponeurotic system suspension and buccinator plication for facial nerve paralysis; This case demonstrates the use of the superficial musculoaponeurotic system for suspension in facial nerve paralysis. This approach allows access to the buccinator, which is plicated to the masseteric fascia to reduce intraoral redundancy.
Review of peripheral facial palsy; A long portion of the facial nerve is located inside the temporal bone from where it gives its main branches. Topographic tests help to localize a lesion clinically, and electrodiagnostic tests are used to determine the degree of damage to the nerve. Bell's palsy or facial nerve idiopathic paralysis is the most frequent cause of peripheral facial palsies; the diagnosis is made by exclusion. The course of the disease tends toward a complete remission in most cases (85%) but some cases (15%) may leave permanent long term sequelae. The treatment usually aims at the cause of the palsy. In Bell's palsy, it is important to follow closely the evolution with the electrodiagnostic tests in order to detect the first signs of degeneration as soon as possible; then surgical decompression is indicated.
Neuronography of the facial nerve; Electrophysiological methods of examination of the facial nerve provide information concerning the degree of nerve damage and the progress c.q. arrest of instituted treatment; they may also be used to assess therapeutic results of peripheral facial paresis. Since 1975, the ORL Clinic of the University of Halle in addition to the traditional methods of functional and topical diagnosis applies electroneuronogaphy to study facial nerve function. So far it has been carried out in 197 patients. Findings prove electroneuronography to be an adequate method for objective determination of facial nerve function. It constitutes a valuable addition to traditional methods of examination, especially in questions of the therapeutic consequences in recent peripheral facial paresis.
Lymphocytic lymphoma involving the middle ear; A patient with lymphocytic lymphoma involving the middle ear had otalgia and facial palsy as his initial symptoms, and the definitive diagnosis was made by means of biopsy of the tumor in the middle ear. Review of te literature revealed only one other case with clinical involvement of the middle ear space.
Facial nerve reconstruction; A retrospective study on 21 patients who had a reconstruction of their facial nerve was undertaken by means of a new photographic method of evaluation. The average of recuperation results was 62.38%. 85% of the patients achieved a good or excellent evaluation. The only individual parameter that showed some influence on the outcome of the surgery was the length of the graft. Compared with a short graft (≤1 cm), the long graft (≥1 cm) is associated with better results. Good and excellent results appeared available for patients whose preoperative palsy had lasted from 18 to 36 months.
Nerve injuries during rhytidectomy. Considerations after 3,203 cases; The potential for injury to the nerves of the face is ever-present in rhytidectomy. Only a thorough knowlegde of the anatomy of the face, adequate surgical experience, and strict adherence to basic operating principles can avoid problems. The temporalis, paraorbitalis, genian, mandibular, and cervicoauricularis areas each offer hazards, which are detailed in this discussion, along with some technical details to avoid both temporary and permanent damage.
Facial paralysis in children - differential diagnostics and therapy; Review based on 121 personal cases from 25 years. 33 paralyses (27.3%) were already present immediately after birth (10 children with malformations, 10 times caused mechanically and in 6 cases by hypoxemic or toxic damages). 88 paralyses (72.3%) occurred in elder infants and children: 37 cases of idiopathic (Bell's) palsy, 23 other diseases of viral origin (meningo-encephalitis, poliomyelitis, complication from polio-immunization), 8 bacterial infections (mastoiditis, purulent meningitis, tuberculous lymphadenitis) 7 tumours and 6 traumatic processes. Congenital palsies presented mostly as central paralyses and acquired ones more frequently as peripherical paralyses. The latter had two peaks in the age distribution, in preschool-children and in the middle school-age. A flow-chart for rational differential diagnostics is presented. According to the good prognosis of facial paralysis in children we recommend only conservative treatment with corticosteroids immediately after onset of the disease. An operative decompression of the facial nerve was never necessary. 38 children were followed-up: two thirds showed complete normalization of the facial function and the remaining third had only slight disturbances. Severe residuals were found in no child. The idiopathic cases have the best prognosis.
Free revascularised muscle grafts reinnervated by cross facial nerve grafts; In an attempt to restore more normal voluntary and involuntary movement in the paralysed face, free revascularised muscle grafts were inserted in 7 patients, all of whom had non-functioning perioral and lower cheek musculature on one side. This procedure was preceded by a cross facial nerve graft in order to supply the nerve fibres to the graft as soon after its insertion as possible. The clinical and electromyographical results are discussed and together have provided sufficient evidence to indicate that the technique works effectively.
Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome; A description is given of a case of Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome in which a woman patient had a facial paralysis with hemifacial swelling on 4 occasions within 3 years. A study of the literature over the last 5 years was made, 25 publications being found. These were examined mainly to gain insight into the course, prognosis and therapy of this syndrome.
Facial diplegie through tick bites; Facial diplegy is seldom met in otology. The etiology through tick bites is exceptional (25 cases in the whole world). The clinical evolution is the same as the one of peripheral facial paralysis, that is to say the affection is curable with sequelae or not. After a short parasitologic recall, the authors connect this paralysis with the neurological form of polyradiculoneuritis.
A case of thalamic germinoma with crossed aphasia in a dextral; A patient, 17-year-old right-handed male, was admitted with chief complaints of headache, abnormality of visual field and speech disturbance. There were pigmentations on the back of hand, foot and the perineum. Neurological examination revealed left homonymous hemianopsia, right slight degree of ptosis, left facial palsy, a mild paresis of the left upper extremity and motor aphasia. Right carotid angiography showed marked unrolling and midline shift of right anterior cerebral artery. CT scan revealed ring-like high density area in the right thalamic region, which was enhanced after contrast infusion. Brain scintigraphy also showed an abnormal accumulation at the same site. The hen-egg sized tumor (40 g.) was almost totally removed by the right fronto-parietal craniotomy. The tumor was characterized histologically by the so-called two-cell pattern with teratomatous components. As postoperative treatment local injection of adriamycin, irradiation and immunotherapy with picibanil were performed, and then left hemiparesis was markedly improved without sign of recurrence. Language evaluation was performed after operation. There were dysarthria, remarkable word amnesia, paraphasia and perseveration. Repetition was also impaired. His speech function was concluded to be a mixed type aphasia mainly composed of Broca's aphasia. The speech function of thalamus and crossed aphasia with dextrales were discussed.
Lymphocytic lymphoma involving the middle ear; A patient with lymphocytic lymphoma involving the middle ear had otalgia and facial palsy as his initial symptoms, and the definitive diagnosis was made by means of biopsy of the tumor in the middle ear. Review of the literature revealed only one other case with clinical involvement of the middle ear space.
Tolosa-Hunt syndrome: A case with associated facial nerve palsy; A 54-year-old man developed a painful right third nerve palsy with signs of involvement of the first two divisions of the trigeminal nerve and, later, ipsilateral peripheral facial nerve weakness. A cavernous sinus venogram demonstrated narrowing of the third portion of the right ophthalmic vein and poor filling of the adjacent cavernous sinus. Resolution occurred with steroid therapy. The Tolosa-Hunt syndrome may be a variant of a larger syndrome of recurrent multiple cranial polyneuropathies without identifiable cause.
Moebius syndrome: One case; The Moebius syndrome is a congenital anomaly characterized by paralysis of the sixth and seventh nerves. In some instances, there may be weakness of the adductors. The other muscles are normal. Visual acuity is not affected. Other congenital defects may be associated: polydactyly, and defects of the ear and of the tongue. The etiology is probably an embryonal aggression, because of aplasia of the facial and abducens nuclei. The impossibility to move the eyes laterally in either direction points to supranucleus involvement by defective development of the medial longitudinal fasciculus. Some people suggest that a myogenic disturbance should be the principal and unique etiology. There is no evolution, and no treatment.
Moebius syndrome associated with benign intracranial hypertension; A patient with Moebius syndrome who developed benign intracranial hypertension is presented. The patient has the following features of Moebius syndrome: bilateral facial palsy, esotropia with severely limited abduction, paresis and hypoplasia of the tongue, bilateral clubbed feet, and thoracic lumbar scoliosis. At age 15, he presented to the hospital with headaches and bilateral papilledema and was diagnosed as having benign intracranial hypertension. The headaches and papilledema resolved on oral steroids. The 2 conditions are discussed with emphasis on their etiologies and pathogenetic mechanisms. An attempt is made to relate the 2 conditions through a common mechanism. Both syndromes may have a disorder of CSF dynamics which leads to an overaccumulation of CSF in the tissues of the central nervous system.
Reeducation in peripheral facial paralysis; When dealing with a case of peripheral facial paralysis kinestherapy implies: good anatomophysiological knowledge about the facial nerve, its vascularisation, the innervated muscles, mimetics, and from the testing manual, practical knowledge of massage amd reeducation to arrive at a delicate reharmonisation. Kinesitherapy proves indispensable for a rapid recovery and complete absence of sequels. Its precise role in the result is, however, difficult to evaluate due to the fact that it is classified in a therapeutic scheme that may be medical or surgical.
Intratympanic injection of steroid for treatment of idiopathic facial paralysis; Intratympanic injection of steroid was performed in patients with idiopathic facial paralysis during a period from 1973 to 1979, and the results of this treatment were analyzed and compared with those of conventional treatment. As the standard determination of the degree of facial recovery, the pointscoring system proposed by May (1970) was adopted in this study. In patients with incomplete paralysis treated within 2 weeks after onset, 92.6% attained full recovery by this therapy and 96.4% by conservative treatment. But in patients with complete paralysis, 69.2% showed full recovery, and 38.2% by conservative treatment. It should be noted that the appearance of incipient remission signs and average length of treatment were considerably shortened by this treatment in patients with complete paralysis. In cases of long standing Bell's palsy and Ramsay-Hunt syndrome, no satisfactory results were obtained. In conclusion, intratympanic steroid therapy initiated within two weeks after onset is worth-while and rational for treatment of Bell's palsy.
Mastoid chloroma as relapse in acute myeloid leukaemia; Leukaemic infiltration of the petrous temporal bone is uncommon but with improved remission rates longer survival in leukemia isolated sites of relapse can be expected more frequently. Mastoid chloroma requires treatment with chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Wide-field mastoidectomy and facial nerve decompression are contraindicated.
Facial nerve paralysis secondary to mandibular fracture; When facial nerve paralysis complicates a mandibular fracture, it may be difficult to locate the point of injury, since the nerve may be injured in the fallopian canal by a secondary temporal bone fracture or in soft tissue by mandibular fragments. Following a review of eight previously reported cases, this paper presents two additional cases, one with bilateral, complete paralyses and the other with a unilateral paresis. In the first, the condyles were driven posteriorly, resulting in bilateral temporal bone fractures, a unilateral external canal stenosis, and a unilateral sensorineural hearing impairment. Good functional return followed decompression of the intratemporal facial nerves. In the second patient, facial function returned spontaneously. When the temporal bone is fractured, therapy follows guidelines for facial paralysis associated with basilar skull fractures from other causes. If soft tissue injury is suspected, the decision must be made whether to explore the nerve or wait for spontaneous recovery.
Congenital cholesteatoma of the temporal bone. (A report on 5 cases); The authors report 5 cases (3 male and 2 female) of congenital cholesteatoma of the temporal bone where the diagnosis was made earlier in each successive case. The first diagnosis was made on the basis of a total paralysis of the facial nerve, the last was made on the basis of a transitory paralysis of the facial nerve associated in the majority of cases with deafness or reduced hearing. Early removal preserves function of the VIIth and VIIIth nerve and is the justification for a systematic X-ray in the Stenver's incidences to be carried out in any facial weakness, even if it is transitory. The surgical approach of choice is the middle fossa approach. There is no drainage necessary because these cholesteatomas are not infected.
Cerebellar ataxia and papilloedema in chronic relapsing Guillain-Barre syndrome (A case report and review of the evidence for possible central nervous system involvement); A young woman presented with flaccid quadraparesis, a right infranuclear facial palsy and limb areflexia following a two-day history of severe streptococcal pharyngitis. She was found to have cerebellar ataxia in the upper limbs with normal deep sensation. Bilateral papilloedema developed a year later during her third relapse. Treatment with high dose of prednisolone on an alternate day regimen basis induced a long lasting remission including improvement of her cerebellar deficit. The mechanism of cerebellar involvement and the pathogenesis of her papilloedema were uncertain. This is in keeping with the views previously expressed by earlier authors.
The stapedius reflex in idiopathic facial palsy; Various aspects of the stapedial reflex responses and facial palsy were investigated. In the first study the initial reflex responses following facial palsy in 120 patients were compared with the outcome. In 42 patients with a present stapedial reflex, the full recovery rate was 92 per cent as compared to 78 patients with an absent stapedial reflex and a full recovery rate of 73 per cent. Twenty-five patients with facial palsy and absent stapedial reflex were followed up. In 21 patients (84 per cent) the return of a positive stapedial reflex was the first sign of recovery, and it preceded any other evidence of recovery by 6 weeks. The third study showed that the stapedial reflex does not participate in the synkinetic movement of post-paralytic patients.
Malignant external otitis due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa in childhood; Malignant external otitis (MEO) is a severe variant of external otitis. As originally described by Chandler in 1968, MEO is an infection of the external ear canal, usually due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is associated with systemic invasion, significant neurologic sequelae, and a high mortality rate. The vast majority of cases have occurred in elderly adults with diabetes mellitus. We present a case of MEO occurring in a 6 yr old child, and have compared the findings in our case with those in the adult literature.
Facial nerve palsy following therapeutic embolization; Ischemic neuropathy is a previously described but rarely encountered complication of therapeutic embolization. Two cases of peripheral facial nerve palsy following embolization of branches of the external carotid artery are reported, and the possible mechanism is discussed.
A case of Ramsay Hunt syndrome with encephalitis; A case of a seventy year old female patient with the left side Ramsay Hunt syndrome and encephalitis has been reported. Neurological impairments of the left acoustic nerve, peripheral facial palsy on the same side and slightly disturbed consciousness were observed. By cerebrospinal fluid examinations prominently increased cells and elevation of protein level were found. The highest titer against herpes zoster virus was x 1024 in serum and x 32 in liquor. Moreover, the titer against herpes simplex virus was elevated to a maximum of x 128 in serum and x 8 in liquor. CT scan revealed low density area chiefly in the frontal lobe and expanding to posterior portion of temporal lobe in the white matter of the affected side. This change was thought to be not the direct infiltration by the infection but an edematous change due to meningitis. About three months later CT scan was done but the low density area had disappeared and there were no enlargement of ventricles or sulci. According to the administration of corticosteroid hormone the clinical pictures of encephalitis improved and the patients discharged without signs of dementia. (Journal received: 21 May, 1982.)
Surgical treatment of leprous facial paralysis in Iran; Leprous facial paralysis appears more frequently in Iran than in other countries. The damaged branch is more often the upper one inducing lagophthalmos and is sometimes associated with a trigeminal anesthesia. The ocular risk is great. When the lower branch is afflicted, it gives an anesthetic deformity and speaking difficulty. As a consequence, surgical treatment is necessary and directed; against lagophthalmos, with static or dynamic methods, against the ptosis of commissura labiorum with several techniques available.
Recent advances in reconstructive microsurgery; Microsurgical techiques, which have already been exploited in other disciplines for a long time, have recently been greatly extended to include the field of reconstructive and plastic surgery, thanks to the progress made in the surgery of small vessels and peripheral nerves. This had led to the appearance of new therapeutic procedures, first in emergency for traumatological surgery: digital replantations (whose indications are now well codified), soon followed by replantations of other segments of the body, accidentally amputated, and providing a sufficient vascular pedicle. But, in addition to emergencies, repair surgery has also undergone a revolution with microsurgical transfers of microrevascularized and, if necessary, microreinnervated tissues. An example of this is our experience of over 110 free transfers since 1974. The free skin flap is one of the major acquisitions. Donor sites are many and various (groin flaps, delto-pectoral flaps, dorsalis pedis flaps, axillary flaps), but two sites offer the original peculiarity of using surplus tissue removed in esthetic surgery, the lateral mammary flap and the inferior gluteal flap. Sensory free skin flaps, which are both revascularised and reinnervated can be used to restore either protective sensibility in a lower member (dorsalis pedis, delto-pectoral, axillary and lateral mammary flaps) or finer and discriminatory sensibility in the hand (first web flaps from the foot, toe pulp flaps). Numerous other revascularized tissue transfers may be used in a wide range of repairs which could not be achieved with traditional techniques: scalp transfers to the hairy areas of the face; fat tissue transfers for hemi-facial atophy; reinnervated muscle transfers for facial palsy; bone transfers for major bone defects; greater omentum transfers to the cranial vault or on the leg; intestinal transfers for the repair of the oesophagus. But microsurgical transfers can also be used to mobilise several tissue structures 'en bloc' with a single vascular pedicle. This procedure includes composite tissue transfers. Musculo-cutaneous transfers may or may not be carried out with reinnervation of the muscle, with maximum use of sensori-motor transfers with skin and muscle reinnervation (neuro-vascular myo-cutaneous dorsalis pedis flap). Osteo-cutaneous tranfers offer an opportunity for daring repairs in lower members (osteo cutaneous iliac flaps with deep circumflex iliac vascular pedicle). Finally, second toe transfers can be used for repair of the thumb or a long finger for some severe mutilations of the hand. All these new methods clearly illustrate the wealth and variety of the possibilities open to reconstructive microsurgery, which has already been promoted from the level of a mere technique (micro-neuro-vascular repair) to become a veritable specialty in its own right (free tissue transfer surgery).
Maximal nerve excitability testing versus neuromyography: Prognostic value in patients with facial paralysis; Neuromyography (NMG) is compared with maximal nerve excitability testing (NET) as a prognostic tool in facial paralysis. Normal latencies, summation muscle action potentials, and test/retest reliability were determined in three groups of subjects. NMG was performed in 33 control subjects of Group 1 to determine test/retest reliability. To determine the range of normal facial nerve conduction latency and amplitude and configuration of the summation muscle action potentials, NMG was performed in 172 otolaryngologic control patients without facial paralysis. NMG and NET were then compared in Group 3, which consisted of 43 patients with Bell's palsy. Fluctuations in NMG were then analyzed in a fourth test series of three subjects from Group 1, in whom summation muscle action potentials at various positions of the electrodes were compared. The high rate of fluctuations observed indicates the need for further assessment of test/retest reliability and standardization of normal values in NMG. Our results indicate that maximal NET is more reliable than NMG for prognosis of facial paralysis.
Hearing impairment and facial palsy as initial signs of Wegener's granulomatosis; In two patients with Wegener's granulomatosis, treatment-resistant serous otitis media was followed by unilateral facial nerve palsy. Later both patients developed uraemia due to extracapillary glomerulonephritis. In one of them, who was treated with prednisone and cyclophosphamide, renal function improved, while in the other patient it remained impaired. Both patients suffered lasting hearing impairment in spite of general improvement during the course of the disease. The facial nerve palsy improved slightly in one, while no improvement was seen in the other. The pssibility of Wegener's granulomatosis or other autoimmune collagen diseases should be considered in cases of treatment-resistant serous otitis media. Early diagnosis and treatment can possibly save the patient from the life-threatening consequences of these diseases.
Diagnosis and treatment of Bell's palsy; The principles worked out in connection with Bell's palsy in the Otorhinolaryngological Department of the University Medical School, Szeged, are summarized by the author. Partly on the basis of the data of the literature, partly on his own experiences, a schema, facilitating the prediction of the prognosis, has been worked out. As it may be concluded from the electro-diagnostical examinations, the course of the disease is decided within the first two weeks. Therefore the patients must be admitted as soon as possible to an institute where the adequate diagnostical methods for the expectable course of the palsy are available and also where the conditions for a surgical intervention are possible. The treatment must always be adjusted to the pathophysiological processes. These latter may be followed by the above-mentioned methods.

Cross-facial nerve anastomosis in the treatment of facial paralysis: A preliminary report on 10 cases; This preliminary communication describes our early experiences with one-stage cross-facial nerve anastomosis in the treatment of complete and recent facial paralysis. We submit that this technique can offer the patient a better result than that obtained by the other methods in current use. Since this paper was submitted for publication, four more cases have been treated and these will be reviewed in due course along with those described in this article. This should allow one to critically review the long term effects of this surgical technique.
Cross-facial nerve grafts and microneurovascular free muscle transfer for long established facial palsy; Cross-facial nerve grafts followed in 4 to 12 months by microneurovascular free gracilis transplantation can produce adequate reconstruction in the lower two-thirds of a paralysed face. The mixed sensory and motor deep peroneal nerve and the small muscle bulk of the extensor digitorum brevis limit its usefulness in facial palsy. The gracilis has proved to be a much superior muscle. A feasible method for total reanimation of unilateral facial palsy is presented.
Facial nerve block in the treatment of hemifacial spasm; 45 patients with hemifacial spasm were analyzed retrospectively. The age in which the initial spasm was ranged from 18 yr to 77 yr, with a median age of 47 yr. Younger children (under 20 yr), and older persons (over 70 yr) were rarely sick. Women are more frequently afflicted than men, in a ratio of about 5 to 1. 40 patients were treated by facial nerve block at the stylomastoid foramen. Facial nerve blocks were done 72 times; 42 times (58%) were needle insertion only. 15 times (21%) were needle insertion with a small amount of pure alcohol, and the remainder (21%) were unsuccessful blocks. Duration of the nerve block effect was generally less than one year. The spasm recurred usually within 6 months in those patients treated by needle insertion only. However, with pure alcohol, it was longer. Unfortunately, the use of alcohol always resulted in a longer duration of facial palsy after nerve block. It was revealed by the enquete that almost all the patients did not consider the facial nerve block as a 'godsend'. The most popular reasons for this were severe pain during nerve block procedure, facial palsy after nerve block, and the inevitable recurrence of the spasm within a year.
The effect of the stellate ganglion block on Bell's palsy; Thirty seven cases Bell's palsy were treated with the stellate ganglion block (SGB). All cases were retrospectively analyzed by sex, age and seasonal rate of occurence plus the effect of SGB on the disease. The following results were obtained. It was in winter that Bell's palsy occurred with the highest frequency followed by spring. Bell's palsy occurred more frequently in males than in females and this was most noticeable in those in their fifties. The cases in which the disease occurred in winter proved worse than those in spring. Within 10 days after the onset, those cases treated with SGB had a good prognosis. However, when this treatment was started later, the prognosis was bad. One case after 25 years had passed, showed a little improvement with the SGB. From these results it is suggested, first, that cold stimulation likely causes Bell's palsy and inhibits recovery from the disease. Second, it is thought that Bell's palsy improved remarkably with SGB when started early after the onset because the increase of the blood flow before the manifestation of irreversible degeneration of the facial nerve is essential. It is concluded that SGB must be started as early as possible after the onset.
Congenital malformations of the ear. Analysis of 94 operations; The 94 operations analyzed were performed on 80 ears in 73 patients with congenital malformation of the ear. Operative findings included 13 patients with a congenital absence of the oval window, 5 patients with vascular anomaly of the middle ear, and 16 patients with congenital cholesteatoma. Six of 13 patients with congenital absence of the oval window had a labyrinthotomy performed to create a new opening into the vestibule. The method of surgical repair in atresia was a canalplasty with fascia graft overlay for the substitute tympanic membrane. A Silastic button was placed over the substitute tympanic membrane to lessen blunting and to anchor the center-hole skin graft in place. Ramsay Hunt syndrome. A case report and a review of the literature; A case of Ramsay Hunt syndrome, though more often seen at the ENT clinic because of the patients' concern with symptoms in the ear, was seen and treated at the Dermatologic Clinic of Chosun University. A 29 year old male patient presented earache, pinhead to rice sized erythematous vesicular eruption on the external auditory canal, auricle and superior auricular area, and facial paralysis, all involving the right side of the face, duration of which were 7 days, 5 days and 1 day respectively. High doses of prednisolone alone made it possible to remit the otalgia, control the vesicular eruption and resolve the facial paralysis almost completely within 18 days in the order of their appearance, indicating that this is one of the more easily treated diseases for dermatologists. Alteration of blink reflexes in hemispheral lesions; Orbicularis oculi responses evoked by supraorbital and facial nerve stimulation were studied in 24 patients with unilateral hemispheral lesions. The direct facial motor response was only altered on the involved side and only in cases of central facial palsy. This influence was more expressed on the involved side. On the basis of changes in latency, duration, amplitude values and in habituation of late responses the effect of hemispheral lesions must be taken for depressing type either on R1 or R2 responses. These data suggest an exteroceptive character of both responses.

Analysis and results of twenty cases of transfacial anastomosis; A study of the 20 cases shows results which are, on the whole, disappointing, although we always obtained active movement of the eyelids. There can be no doubt that ancillary simple procedures (section of the mentalis, frontal myomectomy, tension of the musculo-aponeurotic system and skin elements, or reconstructive surgery of the eyelid) make a major contribution to the symmetry of the face and the protection of the cornea. In the light of these results, we have abandoned transfacial anastomoses in favour of hypoglossal facial nerve anastomosis associated with simple procedures to improve symmetry. Comparative analysis of the results of the two techniques will show which procedure provides the better rehabilitation.
Acoustic neurinoma with massive hemorrhage within the tumor tissue. A case report; In some kinds of benign intracranial tumors, as meningioma, choroid plexus papilloma, pituitary adenoma or hemangioma, it has been reported that subarachnoid hemorrhage or massive hemorrhage within the tumor tissue occurred in some cases. However, literatures on massive hemorrhage from acoustic neurinoma seemed to be rare. Recently we have experienced a case of acoustic neurinoma with massive hemorrhage within the tumor tissue. The patient was a 71-yr-old woman who had suffered from left hearing disturbance for several years and gradually progressive mental deficits and was hospitalized on November 14, 1978. She was diagnosed as having left acoustic neurinoma based on the findings of several examinations. In the period of preparation for the operation, she suddenly developed left facial palsy and left taste disturbance. She complained of mild headache, but consciousness was not disturbed. Non-contrast CT scan revealed an irregular high density region in the left cerebellopontine angle and a high density region by contrast enhancement, which was larger than that on the previous examination. At the surgical operation, 5 ml, liquefied hematoma and about 20 gm coagulated blood were observed in the rostral and medial portion of the tumor. Histological examination verified acoustic neurinoma of Antoni A type containing massive clot as well as hemosiderin-laden cells. The patient expired 8 days after the operation without restoration of consciousness. It was emphasized in the present report that one must take into consideration that a massive hemorrhage from the tumor itself is occasionally one of the causes of aggressive deterioration of clinical symptoms in patients with acoustic neurinoma.
Tuberculous otitis media: A series of 22 patients; A series of 22 cases of tuberculous otitis media is reviewed to assess the diagnostic features of the disease. Significant clinical features are the presence of abundant pale granulations, an unexpectedly severe hearing loss, facial paralysis, the presence of normal mastoid cellular development and a past or family history of tuberculosis of any site. The otoscopic appearances of the tympanic membrane, and the symptom of painless otorrhea are not considered suspicious features. Histological examination of operative material was the diagnostic procedure in 20/22 cases, thus underlining the difficulty of diagnosis in a non-tuberculous general population. Treatment with antituberculous chemotherapy and surgery gives good results and recent indications are that tympanoplastic surgery may be useful.

Granulomatous gingival manifestations of Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome; Of thirty patients with complete or incomplete forms of Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome (MRS), five patients with gingival lesions that microscopically showed the characteristic granulomatous changes are presented, with special reference to their gingival manifestations. In some cases bluish red, small, distinct, and irregular edematous swellings characterized the gingival changes, while in other cases more extensive and diffuse, edematous swellings dominated. All five patients had only vague symptoms from the gingiva. Because of the apparent slowly progressing nature of the gingival swellings and occasional spontaneous regression of the gingival changes, a conservative attitude in the treatment of gingival lesions in MRS is recommended. Orbicularis transposition: Concept of a functional correction of uni- or bilateral paralysis of the lower lip; A concept is described for the correction of the lower lip in cases of uni- or bilateral paralysis following injuries of the mandibular branch of the facial nerve, by transpositioning the affected orbicularis muscle to the innervated parts of the upper lip and the zygomatic muscle respectively. Facial nerve palsy: An unexpected complication following anesthesia by mask. A case report; An adult male patient suffered a partial palsy of the right mandibular branch of the facial nerve resulting from anesthesia under mask. A good airway is usually achieved by tight digital compression around the angle of the mandibulae. As in this case, if continuous bilateral digital pressure is applied on the angle of the jaw to provide a clear airway, the facial nerve is in danger of being pinched between the fingers and the ascending ramus of the mandibulae. To avoid this risk to the nerve, the angle of the mandibulae should be held correctly and the two areas, behind the ramus or above the inferior border of the mandibulae where the mandibular branch is distributed, should not be compressed.
Facial paralysis in children: A study of 99 cases; Ninety-nine cases of peripheral facial paralysis in children treated at Ste. Justine's Hospital over a 10 year period were reviewed. Sexes were nearly equally affected with a slightly higher incidence in female. Cases were distributed quite evenly throughout childhood except for a definitely higher incidence in the 0-2 year old group. Trauma, Bell's palsy, and otomastoid inflammation were found to be the most frequent causes of facial palsy in that group of cases. Cases of otomastoid inflammation did generally well on antibiotics and nearly 70 per cent so recovered completely. Twenty per cent only had to undergo simple mastoidectomy and two cases a decompression. Out of 25 cases of Bell's palsy, 18 recovered totally without surgery and four were decompressed with total or partial recovery. Following this study, the need for a more complete evaluation and somewhat more standardized treatment became obvious. This may permit in the future a more adequate knowledge of the problem and likely a better management.
Steroid therapy in Bell's palsy: Correlation between prognosis and varicella-Zoster virus (VZV) skin test; In treatment of Bell's palsy, 42 patients were treated with steroid hormone and 45 without steroid hormone. About 80% of the patients showed complete recovery; recovery rates were not comparable between groups. However, the palsy of patients undergoing steroid therapy returned to normal earlier than those without steroid therapy. The patients with positive VZV skin test showed better recovery than negative ones. It seems that VZV skin test becomes one of the parameters to show whether paralysis recovers well or not.

Lyme carditis: Cardiac abnormalities of Lyme disease; We studied 20 patients, mostly young adult men, with cardiac involvement of Lyme disease. The commonest abnormality (18 patients) was fluctuating degrees of atrioventricular block; eight of them developed complete heart block. Thirteen patients had evidence of more diffuse cardiac involvement: electrocardiographic changes compatible with acute myopericarditis (11 patients), radionuclide evidence of mild left ventricular dysfunction (five of 12 patients tested), or frank cardiomegaly (one patient). Heart involvement was usually preceded by erythema chronicum migrans and sometimes accompanied by meningoencephalitis, facial palsy, arthritis, elevated serum IgM levels or cryoglobulins containing IgM. The duration of cardiac involvement was usually brief (3 days to 6 weeks). The clinical picture in these patients has similarities to acute rheumatic fever; but in Lyme disease, complete heart block may be commoner, myopericardial involvement tends to be milder, and valves seem not to be affected.
Otic topical agents; Ototopical preparations are available for the treatment of obstruction, dermatitis, pain, and infection of the ear canal and the mastoid and tympanic structures. Most preparations contain alcohol and some type of mild acid, both of which provide nonspecific antiseptic activity against fungi and bacteria. For bacterial infections the combination of neomycin and polymyxin offers of best therapeutic spectrum against common pathogens. Ototoxicity from topical use in man is a theoretic possibility but not a practical problem. Chloramphenicol (otic) is an alternative in infections caused by bacteroides, but not by the more common P aeruginosa. When otic preparations are too painful for application through a tympanic perforation, an ophthalmic preparation may be more acceptable.

Diagnosis and treatment of neuroparalytic zoster keratitis; In severe zoster keratitis, many pathogenic factors are involved. In addition to viral manifestations, the cornea is often affected by anterior uveitis or secondary glaucoma. Neuroparalytic keratitis causes lowered blinking frequency and decreased tear secretion. In addition, zoster ulcerations of the uper lid margin mechanically disturb reformation of the tear film and weaken the lipid layer by necrosis of the Meibomian glands. Ointments reduce break-up time and parasympathicolytic mydriatics further decrease tear secretion. When the average time between two blinks is shorter than the tear film break-up time, a 'dry eye' condition usually develops. The appropriate treatment in such cases is thorough prevention of evaporation.
Brain stem encephalitis: Report of an autopsy; An autopsy case of a 25-yr-old female patient with gradually developing dyspnea and quadriplegia was presented. The patient had an operative treatment of otitis media at the age of 17 when she had a transient postoperative facial palsy. Since then, drowsiness tended to increase gradually. In and after the middle of May 1972, she began to complain of neck pruritus, numbness of a part distal to the bilateral upper extremities and general weakness. These symptoms became intensified gradually, with manifestations of headache, dysphagia and hypersalivation. Due to a fever (38-39°C), she was admitted to our hospital on July 1, 1972. On admission she had bilateral myosis, hyperreflexia of lower extremities and hyporeflexia of upper extremities. Babinski's signs, Chaddock's signs and Mayer's signs indicated abnormalities bilaterally. The general conditions deteriorated gradually following her hospitalization. She became comatous on July 8 and died on the night of July 10. The autopsy revealed bronchopneumonia, gastric ulcer and cystitis. There were mild cerebral swelling an both tonsillar and uncal herniation. Demyelination, gliosis, perivascular cuff, microthrombi and necroses in the lateral side of the medulla, in the basis of the 4th ventricle and around the cerebral aqueduct were found microscopically. Nerve cells were normal. According to available literature, there are two types of brain stem encephalitis; a type without strong changes in nerve cells and axons as in the present case and the other type with these changes like the case reported by Mukaiyama et al. We discussed about these and the etiology.
A case of penetrating cerebellar injury; Reports of cerebellar injuries are less often noted than those of cerebral injuries, because the cerebellum anatomically holds a specific position and many patients with cerebellar injuries die due to direct brain stem injuries or hemorrhage into the posterior fossa. However, if patients do recover from the acute stage in cerebellar injuries, their prognosis is extremely good. A 13-year-old boy fell into a grave and an iron bar pierced his neck. He was admitted to our department for evaluation of disturbance of consciousness. At that time he was delirious and he had right facial palsy, a skew deviation and curious spontaneous ocular movement, but no paresis of extremities. A plain skull roentgenogram showed a fracture of the occipital bone and the intracranial bony fragment. We suspected that the iron bar had penetrated into the posterior fossa, but no surgical treatment was done because CT scan showed only a small hematoma of the right cerebellar hemisphere and deep seated bony fragments. He recovered day by day with conservative therapy and he was discharged with right facial palsy, right auditory disturbance and loss of right gag reflex. These symptoms would be induced by direct injury of cranial nerves. After six months he complained of little interference with his daily life and some neurological deficits. Skew deviation found in cerebellar injuries was first reported by Gordon Holmes. Thereafter there have been many reports about this matter. The relationship between skew deviations and the brain stem or cerebellum has been reported by many authors. It is generally accepted that a skew deviation is associated with brain stem lesions but accurate etiology of skew deviation is unknown. We think that the skew deviation is more likely to be induced by complicated brain stem lesions than by one brain stem lesion.

Bell's palsy - a new concept of treatment; A report is given in preliminary results of an infusion therapy which, in contrast to presently used conservative forms of treatment, is based on both an antiphlogistic and a rheological effect of high doses of cortisone in combination with dextrane plus pentoxifylline. Facial paralysis: 100 years of treatment; In the treatment of patients with unilateral facial paralysis, symmetry of movements is generally the highest aim. Re-innervation of the paralyzed muscles should first be considered. Electromyographically demonstrable denervation potentials indicate that the muscles are still viable. Re-innervation can be obtained by restoring the continuity of the facial nerve, e.g. by end-to-end anastomosis or by insertion of a free nerve graft. In cases where the proximal stump of an interrupted facial nerve is not accessible, free nerve grafts can be used to bring nerve impulses from branches of the normal, contralateral facial nerve across the midline of the face to nerve branches on the paralyzed side. In cases where the facial muscles have degenerated or are congenitally absent, a muscular 'motor' should be brought to the paralyzed side. This can be done with free muscle grafts or with transposed local muscles, usually the muscles of mastication. In order to give these muscles spontaneous dynamic action, cross-face grafts can again be used to innervate them. When patients do not choose or need to undergo these rather extensive operations, or when they are in poor general health, we resort to methods of static correction. Many of these can comfortably be performed under local anaesthesia. Because of the absence of movement and other drawbacks, these methods should, in our opinion, generally be considered last.

Bell's palsy, a discussion of treatment; Treatment of Bell's palsy by intensive galvanic stimulation and by decompression in the second or third week after onset, has not been proved to lead to better recovery. Whether earlier surgical intervention would produced better results remains to be seen and depends on the possibility of making a fool-proof and very early prognosis, which in our opinion is not yet possible. Prednisone is now as popular as electrotherapy was a generation ago, but on equally slender grounds.

Mechanisms of synkinesis; When the facial nerve is injured, changes occur in muscle, proximal nerve, distal nerve, and the cell body in the nucleus. All of these changes contribute to the quality of regeneration and repair. This paper describes the usual processes of neuronal regeneration with the objective of a better understanding of why some injuries inevitably result in poor return of motion and synkinesis, while others recover completely. The possible mechanisms of synkinesis include: imperfect regeneration due to axonal misdirection, demyelination, microglial scarring in the facial nucleus, neuron depopulation, multiple axon sprouting, and misdirection of regenerating axons via vertical anastomotic filaments.

Transmastoid decompression of the facial nerve in Bell's palsy; We describe the technique of decompression of the facial nerve from the geniculate ganglion to the stylomastoid foramen. The decompression was made on 51 patients with Bell's palsy, and the results of follow-up study were compared with those of 77 patients in whom the pyramidal and vertical segments were decompressed. The decompressions were indicated when a severe denervation of the nerve was confirmed by electrodiagnostic examinations. Incidences of notable residual palsy and of pronounced sequelae were always lower in the former group of patients regardless of the operational timing. Notes on some complications in stapedial operations; A number of complications occurring during and after stapedial operations for otosclerosis are dealt with. More particularly, a patient with bilateral dehiscence of the facial nerve canal is studied, where following blood aspiration, paresis of the facial nerve situated just beneath the mucosa developed. The other patients discussed include: a second case with canal dehiscence, a case with acute otitis and n. facialis paresis, and a case with acute otitis and labyrinthitis in whom the sense of hearing failed to recover. It is strongly recommended to carry out the operative intervention under conditions of exceptional acepsis. Also, it is mandatory to perform a careful prophylactical examination of the upper airways before the operation.
Facial paralysis: Differential diagnosis and indications for surgical therapy; The management of patients with facial paralysis is based upon the experience of the author in managing over 700 patients with facial paralysis over a period of 15 years. As our understanding of viral immune disorders becomes clearer, the clinical recommendations may require reevaluation and change.
Restoration of selective facial nerve function by the nerve-muscle pedicle technique; The nerve-muscle pedicle technique for selective reinnervation of paralyzed facial muscles, when combined with a modified muscle-fascia sling and neurotization from the temporal muscle, has been applied in 26 patients to date. The success rate has been 88% for restoration of tonus and 77% for restoration of voluntary motion as well. This procedure offers several significant advantages over other accepted means of reinnervation in patients in whom the seventh nerve itself is not available as a source for restoration of function. It also may have value as a method for rapid restoration of tonus while other means of reinnervation take effect.
Free muscle grafting; The histochemical, histologic, electromyographic and electron microscopic findings in the experimental studies strongly suggest that whole muscle bellies transplanted two to three weeks after denervation will survive and become reinnervated.1-2. The importance of denervation before grafting has been proposed by other authors and more experimental work is needed to make the role of denervation clear. In clinical studies two modifications of the technique of transplantation to the eyelids have improved the results and will appear later in the series. The change of lining of the nasal tunnel from silicone sheet to vein graft eliminated infections of the nasal tunnel with concomitant necrosis of the tendons of he transplant. The transplant of two muscle bellies, one to the upper and one to the lower eyelid, proved to be unnecessary and the elimination of the muscle belly in the normal upper eyelid removed the risk of constriction of the normal rima. The results of the operations to improve eyelid function are satisfactory. In the unsuccessful procedures the failure more often was a result of tenodesis on both sides of the nasal tunnel than a poor take of the muscle graft. In the patients in whom transplant was made to the lips the static support of the mouth was as good as the conventional fascia lata transplant and, in addition, the muscle grafts gave some mobility to the paralyzed half of the lips even if the graft contractions at the paralyzed side, as a rule, were weaker than on the normal side. In the patients, in whom grafts were attached to partially paralyzed muscles the results depended upon whether the recipient muscle had a sufficient number of functioning motor units to support the reinnervation of the graft. It appears that at least 10 to 15 percent of the motor function of the paralyzed recipient muscle must remain to secure adequate reinnervation of the graft.
Nerve suture and grafting to restore the extratemporal facial nerve; A concept for dealing with extratemporal lesions of the facial nerve is based on cadaver studies performed by Meissl. In spite of plexiform arrangement and fiber exchange, areas and fascicle groups can be differentiated within the cross section of the facial nerve which contain a great percentage of the fibers supplying a certain muscle group. An attempt should be made to unite the corresponding parts by direct coaptation, or, if nerve defect exists, by nerve grafts.
Facial nerve grafting: A thirty year retrospective review; It is axiomatic that nerve grafting be considered as an integral part of every ablative or traumatic injury involving the extratemporal main trunk and branches of the facial nerve. The experience with 170 autogenous grafts has established the efficacy of the technique and has proved the high regenerative and adaptive capacities of the facial nerve system.
Microneurovascular free muscle transplantation for reanimation of facial paralysis; The transferred muscle undergoes some degenerative atrophy and its bulk is reduced during the period of reinnervation. In the patients, the acquired contraction of the transferred muscle was weaker than its original excursion. As the rabbit experiments of Terzis et al. have demonstrated, the orthotopical or heterotopical transfer of skeletal muscles diminished their powers of contraction. The acquired contraction therefore is less than that which existed originally. Use of the larger muscles, such as the gracilis and latissimus dorsi muscles (not always transferred in their entirety), obtains better results than that of such smaller muscles as the extensor digitorum brevis muscle. When the transplant is too bulky, the excess portion can later be excised. For reconstruction of the facial expression, better results were obtained with muscles innervated through the seventh nerve either ipsilaterally or contralaterally. In long-standing Bell's palsy, a combination method with cross-facial nerve grafting is now recommended.
Current surgical treatment of intratemporal facial palsy; A lesion of the facial nerve producing facial palsy most commonly occurs in its intratemporal course. Recent progress in microsurgery of the temporal bone has permitted a safe approach to the facial nerve from the internal auditory meatus to the stylomastoid foramen. Today nearly all intratemporal facial nerve lesions are accessible to surgical repair. The knowledge of this possibility is of utmost importance to plastic surgeons involved with the diagnosis and treatment of facial paralysis, because the restoration of continuity of the facial nerve is preferred to any type of substitution operation whenever possible. In order to frequency the most common causes of intratemporal facial palsy are idiopathic or Bell's palsy (39.7 percent), trauma (24.7 percent), tumors (12.5 percent), herpes zoster oticus (6.8 percent), and acute and chronic otitis media (5.5 percent). Electrodiagnosis should be used whenever the slightest doubt in the clinical evaluation of facial movements exists, in order to confirm or exclude total paralysis, and in every patient with complete paralysis in order to assess the underlying condition of the fibers of the motor nerve.
The evaluation and management of the eye in facial palsy; Orbicularis oculi palsy resulting from facial paralysis is often associated with ocular problems, the severity of which is usually related to the degree and duration of the paralysis. This discussion is directed at the evaluation of the patient with orbicularis oculi palsy with specific emphasis on recognition and management of the ocular abnormalities.
New aspects in facial nerve surgery; Practicing logical postoperative treatment requires knowledge about the processes involved in nerve regeneration, which are briefly dealt with. However, it is the opinion of the authors that greater attention should be given to the reaction of the denervated musculature. For effective electrotherapy, recent findings from animal experiments on changes at the membrane of the muscle fiber seem to be of paramount importance, at least from a theoretical point of view. Practical consequences result from these findings, but the physiological behavior of the mimetic muscles is different from that of the skeletal muscles, and the usefulness of electrotherapy on facial musculature is still controversial.
I. Hypoglossal facial anastomosis: Its significance for modern facial surgery. II. Combined approach in extratemporal facial nerve reconstruction; The difficulties encountered in extratemporal facial nerve reconstruction after extensive trauma or following resection of parotid tumors often lead to unsatisfactory functional and cosmetic results. So far it has been common practice to use as a 'regenerative nerve', the original facial nerve. Using this procedure, however, frequently only a portion of the peripheral branches can be reanastomosed. Above all, the 'autoparalytic syndrome' develops in this situation owing to undirected outgrowth of axons, and an aberration of the blinking-reflex motoneurons occurs. Experience has shown that the isolated use of a cross-face transplant is not suitable for satisfactory functional regeneration. Depending on the individual anatomic situation, a number of possibilities are therefore recommended for a combined approach using several 'regenerative nerves'. In this connection, the particular physiologic properties of these nerves have to be taken into account which can help to improve considerably the functional and cosmetic results.
Clinical experiences and results of treatment of facial paralysis by Thompson's method; Before Thompson's treatment of facial paralysis corrective surgery of these lesions had followed indirect and not direct methods. The re-acquisition of the contracting capacity of a denervated muscle, once put in contact with a normal muscle, has marked a decisive and effective turn in paralysis. The uniting of Thompson's method with nervous by-pass from the normal side to the paralyzed side by neuro-surgical method according to Anderl, is opening up continously growing possibilities of recovery for paralyzed facial muscles. Of course, this method is not possible without an adequate staff with micro-surgical experience. The authors present their patients' case histories treated with Thompson's method.
Neurologic abnormalities of Lyme disease; We studied 18 patients with erythema chronicum migrans (ECM), Lyme arthritis, or both who developed neurologic abnormalities. Six of the 14 patients (43%) with ECM remembered having been bitten by a tick at the site of the lesion 3 to 20 days before its onset. Neurologic abnormalities, which appeared either while ECM was still present or one to six weeks after it had faded, included aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, chorea, cerebellar ataxia, cranial neuritis (including bilateral facial palsy), motor and sensory radiculoneuritis, mononeuritis multiplex, and myelitis, in various combinations, but encephalitis and facial palsy each also occurred alone. The usual pattern was fluctuating meningoencephalitis (nine patients) with superimposed cranial and peripheral radiculoneuropathy. At the beginning of the illness, associated symptoms included migratory arthralgias, chills and fever, malaise and fatigue, backache, and myalgias; signs included low-grade fever, malar rash, and lymphadenopathy. Frank arthritis was usually a later finding, beginning 1 to 9 months after the onset of the illness. During attacks, 15 of the 18 patients (83%) had cryoglogulins present in serum, which consisted of quantitatively greater amounts of IgM than IgG, and decreased or disappeared during remission. These findings support the hypothesis that circulating immune complexes may play a pathogenetic role in Lyme disease. Ten patients recovered neurologically within 2 weeks to 8 months, but 8 others continued to have residual weakness or cerebral symptoms. Systemic corticosteroids appeared to suppress meningeal symptoms rapidly, but did not seem to affect established parenchymal lesions. Two additional patients, who could only be classified as having possible Lyme disease, are noteworthy because hemiparesis was part of their clinical picture. Erythema chronicum migrans is the diagnostic marker for the illness. Without it, a course of recurrent meningoencephalitis during at least a period of several months with superimposed cranial neuritis or radiculoneuritis, particularly if accompanied by cryoglobulins or followed by arthritis, is quite suggestive of Lyme disease. When the diagnosis cannot be made on clinical grounds alone, a history of preceding tick bite, onset in the summer months, or geographic clustering with those who have erythema chronicum migrans, Lyme arthritis, or both, may be important clues.
Peripheral facial nerve paralysis; The use of polytomography, electroneurography, and level diagnosis have radically changed the approach to peripheral facial paralysis, and have resulted in a more precise etiology and diagnosis, evolution of the functional state of the nerve at an early stage of the paralysis, more reliable prognosis, and more selective therapeutic indications. Progress in microsurgical techniques in neuro-otology has created the possibility to propose appropriate therapy for all parts of the facial nervous system.
Regional muscle transposition for rehabilitation of the paralyzed face; Masseter and temporalis muscle transpositions may be considered in cases of long-standing facial paralysis and in the congenital absence of the facial nerve or muscles. The basic advantage of this technique is the introduction of a large volume of living and dynamic muscle into the face. Additional advantages include simplicity, the support provided, enhancement of the possibility of myoneurotization, and no loss of other significant function. In many instances, facial movement improves for a period of approximately two years, and the long-range effect would suggest some degree of rehabilitation of the facial muscles. The combined experience with over 100 muscle transpositions indicates the efficacy and success of this technique in selected patients.
Facial rehabilitation: New potentials; There is some clinical evidence to support the theory that in the immediate rehabilitation of the paralyzed face some regionalization and separate movement of the eye, lips, and cheek may be produced. This is not accomplished by specific fascicular connections. It is postulated that a combination of intracranial and extracranial connections, which have not been identified to date, contribute to this phenomenon.
Cross-face nerve transplant; The two stage principle is one of the most important features of the procedure. It allows starting the operation at a very early stage (one to six months). The donor area in the periphery is very well supplied, therefore as many facial fascicles as necessary can be sacrificed on the healthy side. The authors have never noticed any functional disturbances. The nerves leading to the buccinator muscle and those which innervate the lateral pull of the mouth are especially suitable. This weakening of the strong pull of the mouth is of great value for symmetry but unfortunately relapse to the original state is common. The selection of the nerve fascicles on the healthy side must be executed in a deep layer below the muscles because all large branches are located here. The end of the sural grafts should be positioned far back on the paralyzed side to enable easy anastomoses at the second stage. A face lift incision on the paralyzed side and tightening of the skin are of additional value and provide some support to the elongated muscles. The combination of cross-face nerve transplant with other substitutional methods in which muscles are used for reinnervation is very promising. In the author's experience physiotherapy is a very important measure. It should be started after the onset of the palsy and continued until restoration of the face is complete. It is usually applied three times a week with exponential current and at a strength of 20 to 60 milliamperes. Each group of muscles receives a 2 to 3 minutes dosage. It is helpful if the patient can use a stimulation apparatus at home daily for short treatments.
Otoneurosurgery in diseases of the temporal bone pyramid and of the cerebellopontile angle; Surgical treatment was conducted in 25 patients with glomus tumours of the pyramid (5), cystic arachnoiditis of the cerebellopontile angle (5), neurinoma of the auditory nerve (4), paralysis of the facial nerve in fracture of the pyramid (4), choleastoma of the cereballopontile angle (1), gun shot wound of the pyramid (1), and purulent labyrinthitis (1). The pathological focus was approached transpyramidally (13), suprapyramidally (4), and by the combined method (4). In the choice of the method, approach localization and dissemination of the process, as well as the state of the auditory function and condition of the facial nerve were taken into consideration. No lethal outcome followed these operations.
