Gunshot injury to the temporal bone: An analysis of thirty-five cases; By retrospective analysis of 35 surviving gunshot injuries to the temporal bone and by presentation of 6 representative cases, the management and reconstructive procedures of these injuries in the Tulane University affiliated hospitals are presented. The most frequent single injury was facial nerve paralysis (16 cases). followed by external canal injury and conductive hearing loss. Anacusis occurred in 12 cases. In conductive hearing loss the intact posterior wall tympanoplasty with mastoidectomy (16 cases), or the modified radical mastoidectomy (5 cases), allowed middle ear reconstruction. Transmastoid facial canal decompression, combined with the above procedures or with a middle fossa craniotomy, was performed in 6 cases. Delayed facial reconstruction (5 cases) utilized microneural anastomosis between facial-facial and hypoglossal-facial nerves and fascia lata slings. Intracranial complications of thrombosis of internal carotid artery, dural venous lacerations, temporal lobe aphasia, bitemporal hemianopsia, cerebral abscesses and meningitis are also discussed.
Steroid versus placebo treatments in cases of acute peripheral facial paralysis; 30 case of Bell's palsy were included in the study. During 13 days of drug treatment, in 10 cases low doses and gradually decreasing amount while in 10 cases alternate day high doses of steroid (dexamethasone) and in 10 cases placebo only were given. Severity of facial paralysis before treatment and degree of improvement in 7 th and 21 st days after treatment were measured in terms of muscular power of frontal, ocular and buccinator muscles. The aim of the study was to compare the results of steroid and placebo treatments in cases of Bell's palsy. This study demonstrated that there was no difference between steroid and placebo in the treatment of Bell's palsy. 25 out of 30 cases of acute facial paralysis exhibited improvement in 2-5 weeks regardless of the drug given. In 5 cases who showed slow recovery, there was hyperacusia, disturbance of taste and dryness of the mouth. Pregnancy and hypertension seemed contributory factors responsible for delayed recovery.
The treatment of Bell's palsy with electric acupuncture; During the period from March 1974 through August 1978 we treated 21 cases of Bell's palsy by electric acupuncture. Diagnosis was based on neurological examination. The method of treatment is described in detail. Acupuncture points used were located on the afflicted side. Good results were seen in 14 cases (66.67%), 5 cases showed considerable improvement (23.80%), and 2 cases were considered as failure (9.53%). Electric acupuncture is recommended as the method of first choice for the successful treatment of Bell's palsy.
First musculotendinous grafts, with motorizing function, in paralyzed areas; In 1973, the author performed, for the first time in Uruguay, a complete transplant of skeletal musculotendinous units, as autografts. Since that time 6 patients have been operated, which totals 8 muscular transplants implanted as grafts; their contractile functional capacity has remained intact. Thus it has been possible to motorize orbicular areas, palpebral and labial, paralyzed on the opposite side, once they are reinnervated by neurotization from the healthy muscular bed. In this paper the different cases are analyzed; pre and post-operatory clinical and electrodiagnostic evaluation is made; the technique used, described by Noel Thompson in 1971, is set down in detail, with suggestions which render it simpler and improve it by making possible the nervous suture of graft to nerves in the receiving bed.
Identical twins with papilloedema and cranial nerve palsies; Central nervous system involvement has not been reported previously as a manifestation of sarcoidosis in monozygotic twins. Twin sisters developed multiple cranial nerve palsies and papilloedema within a two month period. Clinical features and the course of their diseases were remarkably similar.
Prednisone treatment of Bell's palsy; A report is presented of personal experience with prednisone treatment of 76 patients with severe acute idiopathic facial paralysis (Bell's palsy). The indication for treatment is total or subtotal loss of the motor function, determined by clinical examination. The author advocates treatment of selected patients at an early stage, at the last 5 to 7 days after the diagnosis.
Chronic granulomatous disease. A case report; A case of chronic granulomatous disease is reported. A 1.8 year old boy had suffered from recurrent infections such as cervical lymphadenitis, eczematous dermatitis and perianal abscess in his newborn period. Later he developed left facial palsy, otitis media and intermittent fever. Otoscopic examination revealed a granulomatous mass in the left external auditory meatus, and x-ray showed a diffuse shadow in the left mastoid. Simple mastoidectomy was performed on May 26, 1978. Under intensive postoperative care, the patient has been free from fever and local infection.
Panel discussion: Bell's palsy; The clinical and electrophysiological criterias for medical or surgical treatment of Bell's palsy are: clinical severity (complete, not complete) estimated by muscular testing; psychosocial aspect of the patient; electrophysiological tests. Electroneuronography looks the most used test (<95% of degeneration during the two first weeks good prognosis, ≥ 95% bad prognosis in half the cases); - integrated electromyography can separate these last bad cases (> 20 μV good prognosis, and < 20 μV bad prognosis): 14th day after onset looks the important date for this test. Prednisone or A.C.T.H. therapy avoids 95% of degeneration and surgical treatment looks indicated when the number of the degenerated fibers reaches 90%. The approach is discussed with no consenus: the 2nd and 3rd portions are more often decompressed. Total decompression is advocated by Pulec when eye is dry; he also notes its interest for finding little tumors not diagnosed. (10% of cases of author's decompressions). U. Fisch begins decompression in the last portion and decompresses the nerve until he finds the point where it comes back excitable. The extent of decompression and the approach are determinated by localisation tests (Schirmer-Blatt).
Traumatic facial palsy; On the basis of 67 cases, criteria for surgical treatment of traumatic facial palsy are given. As regards the chronology, of the 37 immediate cases, 26 were operated; of the 30 secondary cases 12 received surgical treatment. The clinical examination must look for fracture in the external auditory meatus. With audiometry and vestibulometry middle ear deafness indicated the 2nd portion while total hearing loss allows a translabyrinth approach. Topographic tests (Blatt, Schirmer) give doubtful results as the petrous nerve or chorda alone can be injured. EMG and electroneurography should be carried out. Among the roentgenographic approaches Schuller, frontal and sagittal tomographic techniques are utilised, although sometimes this diagnosis is quite difficult in practice; if the topographic results remain uncertain a total decompression may be considered. The delay and quality of recovery depend on the type of nervous lesion involved (in 48 operated cases). In 6 nerve section cases recovery took 4 to 7 months. In 21 cases with commotion, 13 recovered for more than 50%. Recovery in contusion and compression cases shows a less favourable prognosis (20 cases observed). The post operative audiologic evaluation showed 2 partial labyrinthisations and 1 middle ear deafness (pocket retraction).
Sclerosteosis in South Africa; Sclerosteosis is a potentially lethal inherited disorder of skeletal overgrowth which has a minimum prevalence of 1 in 60,000 in the Afrikaner community of South Africa. Early presenting features are syndactyly and facial palsy, and the diagnosis should be considered in any infant of Afrikaner stock with these abnormalities. No medical treatment is available, but cosmetic surgery, cranial nerve decompression and prophylactic craniectomy may be of value.
Pseudo-paralysis of the mandibular branch of the facial nerve after platysmal face-lift operation; With the increasing popularity of platysmal face lifts, the anatomy of the cervical branch of the facial nerve should be noted. The postoperative appearance of lack of ability to retrude the corner of the mouth, in someone who had a 'full denture' smile preoperatively, could possibly be due to severance or stretching of the rami of the cervical branch of the facial nerve, rather than an injury of the facial nerve of the marginal mandibular branch.
Three cases of tuberculous otitis media; Three cases of tuberculous otitis media are reported. In two adult cases, vertigo, facial palsy and severe hearing impairment appeared three months after the onset. The latter two symptoms persisted in spite of the surgical and medical treatment. In a child case, an early diagnosis prevented the patient from any sequelae. Necrotic changes of the ear drum, external auditory canal or tympanic cavity were characteristic in all these cases. It seems important, in case of necrotic otitis media, to take tuberculosis into consideration.
Guillain-Barre syndrome in Singapore. The pattern of Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute polyradiculopathy) in Singapore. A critical analysis of 46 cases; 46 cases of Guillain-Barre syndrome or acute polyradiculopathy are analysed. The disease affected all age groups and both sexes equally. A relatively higher incidence among Malays and absence among Indians was observed. One third of patients had preceding upper respiratory tract infection. Relapse rate was at least 5% in the short period of follow-up. Most patients developed maximal signs and symptoms within two weeks but some ran a subacute course for two months. The distribution of muscle weakness was noted in detail. Almost all patients had weakness of the lower limb; one-third had facial palsy and one quarter had respiratory muscle weakness or bulbar paresis. Severe sensory loss was virtually absent. Areflexia was a cardinal sign. Presence of bilateral radicular pain as elicited by a positive Laseque's sign was found to be an important bedside diagnostic clue, being present in 95% of cases tested. Two district clinical variants were observed - the Miller-Fisher Syndrome and an ataxic (pseudo-tabetic) form that ran a protracted course. 60% had raised CSF protein. Nerve conduction studies were of diagnostic rather than prognostic value in doubtful cases. Mortality rate was below 3% although 5 patients required assisted ventilation. Follow-up revealed that full recovery was the rule within 6 months with or without steroids, and that with prolonged weakness or ataxia they continued to recover even as long as after two years.
Neuromyopathic ptosis. A new surgical approach; Neuromyopathic ptosis is a progressive disorder frequently associated with other ocular abnormalities. These include dry eyes, absent Bell's phenomenon, protractor weakness, and heterotropia. Thus, correction of this ptosis has not been well described and is avoided by many surgeons. Since ptosis usually occurs early in life, correction is of functional, economic, and cosmetic importance. Clinical and histologic findings suggest that degeneration and defects of the levator aponeurosis contribute to the ptosis. During the past two years, we have used the aponeurotic approach to correct neuromyopathic ptosis. We describe 19 eyelids with a minimum one-year follow-up. Most eyelids were purposely under-corrected. A mean lid elevation of 3.3 mm with good symmetric results was obtained. Procedures were performed under local anesthesia. Advantages of this technique are (1) patient cooperation for adjustment of lid height and contour at surgery; (2) preservation of other suspensory structures (Muller's muscle and Whitnall's ligament); (3) easy adjustment of lid height postoperatively; (4) preservation of all tear-producing structures; (5) avoidance of corneal irritation from posterior sutures; and (6) maintenance of anatomic planes, which simplifies reoperation, if necessary. We believe this conservative approach corrects most eyelids with neuromyopathic ptosis.
Advances in plastic and reconstructive surgery in E.N.T.; Current surgical methods and tendencies are reviewed from an oto-laryngological viewpoint. In lope ears the combined method has stood the test very well. Reconstruction in anotia is not always satisfactory; the combination with deformities of the external auditory canal, of the middle and the inner ear, as well as of the facial cranium must be taken into account. The replacement of parts of the pinna is a minor problem. Reference is made to the possibility of reimplantation of separated parts. Current operations for deformities of the nose are mentioned. The use of conserved cartilage is described. In frontal defects paladon has proved a very successful inlay. Partial defects can be closed by pedicled island flaps. Stenosis of the larynx is no longer treated by bolt inlays of long duration; the implantation of septal cartilage including its mucoperichondrium leads much quicker to a permanent and adequate lumen. Smaller tracheal stenoses can be treated by circumscribed local management. Larger stenoses need either extensive plastic operations with large flaps or transversal resection. After total laryngectomy a specially formed canal between the upper and of the trachea and the hypopharynx allows a new voice to be developed. The transplantation of denervated muscles in facial palsy, special operations in paralysis of deglutition and some general problems are mentioned briefly. A voluminous list of recent literature gives the opportunity of studying further details.
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and related diseases; Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, progressive bulbar paralysis and spinal progressive muscular atrophy should be regarded as one nosological unit. They are the most frequent manifestation types of degenerative diseases of the pyramidal motor system leading to gradually progressive atrophic and/or spastic paralyses. The cause is not known; occasional familial occurrence suggests genetic determination. The diagnosis has to be made on clinical grounds. No treatment is known. The prognosis is unfavorable; a few special hereditary types run a relatively benign course.
Herpes zoster oticus. Uncommon but recognizable cause of facial paralysis; Herpes zoster oticus, an uncommon but recognizable cause of facial paralysis, can be identified from the characteristic auricular vesicles. Manifestations can include otic vesicles, facial paralysis, decreased hearing, dizziness, and severe ear and facial pain. Topographic and nerve excitability studies help determine extent of involvement and probable prognosis. Although therapy remains controversial, outcome in a few cases has suggested that systemic steroid therapy is beneficial.
Immediate improvement in facial paralysis after surgical decompression; 17 cases of severe facial paralysis were studied before and after microsurgical decompression, by quantitative electromyography (electromyogram integrated in volts) at the site of the zygomatic arch. In 76% of cases, no significant improvement was measured. Immediate improvement occurred infrequently (12%), was short-lived and did not have any influence on the final result.
Auricular tuberculosis with regressive facial palsy after surgical intervention; The authors have observed the complete regression of a facial palsy in a tuberculous otitis by precocious decompression of the nerve and anti-tuberculous medical treatment.
Hypoglossal-facial nerve anastomosis for reinnervation of the paralyzed face; The hypoglossal-facial nerve crossover is a valuable surgical procedure for the treatment of certain types of facial paralysis. It is most effective when used as an integral part of a primary ablative operation for the treatment of cancer in this region. In the treatment of long-standing facial paralysis, its application requires an intact peripheral facial nerve system and some functioning mimetic muscles with an obliterated proximal facial nerve segment. It is recognized that other procedures are available for repair in patients who meet essentially these same criteria. The disadvantages are minimal intraoral crippling, mass movements of the face and, in some instances, hypertonia of the face. The advantages are improved facial tone, protection of the eye, intentional facial movements controlled by the tongue, and movements associated with physiologial functions of the tongue.
Electrodiagnostic methods for determination of prognosis and therapeutic criteria in facial nerve paralysis; The function of the facial nerve can be examined by four electrodiagnostic methods. In the nerve excitability test and electroneurography with determination of the distal latency, the facial nerve is stimulated over the stylomastoid foramen. Chronaximetry and electromyography are performed in the muscles. Whereas chronaximetry renders an impression of the severity of neural lesion, electromyography can also determine the onset of reinnervation activity. Early prognosis within 6 days of onset can be determined only by nerve excitability test and electroneurography, preferred by us, which assesses the muscle potential. If the potential amplitude decreases more than 35% within two days and the muscle potential disappears between the fourth and sixth day, total degeneration of the nerve with poor prognosis is indicated. Such data can be gathered by at least two electrodiagnostic investigations preferably on the third day after onset and one to three days later. The cosmetic disfigurement through peripheral facial nerve palsy poses immediately the question of prognosis and of the therapeutic possibilities. Usually, this question can be answered by clinical examination alone. As soon as paralysis of facial muscles exists, prognostical statements can be made by electrodiagnostical methods alone. Because of the possibility of operative treatment, it is necessary to assess the unfavorable courses early.
A spectacle device to treat facial nerve paralysis; We describe a new method to prevent ocular complications in facial nerve palsy. A device mounted on a spectacle frame senses the blink of the normal eye and closes the lids of the paretic eye by levers which rest on the upper and lower lids. It provides a physiologic replacement of function and prevents corneal exposure.
Rare care of Ramsay Hunt syndrome associated with herpes zoster of the glossopharyngeal nerve; The authors describe a rare coexistence of Ramsay Hunt syndrome with glossopharyngeal zoster in a 67-year-old patient. A trial of systematization of the nomenclature of Ramsay Hunt syndrome is suggested, on the basis of certain anatomophysiological data. It is concluded that in zoster involvement of the sensory elements in the geniculate ganglion and in otic ganglion should be accompanied by taste sensitivity disturbances, but often the patients fail to notice these disturbances and routine taste testing shows also no such tase impairment. Routine use of electrogustometry is postulated since this makes possible diagnostic-prognostic assessment followed by selection of appropriate treatment.
On the repair of the injured facial nerve; Seven cases of traumatic peripheral facial palsy are presented. Three patients were treated with a technique of anastomosis between the two facial nerves as devised by the author.
Minimal decompression of facial nerve in its paralysis; A partial decompression of the facial nerve consists in fenestration of its tympanal part (area from projection of incus long process to pyramidal process) with epineural membrane dissection. The patients were operated on 45-70 days from the beginning of disease (after the failure of conservative therapy) in the presence of deep paralysis without amelioration. A parallelism between facial nerve and chorda tympani states was marked: in hyperemia and edema of the latter the analogous changes are seen in the facial nerve. In all patients who had undergone surgery the positive results were obtained. The authors consider that surgery should be performed early.
Surgical treatment of early facial palsies in cases of longitudinal fractures of the temporal bone; Longitudinal fractures of the temporal bone are complicated by facial palsies in 10-25%. According according to the results of Fisch the lesions of the facial nerve are situated at the labyrinthine segment of the nerve. The most frequent lesion is the impression of bone fragments in the Fallopian canal. Clinical controls of the progredience of the palsy and tomographies are necessary. The only successful therapy in cases of early facial palsies due to longitidunal temporal bone fractures is the total decompression of the facial nerve with the combinated transmastoid approach and middle fossa approach.
Review of long-term results in supportive treatment of facial paralysis; The author has reviewed approximately 150 patients who were treated with supportive measures for facial paralysis. He found that in the patient's view an adequate result requires establishment of a proper lip sphincter - either by restoring muscular tone, or by creating an anatomical framework to which can be added either a motor unit or stabilization to aid the opposite intact muscle. He also found lasting value from dampening contralateral spasticity, and from the use of such ancillary procedures as the face lift, the brow lift and the creation of a nasolabial fold. It is important for the physician to help the patient acquire a tranquil face during speech and emotion by persevering in mirror training and mimetic gymnastics.
Facial nerve palsy in acute leukaemia; During a three year period, of 62 children and adults seen with lymphoblastic leukaemia 6 developed unilateral facial paralysis during the course of their disease, compared to none of 54 adults and children with acute non-lymphatic leukaemia seen during the same period. In all cases the problem arose in patients with refractory disease and was associated with the development of resistant bone marrow infiltration. The neuropathy showed no obvious response to intrathecal therapy and whilst meningeal infiltration was present at some stage in all but one of the 6, this waxed and waned independently of the facial palsy. Four of the 6 cases described had stigmata of the T-cell variety of lymphoblastic leukaemia, which is a significantly higher proportion than would be expected by chance. This apparent association with T-cell disease has not been previously recognised.
Trigeminal neurotization of paralyzed facial musculature. Modification of the Lexer-Rosenthal surgical procedure; The authors introduce a modification of the Lexer-Rosenthal surgical technique for reinnervation of the facial muscles by trigeminal neurotization in patients with facial paralysis. Four patients with such paralysis were seen in the Cranial Nerve Research Clinic, Oakland, Calif. Three of the four patients had their paralysis surgically treated, and recovery of facial motion was compared with that in one patient, in whom spontaneous trigeminal neurotization occurred. Those patients whose facial paralysis was surgically treated had fair to excellent results, and the technique is considered superior to alternative hypoglossal or spinal accessory anastomosis.
Pathophysiological effects of Mobius syndrome on speech and hearing; The effects of Mobius syndrome (MoS) on the functioning of the peripheral speech and hearing mechanisms has not hithertofore been described, to the author's knowledge. Speech and hearing function of an 8-year-old MoS speaker was studied. Data were obtained from several sources. These included: electromyography of the facial muscles, physical examination of the peripheral speech mechanism, speech and language test batteries, audiological evaluation, and acoustic analyses of the speech signal. A pathologic condition was found to exist in a number of cranial nerves and in structures in the oral cavity. This resulted in consonant and vowel misarticulations, which notably affected speech intelligibility. Middle ear dysfunction was also present. Neurological mechanisms are discussed to account for these pathologies in human communication. Strategies for speech therapy and future research in MoS are presented.
Peripheral facial paralysis secondary to metastatic malignant melanoma. A clinicopathologic report; We report a case of disseminated malignant melanoma in which the initial sign was an isolated peripheral facial palsy on the left side. The cause of the palsy was established five months later, with the appearance of metastatic axillary nodes. The temporal bones demonstrated tumor infiltration within the marrow spaces of the petrous apices bilaterally. The left facial nerve was also extensively involved with melanoma to the level of the geniculate ganglion.
Bell's palsy: Beneficial effect of treatment with adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) in patients with a poor prognosis; In 111 patients with idiopathic peripheral facial paralysis (Bell's palsy) the prognosis was established during the first days of the disease, using sialometry and the stapedius reflex test in 102 patients. A poor prognosis was indicated in 36 patients. Treatment with adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) was commenced within 10 days (in the majority within 5 days) of the onset of the paresis in 31 of those patients with a poor prognosis. The recovery rate in the ACTH treated group was superior compared with the untreated control group of patients with a poor prognosis. The difference is statistically significant. Those patients with a good prognosis were not treated but merely followed up. Some factors which could influence the results of the treatment are considered.
Meningococcal meningitis in children; Forty-four cases of meningococcal meningitis in children at one hospital between 1971 and 1975 inclusive were studied to document the course and complications of this disease in children in the current therapeutic era. The mortality was 5%. Of the 41 survivors 76% were healthy 1 to 5 yr after the episode of meningitis. Permanent severe sequelae (facial palsy, optic atrophy and ptosis) were seen in 3 (7%) of the survivors, and mild hearing loss, hyperactivity and nervousness were noted in 7 (17%). Electroencephalography was not useful in determining management or prognosis. Both the mortality and the frequency of early and late complications among the survivors were lower than those reported from earlier studies.
Nicolaus A. Friedreich's description of peripheral facial nerve paralysis in 1798; In 1798, Nicolaus A. Friedreich of Wurzburg published a detailed clinical account of three patients with idiopathic peripheral facial nerve paralysis. His astute observations of onset, physical findings, natural course, treatment, and recovery preceded those of Charles Bell by 23 yr.
Neuropsychic manifestations in systemic lupus erythematosus (author's transl); Thirty-three cases of systemic lupus erythematosus in women are studied in retrospect. Eight patients (24 percent) presented a total of ten neuropsychiatric episodes that could be attributed to the underlying disease. The neuropsychiatric manifestation that was most often observed was cerebrovascular stroke (40 percent) followed by psychic disturbances and convulsions. A facial paralysis coinciding with an hypertensive crisis was noticed in one case. Another patient presented a peripheral sensitive neuropathy. Five episodes occurred prior to diagnosis or during the first year of the disease. In two patients the neuropsychiatric manifestations constituted the initial symptom of systemic lupus erythematosus. ECG proved to be one of the most valuable diagnostic tools among the complementary studies. It was altered in cases of organic pathology and normal when disturbances were of psychic origin. The C3 fraction of the serum complement revealed a definite difference between patients with and without neuropsychiatric manifestations. Concentrations were lower in persons which psychic disturbances than in patients without them. The pathogenesis of neuropsychiatric manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus is discussed. They cannot be attributed exclusively to coagulation disturbances nor to treatment with corticosteroids. The immediate prognosis of neuropsychiatric episodes was good: there was partial or total recuperation in eight of the ten episodes. However, the long-term course of systemic lupus erythematosus shows that these manifestations represent an unfavourable prognostic factor in this disease.
Facial rehabilitation with temporal muscle. New concepts; Facial rehabilitation, utilizing the transposed temporalis muscle, was performed. Three new innovations of this technique include: (1) The whole muscle is transposed into the face to accomplish augmentation, support, protection for the eye, and movement. (2) Following transposition of the temporalis muscle, its nerve supply is lysed at the foramen ovale. Nerve substitution by a free, autogenous graft from the proximal segment of the ipsilateral facial nerve or crossfacial sural nerve is accomplished. This technique substitutes the facial nerve axons and nuclei for the trigeminal nerve in this muscle and thus eliminates movement on mastication and facilitates the possibility for expression. (3) This muscle may be transposed with a portion of the temporal and parietal bones to add bony architecture to the cheek and orbit.
Facial palsy and its conservative treatment. II. Bell's palsy; Pathology, etiopathogenesis, pathophysiology, symptomatology and diagnosis of Bell's palsy are discussed. Among peripheral facial palsies of diverse origin, Bell's palsy is most frequent. It is acute entrapment lesion of the facial nerve in the fallopian canal but not caused by obvious pathology of neighboring structures as, e.g., otitis media. Contrary to previous opinion, this entrapment takes place regularly in the labyrinthine segment and its introitus (Fisch and Esslen 1972). Pathophysiology of Bell's palsy is the same as in other sorts of acute entrapment neuropathies. Primary edema of the facial nerve (inflammatory or non-inflammatory) causes pressure rise in the facial nerve which in turn leads to secondary edema. In this way, a vicious circle may arise damaging both nerve fibres and vessels of the facial nerve. Diagnosis of Bell's palsy is stated in particular by means of examinations mentioned in chapter three and by means of its typical course as described in chapter four. Attention is paid especially to the examination of the region of the internal meatal fundus and its nervous structures. Permanent facial paralysis does not take place in Bell's palsy and another cause, especially space occupying lesions, must be looked for.
Facial palsy and its conservative treatment. III. Treatment of various kinds of peripheral facial palsies; Treatment of Bell's palsy and other types of peripheral facial palsies are discussed separately. Because Bell's palsy is an acute entrapment neuropathy, only immediate decompression of the labyrinthine segment of the facial nerve performed in the early stage of the disorder may be effective. This decompression may be either pharmacological, using glucocorticoids, or surgical. Pharmacological decompression may be carried out either by systemic or local administration of glucocorticoids. Systemic administration is well known but not generally used because it is not without risk. Moreover, due to numerous contra-indications to the general administration of glucocorticoids, approximately 30% of all patients suffering from Bell's palsy must not be treated in this way. In patients without contraindications, systemic administration of glucocorticoids ought to be abudant. Nevertheless, even in carefully selected patients (i.e., without known contraindication), complications occur in 1-2% of cases. Compared to general administration of glucocorticoids, application of ACTH is even less effective and more dangerous.
Facial palsy and its conservative treatment. I. Anatomy, pathophysiology and examination of the facial nerve; Basic anatomical data concerning the facial nerve, especially its petrous portion, are summarized in the introduction. Contrary to other nerves of a similar diameter, the facial nerve consists of one single thick fascicle, in its labyrinthine and tympanic segment, surrounded by a tight perineural sheath. The introitus of the fallopian canal in the fundus of the internal acoustic meatus is the narrowest part of the whole fallopian canal - this fact being of crucial importance in cases of facial nerve entrapment. In chapter II, the most important facts concerning pathophysiology of the facial nerve are reviewed. The different grades of facial nerve injury are discussed and compared with the classification of Seddon, Sunderland and McComas et al. According to clinical observation and anatomical peculiarities of the facial nerve, a more accurate classification of grades of facial nerve lesions has been proposed: subclinical lesion (with local slowing of conduction velocity), local neurapraxia (excitability of the peripheral part of the affected nerve fibre preserved), extended neurapraxia (nerve fibre excitability lost) and partial neurotmesis (including both axonotmesis and lesion of the endoneurium). Pure axonotmesis which is not followed by aberrant regeneration is not observed in facial nerve lesions. Extended neurapraxia is sometimes called degeneration (denervation), less exactly, but this stage is reversible and may not be followed by true axonotmesis in all cases. New classification of the grades of facial nerve lesions seems inevitable because of discrepancies between previous classifications and clinical observations. In chapter III, various kinds of facial nerve examinations are reviewed critically. Without a doubt, examination of the motor function of the facial nerve is the most important. In cases of paresis, careful testing of the strength of mimic muscles ought to be carried out. When paralysis occurs, muscle testing has to be replaced by nerve excitability studies, especially the maximal nerve excitability test or evoked electromyography. When performing evoked electromyography, attention should be focussed on the amplitude of the evoked muscle action potential which is proportional to the number of motor fibres affected only by local neurapraxia. Among numerous methods of facial nerve examination, only nerve excitability studies enable us to differentiate between local and extended neurapraxia - this fact being of paramount importance during follow up of acute facial palsies. Among other methods of examination, Schirmer's test of lacrimation, otoscopy, X-rays of the petrous bone, examination of the function of neighbouring nervous structures, etc., are very important. Finally, the exact site of a facial nerve lesion and its cause ought to be determined. When applying rules of topognosis of the lesion to the facial nerve, the greater resistance of small diameter nerve fibres to damage (i.e., secretory fibres) must be borne in mind.
The clinical characteristics and diagnosis of the middle ear tuberculosis in recent years; A case of tuberculous otitis media is reported. The patient was a 45-yr-old male who had fistula symptom, bilateral facial paralysis and complete deafness. The authors reviewed 25 cases (30 ears) of tuberculous otitis media reported in Japan since 1965. They noticed the remarkable transition of clinical pictures of tuberculous otitis media in recent years. A granulous type of tuberculous lesion was frequently found in the recent cases. Based on the characteristics of the recent cases, the authors established the new criteria of the diagnosis of tuberculous otitis media: chronic otitis media resistant to various antibiotics except for antituberculous agents; a marked formation of granulation tissue in the tympanic cavity and its extension to the external ear canal; disorder in bone conduction; presence of active and/or cured lung tuberculosis; accompanying of the periaural lymphadenitis in children; positive intracutaneous tuberculin reaction; facial paralysis. Chronic otitis media presented with 3 out of 7 items should be suspected as tuberculous. Chronic middle ear disease presented with 5 out of 7 items can be clinically diagnosed as tuberculous otitis media. The final diagnosis should be established by biopsy of the lesion or by bacterial examination. The treatment consists of antituberculous agents and surgical removal of tuberculous regions.
Bell's palsy and secondary syphilis: CSF spirochetes detected by immunofluorescence; Although Bell's palsy is usually idiopathic, occasional cases may have an identifiable infectious cause. When facial paralysis results from syphilis, it usually develops during the tertiary meningovascular stage. In this article a 30-year-old man with secondary syphilis is described who developed facial paralysis associated with acute syphilitic meningitis. Spirochetes were identified in the cerebrospinal fluid by immunofluorescence using standard reagents from the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test. Patients with Bell's palsy should be screened for syphilis with a blood FTA-ABS test, and treatment with corticosteroids should be considered only after an infectious cause has been excluded.
Clinical observation of Bell's palsy; This paper results from a clinical study of 50 patients with idiopathic facial palsy (Bell's palsy). Incidence of Bell's palsy is constant in each year. Bell's palsy occurs most commonly in adults (20-40 yr). Both sexes and both sides are equally affected. Bell's palsy is slightly more frequent in cold weathers in the younger age group. One third of the patients have preceding histories of infection (12 cases), exposure to cold (4 cases) or compression (3 cases). It is suggested that some cases of Bell's palsy are due to viral infection or ischemia of the facial nerve. 60% of the patients recover completely within 50 days (rapid recovery), and most of the rest recover in 3 mth. If there are signs of recovery of facial palsy before the 20th day, rapid and complete recovery can be expected. The age of the patients and therapeutic measures, including administration of steroids, have little influence on the prognosis of facial palsy. Hyperacusis and pain behind the ear seem to be unfavorable prognostic symptoms.
Latent viruses and Bell's palsy in children; 4 Children with unilateral facial palsy - Bell's palsy (BP) - had serological evidence of primary infection with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Concomitant infection with cytomegalovirus (CMV) was demonstrated in 1 child while in all 4 children a rise in antibody titers to an additional one or two viruses was demonstrated. The viruses involved were herpes simplex, CMV and adenovirus which are latent in humans. Immunosuppression induced by EBV and steroid treatment may cause reactivation of these viruses resulting in rise in antibody titers. The need for prolonged serological follow-up for possible reactivation of latent viruses in BP is emphasized.
Myxoma of the mastoid with destruction of the facial nerve; A case of Myxoma of the mastoid with initial facial spasm followed by palsy of the nerve is reported. After removing the tumor the nerve has been reconstructed from the second knee until the stylomastoid foramen. The probable origin of the tumor is discussed.
Results of conservative therapy in 'idiopathic' facial paralysis; The results of conservative therapy in 160 patient with so-called idiopathic facial paralysis are reported. In 94.2% of the patients, a complete or far extending normalisation took place. In incomplete paralysis the number of patients restored to health was about 96.1%, and 93.3% inomplete paralysis. We treated with salicyl-pyrazon-derivatives or combined with corticosteroids and with antibiotics, resp., sulfonamids combined with corticosteroids. Physical therapy was applicated additionally in every case. Recovery did not depend on the sort of medicaments which were chosen.
The dissociated effect of treatment with ACTH on sequelae of Bell facial paralysis; The authors treated homogenous groups of patients with similar drugs and added ACTH in one group, noting a net improvement of synkinesis and hypertony, as well as better motility in light cases, probably secondary to more supple scar tissue while an insignificantly severer motor disturbance occurred in the severe forms of the paralysis. The authors suggest a selective favourable effect of ACTH only for the recovery of the connective tissue, while no effect is obtained in the regeneration of axons.
Tympanoplasty and tuberculosis of the middle ear; This report concerns 6 cases of middle ear tuberculosis. Typical clinical signs for this infection nowadays consist in a pale-colored mucosa, spontaneous facial paresis, pneumatization of the mastoid and in a changing performation of the tympanic membrane. These signs can occur single or in combination. Under a specific chemotherapeutic treatment even in tuberculous infection of the middle ear tympanoplasty can be performed without danger for the newly transplanted tympanic membrane. One should consider tuberculous infection especially in cases when for apparently inexplicable reasons necrosis of the transplant occurs postoperatively.
Faciofacial anastomosis; Facio-facial anastomosis represents an important therapeutic contribution to the difficult treatment of peripheral facial paralyses. Though difficult to perform, this procedure has been rendered possible by the considerable progress brought by the operative microscope and the microsurgical techniques; it opens up a new way for these patients. However, only experience and the practice of this new surgical method will determine its value in the future.
Treatment of acute otogenic neuritis of the facial nerve; Methods of treatment of 200 patients suffering from acute neuritis of the facial nerve occurring in 42 patients with acute otitis media and in 158 patients with chronic otitis media are reported. Paracenthesis and conservative treatment of acute otitis media from the first day of the nerve affection, and complex surgical (operation on the ear and partial decompression of the facial nerve) and conservative treatment of chronic purulent otitis media are recommended. The results of treatment are briefly analyzed. Of 200 patients, complete restoration of the facial nerve function was achieved in 174 cases. The cosmetic effect was good in 6, and satisfactory - in 20 cases.
Facial nerve injury secondary to lateral displacement of the mandibular ramus; The authors describe two cases of facial nerve injury after external dislocation of the mandibular ramus, an event not found in the reviewed literature. They discuss the possible pathogenesis and outline the therapy.
Peripheral facial paralysis and post-antirabies-vaccination polyneuroradiculitis; A case of facial diplegia with albuminocytologic dissociation of cerebrospinal fluid after antirabies vaccination prompted the authors to attempt a retrospective study of post-antirabies-vaccination neuropathies, with facial or extensive involvement. Fifty-seven cases are considered. Irrespective of vaccine type, certain clinical similarities emerge, notably the age of occurrence (adult), the early onset of the paralysis (during vaccine therapy or in the following week), and the prognosis (good survival rate, severity of functional impairment varying with extent of involvement). The authors attribute the main pathogenic role to the peripheral myelinic basic protein contained in varying proportions in conventional vaccines, the corollary being that such accidents should disappear completely with the new vaccination based on tissue culture material. A therapy program comprising the discontinuation of vaccine therapy and administration of corticoids is proposed.
Unusual symptoms of acoustic neuromas; Two cases of acoustic neurinoma with an atypical onset are described. The first case manifested itself with facial paralysis without discernible cause; surgical decompression of the facial nerve was attempted. The second patient presented sudden deafness after an injury to the cervical spine, followed by a syndrome suggestive of vertebrobasilar insufficiency. Arteriography revealed vascular displacement of tumoral origin. It is emphasized that transorbital radiography should be carried out in every case of unilateral inner-ear deafness.
Cerebellar atrophy; The cerebellum, being a special branch of the CNS has functional, structural and biochemical aspects of its own, which explains the existence of specific cerebellar affections. Thus, cerebellar atrophy is a manifestation of a persistent biochemical dysfunction, which may be of genetic origin or induced by any of a number of agents. It is not of fundamental interest to the physician, but sometimes serves as a clear sign of neurotoxicity, as the consequence of which a systemic disease may be discovered or a therapy changed.
Attempts to isolate virus from human trigeminal and facial ganglions; Herpes virus hominis type 1 was isolated from the trigeminal ganglion (ganglion semilunare, gasserian) in three out of 20 randomly selected autopsies. Two of the three patients had been treated with immunosuppressive or cytostatic agents. Clinical signs of herpes infection were not observed during the previous 6 months. No virus was isolated from the facial ganglion (geniculate ganglion) in the same 20 cases. The findings are discussed in relation to the viral etiology of acute peripheral facial palsy.
A case of Wegener's granulomatosis, presenting otological symptoms; A rare form of Wegener's granulomatosis is reported by the authors. The disease began in the form of acute otitis, and the classic form developed after a bilateral complete hearing defect, peripheral vestibular lesion, and facial paresis. The patient died. Attention is called by the authors to the importance of early diagnosis, since by early adequate treatment (steroids and cytostatic drugs) remission may be obtained.
A case of spontaneous pontine hematoma in patient suspected of pontine glioma and multiple sclerosis; A case of spontaneous pontine hematoma in a young boy, with remitting and relapsing clinical course of up to 11 years, suspected of having pontine glioma or multiple sclerosis is reported. Differential diagnosis of these are mentioned with reference to the authors' cases of pontine glioma. This patient was a man aged 16. At 5 years of age he had his first episode of double vision. 20 days after the first episode, gait disturbance, left facial palsy and consciousness disturbance developed. Neurological and neuroradiological examination revealed a pontine glioma and radiotherapy was administered. All signs and symptoms resolved except for bilateral abducens palsy. Four months later, he again complained of gait disturbance and facial palsy. Examination revealed bilateral conjugate ocular palsy, left facial palsy and cerebellar ataxia. These symptoms again resolved spontaneously, except for bilateral abducens palsy. At age 16 years, having been asymptomatic for 10 years, he suddenly noticed loss of taste. At that time sensory disturbance of the left side of himself, right hearing disturbance, dysarthria and retardation urinae. Neurological examination revealed bilateral optic atropy, bilateral abducens palsy, left facial palsy, right hyperacuisis, dysarthria, left hemiparesis, hypesthesia of the left side of the body and left cerebellar ataxia. The vertebral angiography was no evidences of mass lesion and vascular anomalies. Computed tomography demonstrated a pontine hematoma. Conservative therapy was performed and these symptoms cleared, except for bilateral abducens palsy.
Some remarks on the occurrence, diagnosis and results of therapy of peripheral paralyses of facial nerve; In a statistical group of 300 patients with peripheral paralysis of facial nerve from the total of 20,749 hospitalized patients of the Otolaryngological Clinic of Medical Academy in Erfurt (GDR), the subjects are divided into 7 groups according to the cause of the disease. A detailed examination indicated only 29% of etiologically obscure cases. The introduced therapy including surgical therapy in indicated cases resulted in a complete regression in 75% of cases, improvement in 17%, while only 8% of patients were not influenced by the treatment. The authors are of the opinion that a timely diagnosis of the etiological factors of the disease, as well as a timely, whenever possible, causal therapy including surgery, would enable to decrease the percentage of unsatisfactory therapeutic results.
Selective neurectomy in hemifacial spasm: an anatomo-pathologic finding; Today the treatment of choice in hemifacial spasm is selective neurectomy of the branches of the facial nerve. Palliative surgery has improved experience in the treatment of facial palsy. An anatomical finding is reported which could contribute to a better understanding of the etiology of facial spasm.
Effects of obstetrical interference on the newborn; The effective obstetric intervention on newborns have been analysed. Forceps delivery leads to a high incidence of morbidity rate, facial palsy and intracranial injury. The outcome of the neonate is further modified by the indication for forceps application as well as associated factors such as poor ante-natal care, poor socio-economic status and parity of the mothers, which have been responsible for a high perinatal loss as compared to the controls. A high incidence of the respiratory distress syndrome was observed in cesarean-delivered infants as compared to infants delivered by the vaginal route. Internal podalic version was hazardous to the neonate, with a greater predilection to ward asphyxiation, still-birth and higher perinatal loss.
Notes on the acute suppurative forms of otitis media, running a prolonged course; A series of 38 patients with otitis media purulenta acuta is reviewed. In 9 cases (23.7%) the suppurative process runs a torpid, protracted course, with combined or perceptive hearing loss. Reduction of the protective power of the organism due to diabetes mellitus, multiple myeloma, heart defect and postpartum period is accepted as a contributory cause. Infection is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus and influenza viruses, independently or in combination. Despite the treatment performed in 2 patients the otitis became chronic, one patient developing otitis media serosa with labyrinthitis and practical deafness, while the other patient was discharged as cured but with substantial impairment of the sense of hearing. In two of the patients with influenza otitis, untimely exudate evacuation resulted in the development of otitis serosa with labyrinthitis (in one case), and facial palsy (in the other).
Facial paralysis occurring during progressive chronic otitis. Reflections based upon 32 cases; The authors report their experience with 32 cases of facial paralysis occurring during progressive chronic otitis. Twenty were preoperative. The conclusions which may be drawn are as follows: (1) In general it occurs in cases of severe chronic otitis with large destructive cholesteatomatous and osteitic lesions. (2) Surgery is often difficult, long, and full of unexpected findings and risks. (3) The development of facial paralysis in a case of progressive chronic otitis is an indication for immediate surgery, on the same basis as a fistula of the HSCC, which is, in fact, often present in association. (4) The lesions encountered are much more extensive at the time of secondary (11) rather than at primary surgery (9). (5) The extent of the lesions (13 cases of fistula or labyrinthine destruction) and auditory impairment (16 kophenias or subkophenias) are such that tympanoplasty is useless. The authors report their long term results: 13 cases of complete recovery, 4 nil and 3 partial (2 as a result of a superficial cervical plexus graft). They raise the problem of the management when a markedly contused nerve is discovered: simple liberation with incision of its sheath or immediate graft? The other 12 were postoperative. Five were cases operated upon by the authors. There was 100% recovery in all cases, but 1 patient, in whom the nerve followed an atypical course, required decompression surgery. In the other 7, the authors performed 3 decompressions followed by an excellent result, apart from 1 case in which the nerve was markedly contused. In 2 cases a superficial cervical plexus graft and a XII-VII anastomosis proved necessary.
Post-embolisation lower motor neurone facial paralysis. Report of one case, discussion, prevention; In the light of one case of postembolisation lower motor neurone facial paralysis, it was felt to be of interest to draw attention to the possible role played by the middle meningeal artery: - in the etiogenesis of certain peripheral problems affecting the facial nerve during embolisation of the medial maxillary ; in the indirect recognition of a dangerous anatomical distribution. The easy identification of its endocrine branch and of the stylo-mastoid artery should reveal the mode of arterial distribution of the facial nerve: and hence to assess the risks run by patients during embolisation, according to the territory and the equipment.
'Congenital' cholesteatomas of the supralabyrinthine region; Twelve cases of congenital cholesteatomas developing in the region of the geniculate ganglion are presented. The diagnosis was made from a radiological sharp-cut erosion of bone found medial to the superior semicircula canal and superior to the internal auditory meatus in presence of progressive facial palsy. The main problems of the surgical treatment of the presented lesions were: 1. the presence of an unsuspected large fistula of the basal turn of the cochlea; 2. the necessity of resecting the superior semicircular canal in order to drain the supralabyrinthine region; and 3. extensive re-routeing and grafting of the facial nerve. The etiology of the presented cholesteatomas is discussed on the basis of the migratory theory and metaplasia of the first epibranchial placode.
Neural neurotization; Controlled experimentation using dogs has demonstrated that free nerve-end insertion into a denervated muscle that has lost its motor nerve at the point of entry into that muscle can sprout axons at its implanted end to unite with neuromuscular endplates, either preexisting or new, and result in a functioning muscle. Clinical applications can be found in the treatment of facial paralysis and traumatically induced avulsions of large muscles.
Unexpected complications following therapeutic embolization; Unexpected complications may follow therapeutic embolization, even though no apparent technical errors have occurred. This report included 4 cases of facial palsy following middle meningeal artery embolization, one case of aspiration pneumonia following glomus tumor embolization, and a case of pulmonary embolization following embolization of a spinal arteriovenous malformation.
Facial reanimation in Mobius syndrome; The psychosocial deformity associated with total lack of facial animation (as seen in Mobius syndrome) is an extremely crippling situation. This inability to show hapiness, sadness, or anger by facial expression frequently results in severe introversion and a reclusive personality. Restoration of even a minimal degree of controlled facial movement is beneficial. Recent experience in the treatment of two patients with this syndrome using both dynamic and static procedures has been most rewarding. Operating simultaneously on both sides of the face poses some problems that are different from those in the patient with unilateral paralysis. The operative details are described, with preoperative and postoperative evaluation.
Functional and topical diagnosis of peripheral facial paresis and results of treatment; In the ENT clinic of the University of Halle in the period 1966 to 1976, 780 patients with peripheral facialis paresis could be treated conservatively or surgically. The causes of the condition for which the patients came for treatment were otogenic damage, traumatism, iatrogenic causes and, in the majority of cases, the so-called idiopathic pareses. An account is given of a programme of examinations of the functional and topical diagnosis, that proved its value in particular in the indication of the therapy of choice. The functional results have, it is true, greatly improved, but the number of so-called defective cures is too high, in the opinion of the authors, and is avoidable. Emphasis is laid on the examinations that are available for the surgical indication.
Peripheral facial nerve paresis; Peripheral facial nerve paresis produces a certain amount of dismay and anxiety not so much in its threat to health but more for its severe cosmetic impact. In spite of the numerous therapeutic approaches to this frequently occurring nerve injury, many questions about these different approaches have sofar remained unanswered. Narrowly connected with this is the selection of necessary diagnostic measures from a large number of possible measures. Based on experiences gained with 446 patients who were examined electrodiagnostically, practical procedures for diagnosis and therapy are outlined.
Angiographic study of facial paralyses; Many arguments lead us to think that a possible etiologic factor in idiopathic Bell's palsy is the ischemia of the facial nerve and that angiography could help in diagnosis: the rapid progress of the paralysis; the correlation between Bell's palsy occurring after embolization of the internal maxillary artery, the middle meningeal artery, the occipital or posterior auricular artery, and their participation in the blood supply of the facial nerve; the already known ischemic third nerve paralysis reported in diabetes and extending further to the facial nerve. Even if it is technically impossible to study Bell's palsy by angiography, it is interesting to understand and consider some applications of embolization and perhaps to envisage a new kind of treatment.
Rehabilitation of peripheral facial paralysis by means of kinesitherapy; The use of kinesitherapy to treat peripheral facial paralysis is still an infrequent procedure. All types of this condition, however, can be rehabilitated, without, of course, prejudicing surgical decompression at a later date. These include facial paralysis due to cold, trauma, ear diseases, and parotidectomy. Muscle reactions have to be tested before starting treatment. The therapeutic procedures used must follow a precise pattern: application of heat, electrical stimulation under strictly defined conditions, passive and active kinesitherapy. About one hundred patients have been treated with these different methods over the last few years, and the authors report excellent results.
The surgical treatment of extratemporal facial paralysis: An overview; At present there is no single surgical approach that is ideally suited to rehabilitation of the paralyzed face. Dynamic reconstruction and neural reconstitution are usually preferred to static methods, except under special circumstances. Experience with over 150 autogenous facial-nerve grafts using epineural suture technique has resulted in return of movement in 95% of properly selected patients. When grafting is not feasible, as in the obliterated central facial nerve, hypoglossal-facial-nerve crossover is a simple and powerful source of reinnervation, usually resulting in minimal intraoral crippling and mild mass movement. A newer procedure, the cross-face nerve graft, is an alternative to hypoglossal crossover, although it results in less axonal input and longer regenerative time. In cases of long-standing facial paralysis with muscle atrophy, temporalis and masseter transfers are dependable and may sometimes be combined with a nerve graft.
The tongue flap for reconstruction in a case of Mobius syndrome. A case report; This paper deals with the extension of the tongue flap technique for reconstruction of deficient perioral structures in a case of Moebius syndrome. Some important surgical considerations, such as the vascularisation of the tongue, design of the flap, location of the flap base etc, are discussed and the operative procedures and the result are demonstrated.
Intracerebral cavernous hemangioma. A case report; The authors report a case of intracerebral cavernous hemangioma diagnosed by cranial CT. A woman, aged 27, suffered from Jacksonian epilepsy since 20 yr of age. The seizure involved only the left hand at first but gradually deteriorated to general convulsion with unconsciousness and postictal left hemiparesis in the last two years. Neurological examination on admission revealed left facial palsy, left hemiparesis and left paresthesia with increased left tendon reflex. Lumbar puncture showed clear CSF and normal pressure. Skull radiograms and brain scintigram revealed no abnormality. Right carotid angiograms revealed the avascular area and the stretched ascending branches of the middle cerebral artery in the parietal region. Surgery disclosed a subcortical demarcated dark red tumor, 3 cm in size, accompanied with hematoma. The tumor had no remarkable feeding arteries and draining veins. Histology comfirmed a cavernous hemangioma with thrombosis in multiple vascular spaces. Her postoperative course was uneventful. The authors discuss the radiological findings of intracerebral cavernous hemangioma especially those of angiography and CT scanning with a review of literature.
Rehabilitation of peripheral facial paralyses: surgical possibilities; If the plainness resulting from paralysis of the facial nerve has a high psychological repercussion, these lesions can generally be improved with surgical treatment. An etiological treatment is often indicated: decompression or repair of the nerve (suture or graft). It has to be tried. When the treatment fails or is impossible, another treatment has to be carried out. Its indication depends on the clinical picture, on the etiology, on the electromyographic investigation and on the patient's wish. The only palliative treatment, which can restore an emotional and symmetrical face, is the trans-facial graft; if it cannot be carried out, neurotization will be tried and exceptionally a transplantation. Only in case of failure or of impossibility will palliative methods adapted to every case be used (myoplasty, Muhlbauer's magnets).
Bilateral sudden temporary blindness in a 14-year-old boy; A 14-year-old boy with a very rapid impairment of vision leading to complete blindness within less than 24 h is presented. Edema of discs, upward gaze palsy, unreactive pupils, left hemiparesis and central facial nerve palsy were the main clinical features. Under steroid treatment the hemiparesis and facial nerve palsy gradually disappeared and an impressive recovery of visual function was observed. The possible causes and the differential diagnosis of sudden blindness in childhood are discussed.
Peripheral facial nerve paralysis of dental origin; The etiology, diagnosis and treatment of peripheral facial nerve palsy are discussed. Four cases of facial nerve palsy following dental procedures are reported. Following a revision of the world literature during the last 23 years, the 25 cases of facial nerve palsy documented are analysed and divided into four groups on the basis of etiology, speed of onset and recovery and modes of treatment suggested.
Vestibular neurectomy; Vestibular neurectomy technique used for the standard middle fossa approach and for a total translabyrinthine VIII nerve section is described. The middle fossa approach has been used in 49 cases of mainly Meniere's disease and basically the same approach for nerve decompression has been used in 19 cases of facial paralysis, 15 being due to Bell's palsy, 2 to petrous pyramid cholesteatoma and 2 to facial nerve schwannoma. In unilateral Meniere's disease with no further fluctuation in hearing, vestibular neurectomy gives good results in alleviating vertigo.
Concerning etiopathology and treatment of facial paralysis (Bell's palsy); The seventh cranial nerve is a complicated structure which contains sensory and parasympathetic elements in addition to the motor fibres. Following some introductory comments on its embryology and anatomy, the problems of localisation and the clinical symptoms of central and peripheral paralysis of the facial nerve are discussed. Further on there is a more detailed description of defined clinical syndromes, crossed paralytic types, peculiarities in infancy, important criteria concerning differential diagnosis of cerebral excitement and, finally for the practising doctor, special up-to-date clinical pictures showing paresis of the facial nerve.
Surgical treatment of hemifacial spasm associated with tortuous vertebrobasilar system (author's transl); Surgical treatment of hemifacial spasm associated with tortuous vertebrobasilar system was reported. A patient was 63-year-old female, who first experienced mild and intermittent muscle twitching around her left eye twenty years prior to admission. Five years later, the twitching extended to all the facial muscles on the left side. She was treated with facial nerve block, which resulted in facial palsy for about one year. Because of recurrence of the hemifacial spasm, she was admitted to the Neurosurgical Department of Bokuto Municipal Hospital on October 12, 1977. Neurological examination revealed no abnormalities except for left hemifacial spasm with slight muscular weakness. Electromyogram showed severe twitching and synkinesis of all the muscles of facial expression. Vertebral angiogram on the left side disclosed pronounced elongation of the vertebral and basilar arteries, which extended into the left cerebellopontine angle. Compression of the facial nerve root exit zone at the brainstem by the vertebral artery was considered to be the cause of the hemifacial spasm. Suboccipital craniectomy was carried out on November 29, 1977. The vertebral artery extended into the cerebellopontine angle, and adhered to the facial nerve. After mobilization of the vertebral artery from the facial nerve, a small prosthesis of non-absorbable spongy material (Teflon felt) was interposed between the vertebral artery and brainstem. Postoperatively, the hemifacial spasm disappeared, but the facial palsy, which had been observed preoperatively probably due to previous facial nerve block and long-standing hemifacial spasm, remained. The function of the acoustic nerve was preserved. Recently vascular compression of the facial nerve root exit zone has been reported as a major cause of hemifacial spasm, but such abnormal vessels are rarely demonstrated angiographically.
Idiopathic facial palsy due to Zoster (follow-up and indications for treatment); Idiopathic facial paralysis and paralysis due to zoster appear to be the result of pathological processes with identical sequelae: anoxic oedema of the nerve which is constrained within the inelastic confines of the Fallopian canal. In all cases, discovery of facial palsy should indicate urgent medical treatment in which vasodilators and steroids play an essential part. Other forms of treatment are debatable. At the same time as treatment is instituted, clinical assessment with electrophysiological studies of the paralysed neuromuscular complex, and tests to localise the lesion, both of which should be repeated and compared, allow the severity of the palsy to be determined, and the timing of later decompressive surgical treatment to be planned. No test in current use will give the information necessary to decide on very early operation. Where decompression is indicated, the authors use the technique of Professor P. Fleury which involves an enlarged endaural and transmeatal approach to a furrow which is sculpted in the posterior wall of the EAM while conserving bony support anteriorly - an essential feature; this allows easy decompression of the nerve in its second and third portions without risk to the hearing, and with maintenance of a strictly normal otoscopical appearance and a normal mastoid. A modification of this technique will even allow decompression of the geniculate ganglion. Finally, review of the post-operative results encourages decompression of the nerve during the second month, in order to obtain maximal recovery of the best quality.
Facial palsy occurring during active chronic otitis media (a report of 32 cases); The authors review their experience with 32 cases of facial palsy occurring in active chronic suppurative otitis media. 20 cases were preoperative. They have drawn the following conclusions from studying these cases: Paralysis usually follows severe chronic otitis involving vast destruction by cholesteatoma and osteitis. The operation is often difficult, lengthy, and full of suprise findings and risks. The appearance of a facial palsy during active chronic otitis media is an indication for urgent surgery, in exactly the same way as a fistula of the lateral semi-circular canal, which is in any case often associated with it. The lesions discovered are often more extensive when the procedure is a revision one (11) than when it is a primary procedure (9). The extent of the disease (13 fistulae or destruction of the labyrinth) and of the effect on the hearing (16 cases of total or subtotal deafness) preclude any attempt at reconstruction. The authors report their longterm results: 13 cases with complete recovery, 4 with no recovery, 3 with partial recovery, 2 of which had a graft from the superficial cervical plexus. They discuss the problem of the action to take if the nerve is found to be grossly damaged: simple decompression with incision of the sheath or immediate graft? The other 12 cases were post-operative. 5 of them were operated on by the authors. All had 100% recovery, but in one of them the facial nerve took an unusual course, and revision surgery for decompression was necessary. For the other 7, the authors carried out decompressions in 3 and these were followed by an excellent result except in one case where the nerve was very contused. Two further cases were dealt with, one by using a graft from the superficial cervical plexus, and the other by a XII-VII anastomosis.
Traumatic facial palsies undergoing surgery. A report of 24 cases; The authors draw three conclusions from their experience, bearing in mind the fact that they have never used the middle fossa approach except in cases of fracture involving the first portion of VII. The fact that tomography is often unsatisfactory, a number of fracture lines being invisible on the X-ray. The importance of enlarged endaural and transmeatal approach which gives an excellent view of the nerve and ossicular chain so that the necessary surgery can be carried out at leisure. Conservation of the sulcus allows return to a strictly normal anatomical appearance once the tympanomeatal flap has been replaced in position. Above all, a point which seems fundamental to the authors, operations on the VIIth nerve should be undertaken before the sixth week.
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Clinical features and prognosis; The clinical diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis was identified in 668 patients who were followed up for periods up to three years. This disease was found to be more common in women than previously believed. The five-year survival for all patients was found to be 39.4%, but younger patients had a substantially better prognosis than those in whom the disease was diagnosed when over the age of 50 years. When the mode of onset was considered, the spinal form was associated with a threefold better five-year survival than the bulbar form.
Idiopathic hematoma of the parotid area with facial paralysis; A case of hematoma of parotid area is reported. A 3-year-old child developed a swelling of the right parotid area and facial paralysis of the same side of his face. Blood was evacuated by needle aspiration from the swelling area, and facial paralysis disappeared immediately. Operation disclosed a hematoma in the outer surface of the parotid gland. The patient had no history of injury or previous operation around the parotid area. The cause of the hematoma was unknown.
Neurological, neuropsychiatric, and neurosurgical aspects of hyperostosis corticalis generalisata against the background of the clinical picture of Van Buchem's disease as a whole; In Van Buchem's disease bone formation dominates over the resorption of bone. There is pronounced osteosclerosis of the petrous bones and afterwards considerable enlargement of the mandible and chin. As this inherited syndrome progresses over the years, intracranial space is reduced. There is early compression of cranial nerves, e.g. peripheral facial palsy and trigeminal neuralgia. Later on, there may be anosmia, diminishing vision resulting from optic atrophy; moreover exophthalmus. The third and fourth nerves become affected if the superior orbital fissure is narrowed. Compression and deformation of the brain may lead to symptoms such as aphasia, hemianopsia and epilepsy. In advanced stages, the sellar hyperostosis causes injury to the hypophysis resulting in hypopituitarism, sometimes in pan-apituitarism. The spinal cord may also be compressed. A long cavity was seen in the cervical part of the spinal cord of one patient, causing a syringomyelia-like symptomatology. In the pathogenesis of Van Buchem's disease many factors play a role. Firstly one is confronted with an abnormal genetic predisposition, manifesting itself in a disturbed equilibrium between the activity of osteoblasts, stimulated by calcitonin, and that of the osteoclasts, activated by parathormone. If the thyroid gland produces a too high calcitonin level in plasma, strumectomia is indicated, followed by substitution-therapy. In the course of Van Buchem's disease the following stages may be distinguished: The early stage is characterized by irritation and/or paralysis of cranial-, sensory- and spinal nerves; The mature stage is characterized by brain- and spinal cord compression. At autopsy we found that the basal face of the frontal lobes of one patient showed a marked symmetrical impression, caused by pressure of the hyperplastic orbital parts of the frontal bone. Furthermore, an aspecific chronic arachnitis was found, causing a constriction of the optic chiasm. A slowly progressive pressure of the bone of the skull may cause, in that stage, neurological and psychiatric symptoms, such as deficient motor-coordination, reduction of memory and other psychic symptoms; The final stage is characterized by increased intracranial pressure followed by brain atrophy. Microscopic examination brought to light that strange extravasations had come about in the cortex and sub-cortex. We termed them 'pseudo-plaques'. They contained lipoproteins. Their shape varied from drop-like, rope of pearls, stars, rosettes, bunches of grapes or mulberies. The extravasations originate from the capillaries, penetrating their biochemically changed walls. These effusions inundated the cerebral parenchyma and brought about vasal compression into the environment, resulting in encephalonecroses, filled with exsudation. After some time the necrotic brain contained fatty acids. Glial fibrillar structures may be found in the final stage of the disease in the remnants of necrotic foci, resembling 'plaques trichosiques'. They are, however, not identical to genuine Alzheimer fibrillar plaques.
Diagnosis and therapy of so-called malignant external otitis; The malignant external otitis is characterized by the following symptoms: Severe neuralgic pain in the deep ear region is found in the elderly diabetic cases with a facial palsy due to the infection of the outer ear. In more than 50 percent of the cases with a facial palsy due to the infection the further course was lethal (Chandler 1968). A new surgical treatment of the malignant external otitis (Naumann 1977) is presented: After the adequate excision of all infected tissue and cartilage a perforated polyethylene-tube is placed into the infected area along the base of the skull. The combined therapy of a parenteral and local administration of antibiotics helps to improve the bad prognosis of the malignant external otitis.
Electro-acupuncture in otolaryngology; As an introduction to electro-acupuncture, the author discusses the basic theory of classical acupuncture as well as the therapeutic applications of low frequency positive or negative half-waves. Electro-therapy using specific points of acupuncture which refer to selected organs can now be carried out with a compact apparatus called ELBION. This instrument had originally been designed by the author for reliable and uncomplicated applications in oto-rhino-laryngology. ELBION thus permits the realization of a complete electro-acupuncture (EAP). Typical indications for EAP, as confirmed by the author, include influenzal anosmia, Bell's paralysis and central equilibrium disturbances of the neurovasuclar type. EAP serves as a most helpful additional treatment in cases of frontal sinusitis, various kinds of neuralgia, cervical otalgia, as well as sialoses of obscure or chronic genesis.
Facial paralysis in children; Facial-nerve paralysis in children is uncommon, but it is not as rare as was once thought. Most of these paralyses occur later in growth and development as a result of acquired causes, (traumatic or infectisus) although a significant number occur during the neonatal period. infectious) of the presence of associated congenital anomalies, particularly as exemplified by congenital unilateral lower-lip palsies, the early diagnosis of neonatal facial paralysis assumes considerable significance for effective clinical managment. Treatment considerations take primary importance in the acquired facial paralyses and depend on standard tests for facial-nerve function as well as topographic tests for lesion localization. Persistent or recurrent 'idiopathic' facial paralysis requires a thorough diagnostic evaluation, which takes precedence over therapeutic considerations. In most cases, a known cause will be uncovered and will help determine any therapy required.
Bell's palsy; There is still no universally accepted treatment for Bell's palsy. Most physicians use some form of medical therapy for affected patients. Although surgical decompression of the intratemporal facial nerve in patients with Bell's palsy is still highly controversial, there are instances in which it has proved beneficial. Such surgery, though, is based on sequential testing of facial-nerve function and the demonstration of progressive compromise to function (in spite of conservative medical management). More prospective, controlled, double-blind studies employing both medications and surgery are needed before an effective protocol for therapy can be established.
Rehabilitation of the face after facial nerve paralysis; The evolution of surgery for facial rehabilitation has been a fascinating study, beginning with static support and evolving through nerve grafts, muscle grafts, and nerve-muscle grafts. In spite of outstanding recent contributions, there are still patients in whom reconstruction is not possible. In these patients, symmetry and mimetic function must be restored by alternative procedures, such as muscle transfers, myomectomies, neuronectomies, rhitidectomies, and the like.
