At the present time, static symmetry is considered less desirable in facial rehabilitation if dynamic symmetry and motion of the face can be achieved. In principle, the proper innervation of the muscles of facial expression is by the facial nerve itself. This is possible following injury or surgical resection through direct nerve anastomosis or autogenous grafting. This restoration of the neuromuscular mechanism yields a physiologic result that may approximate the preinjury state and is reflected in the cosmetic and functional recovery achieved. However, in the current state of facial-nerve rehabilitation, one must realize that there is a continuing evolution of ideas. The future holds prospects for many new and exciting concepts that must yet come to clinical reality.
Surgery of the facial nerve; The solved and unsolved problems of intra- and extratemporal surgery of the facial nerve are discussed by the authors. On the basis of an evaluation of the various diagnostic methods, the difficulties and deficiencies of prognosis are outlined. The data of the recent literature and personal experience gained in the material are dealt with, taking into consideration the technical performance of the reconstructive operations and the expected function. The results of 21 intra-, 11 extra- and 16 combined transplantations are reported. On the basis of the results, it is emphasized that in case of transplantation not so much the length of the transplant as the degree of the lesion is of decisive importance regarding the time of regeneration. Also, the earliest possible reconstruction is to be taken into consideration. In the author's opinion, in case of Bell's palsy, the discission of the nerve sheath is not an obligatory, but rather a facultative principle, regarding the importance of the conservation of the nerves in the epineurium. In case of Bell's palsy, the exclusion diagnosis must be confirmed exactly by as many as possible examination methods, since behind the clinical picture of Bell's palsy severe morphological changes (neurinoma, tumor metastasis, cholesteatoma, etc.) may be hidden.
Peripheral facial palsy: diagnosis, prognosis and treatment; If the diagnosis of peripheral facial palsy is relatively easy thanks to the clinical and electrophysiological data and to the functional tests, the prognosis of a clinical facial palsy is more difficult to establish. Taking into account their personal experiments and the data in the literature, the authors describe the means which allow the formulation of prognosis on which depends the treatment (medical or surgical). They have tried to establish a well defined program which will be used later as a basis for a longitudinal study realized in common by neurologists, otorhinolaryngologists and neurophysiologists.
Prognostic value of minimal excitability of facial nerve in Bell's palsy; Nerve excitability is useful for prognosis in Bell's palsy. Minimal excitability values (MEV) were obtained by stimulating the facial nerve and recording the effective current (mA) required to evoke a minimal visible contraction of frontalis, orbicularis oculi, orbicularis oris, and mentalis muscles respectively. Serial MEVs were performed on 100 patients with facial palsy, of whom 87 were followed for 6 mth or to complete recovery; 61 patients were treated with steroids of whom 57 had good recovery. Serial MEVs were not only useful for prognosis, but also helpful in regulating the dosage of prednisone.
A case report of tentorial meningioma with complete unilateral facial palsy; A 41-year-old housewife complained of a gradually progressive facial palsy of 4 years' duration, deafness, intermittent facial pain and strain of the left shoulder. Neuro-otological examinations revealed total deafness, canal paresis in the left ear and no response of body sway to galvanic stimulation of the left side, and slight disturbance of optokinetic nystagmus to the right. Slight paralysis of IX, XI and XII cranial nerves was recognized, but not other neurological signs were noted. Electromyographic findings of the left facial muscles showed no response in voluntary and evoked movement. Electroencephalography demonstrated an abnormal slow wave focussed at the left parietotemporal region. Electrocochleography showed a retrocochlear lesion. CT scan and angiography (CAG, VAG) revealed a large tumor growing to the middle fossa from the posterior fossa of the left side. Since the tumor was adherent to the base of skull and the petrous bone, subtotal resection was performed and the tumor was confirmed as meningioma (spindle cell type) histologically. The author discusses the differential diagnosis of tumors at the cerebello-pontine angle, especially neuromas of the acoustic, facial and trigeminal nerves, and intracanalicular hemangioma.
Treatment of Bell's palsy in pediatrics; A series of 22 consecutive cases of idiopathic Bell's palsy are presented, 9 patients obtained return to the normal facial function without treatment and 2 more have had an importnat degree of recovery and it is expected they return to the normal facial function. Two cases did not show any recovery as they were cases with a chronic evolution and facial nerve degeneration. They did not receive any treatment. Facial nerve decompression was indicated in 8 cases; one hundred percent normal function was the result in 6 patients and a good result was obtained in the remaining 2 and complete recovery was expected shortly after.
Speech, language and hearing in moebius syndrome: A study of 22 patients; A comprehensive profile of communicative disorders in patients with Moebius syndrome was attempted. Seven patients were evaluated by the authors and the findings were added to 15 contributed case-histories. Most patients demonstrated some degree of dysarthria due to congenital paralysis of the facial nerves. Other problems such as cleft palate, hearing loss, mental retardation and delayed development of language were found in a few of the patients. As most of the older children in the sample and in reports in the literature eventually developed intelligible speech, a program of oral language stimulation and compensatory adjustments would appear to be the procedure of choice.
Tuberculous otitis media with complications; Tuberculous otitis media, although uncommon today, is still a differential diagnosis of suppurative otitis media. Our patient's otitis progressed from a draining ear with hearing loss to include facial nerve paralysis and meningitis. Several surgical procedures including radical mastoidectomy were insufficient to halt progression of the disease. After culture of acid-fast bacilli from the aural drainage and the cerebrospinal fluid, antituberculous chemotherapy was started and the patient responded well to treatment.

The most common causes, place of damage, errors in the treatment and medical-jurisdictional aspect of the problem are presented. Bell palsy: Muscle reeducation by electromyograph feedback; The present case study investigated the efficacy of feedback in restoring muscle control to facial muscles which had been affected by Bell palsy. The subject, a woman, was provided an analog tone as feedback for modifying the muscle activity on the paralyzed (right) side of her face to match that of her nonaffected (left) side. The results showed a statistically significant shift in muscle activity in masseter, zygomaticus, and orbicularis oculi muscles. Posttreatment levels closely approximated the nonaffected side, and resulted in more normal facial characteristics with respect to jaw position and symmetry of smiling. Bidirectional control of the zygomaticus was also demonstrated.
Anastomosis of masseteric nerve to lower division of facial nerve for correction of lower facial paralysis. Preliminary report; Another method to reanimate the corner of the mouth in facial paralysis is by reinnervation of the perioral musculature. The authors have done this in 3 cases by anastomosing the masseteric nerve to the nearby lower division of the facial nerve. The results varied, but are promising.
Traumatic facial palsy due to head injury; 49 cases of traumatic facial palsy due to head injury and 75 cases of Bell's palsy were examined. Traffic accidents with traumatic facial palsy are most frequently observed in elementary-school aged pupils than adults. In the traumatic facial palsy, male patients are observed far more frequently than female patients for ages from 20 to 39, the former having head injury more often. On the contrary, among patients with Bell's palsy of the same ages, the occurrence rate is almost equal for male and female. In cases of traumatic facial palsy, no correlation was noted between the recovery rate and the age of the patient. Head injury with traumatic facial palsy is observed most frequently in the temporal region. The lesion of the facial nerve inferred from the clinical symptoms does not always correspond to surgical findings. The EMG showed 3 types: the first type is observed mostly in the group with onset of facial palsy within one week from the date of injury, and this type of facial palsy recovers in several months. The second type is observed mostly in the group having onset of facial palsy within a month and this type also recovers in several months. The third type is observed mostly in the group with onset occurring within one hour; this type rarely shows recovery. In Bell's palsy, no such types with regard to the lapse of time could be clearly observed. Surgical indications are as follows: most cases of immediate traumatic facial palsy have a good surgical indication if there is no sign of recovery after several weeks. In the delayed traumatic facial palsy, because most of the cases show gradual recovery on EMG, after several weeks, it is not too late to perform surgical operation after 2-2.5 mth. Macroscopic evidence or dislocation of ossicles, etc. are helpful in dictating the surgical indication.
Electromyographic biofeedback in the reeducation of facial palsy; Electromyographic biofeedback techniques have been successfully applied in various neuromuscular disorders. Data on the use of this technique in reeducation of facial paralysis after initial surgical correction are scarce. The authors have developed a treatment program consisting of EMG biofeedback with the use of the Basmajian-Emory myotrainer. Two case reports are presented which show successful results after a 3 month training period.
Bilateral facial paralysis; Three patients with bilateral facial paralysis are described. The second patient had bilateral facial paracysis combined with acute polyradiculitis with tetraparesis and respiratory difficulties. The third patient was admitted with isolated facial diplegia, a possible monosymptomatic form of the Guillain-Barre syndrome. The various possible causes of bilateral facial paralysis are discussed.
Otogenic lesions of the facial nerve; The prognosis for facialis paresis decisively depends on the time and type of treatment carried out. The diagnosis rests basically on the otological findings and on the results of X ray and functional middle and inner ear examinations. Between 1955 and 1975, 3938 patients with a chronic otitis media were operated in the Halle University ENT clinic and 48 patients were treated for a preoperative peripheral facialis paresis. Iatrogenous operation determined lesions have become more rare due to improved surgical techniques, although they still occur in about 1% of all cases. Follow up operations (1.9%) appear to be more dangerous than first time operations (0.9%). The treatment results underline the necessity for a very critical attitude in otogenous lesions of the facial nerve. Nothing could be worse for the prognosis than a hopeful waiting.
Spinofacial anastomosis; Removal of large acoustic neuromas may still be followed by facial nerve palsy. The results of fourteen cases of spinofacial nerve anastomosis have been studied and compared with the results of spinofacial and hypoglossalfacial anastomoses reported in the literature. Other standard treatments of facial palsy have been briefly reviewed and criteria developed by which the most appropriate therapy for facial paralysis may be selected.
Treatment of facial spasm. A new technique; Facial spasm is not so rare in Japan, but the etiology and treatment are not established. Several treatments (facial nerve block by alcohol injection, neurotomy, drug therapy and stellate ganglion block) have been tried. Wakasugi's physical block method, facial nerve block by needle insertion, is the most popular one. However, the technique is rather difficult for us and the result is not constant. Moreover we sometimes experienced that Bell's palsy was prolonged, and dizziness or inner ear disturbance was complained about. According to this technique the peripheral nerve branch of the facial nerve is found by electric stimulator under neurolept analgesia and a small amount of pure alcohol (usually 0.1 ~ 0.2 nl) is injected.
The effect of stellate ganglion block on peripheral facial palsy: A proposed method of reporting; 86 cases of peripheral facial palsy have been treated. 100 percent function recovery was found in 75% of patients and 80 percent function recovery was found in 15% of patients who received stellate ganglion block within 2 weeks after the onset. 100 percent function recovery was found in 10.5% of patients and 80 percent function recovery was found in 26.3% of patients who received stellate ganglion block within 3 months after the onset.
Rehabilitation of leprosy patients in a comprehensive control programme in Gudiyatham Taluk of Tamil Nadu; The Research Project had been in progress from April 1, 1968 to March 1975 at Gudiyatnam Taluk of Tamil Nadu and it was financed by the Social and Rehabilitation Service of the Department of Health, Education and Welfare of the United States Government. The report is a book (covering 131 pages) on rehabilitation of leprosy patients. The results of the study are described in 8 chapters. This is a very useful index for leprosy patients with disability, whose condition is summarised in a 6 letter code. As a result of studying 5677 unselected leprosy patients, it was found that 33% showed some disability or other, and that involvement of upper limbs was more common than that of lower limbs. In the management of lepromatous leprosy folate and B-12 supplements may be valuable because of the high prevalence of folate and B-12 deficiency. Liver biopsies were done on 240 patients. Among 101 patients who showed no acid-fast bacilli in skin smears 22 patients revealed leprous granulomata in the liver. There was a sharp rise of leprous lesions in the liver as one moved from the polar tuberculoid (TT) to the polar lepromatous (LL) type. The clearance of these lesions depended on the duration of treatment. There was no significant correlation between the presence of tuberculoid granuloma in the liver and liver efficiency tests. A study of the social problems faced by 100 deformed and 100 non-deformed leprosy patients in the author's area revealed that the family and neighbors were friendly to 96-99% of non-deformed patients and to 84% of the deformed patients. Results of the study of nerves in 540 leprosy patients belonging to the 4 clinical types of leprosy were recorded. Electromyographic study of the muscles of the face has revealed the phenomenon of mis-reinnervation of these muscles in leprosy. Among 2416 leprosy patients with disability, the greatest prevalence is in the 2 decades over 30 yr. Deformities of the face were the most frequent single involvement. Regular administration of DDS in patients suffering from bacilliferous types of leprosy has been found to have beneficial effect on nerve function. It was proved that trophic ulcers can be treated at the home of the patients with plaster of paris (POP) casts or felt pad dressings. Under the local conditions, the patients were averse to having immobilization with POP cast at home. Fissures of anhidrotic feet were tested by soaking the feet for 45 min in water followed by a liberal application of vaseline and application of rubber latex solution to form a boot. When the boot was removed after 3 wk, fissures and hyperkeratosis had disappeared. In cases where repeated ulceration took place in the same area of the sole of the foot, devices to relieve weight bearing were necessary (e.g. fixed ankle brace walker and patellar tendon bearing shoes). These were provided for the village patients resulting in a significant decrease in the prevalence of plantar ulcers. Great deal of attention was paid to the retraining of farm workers who had to use plough and other tools in their normal work. Teaching of safe cooking methods also formed part of the training for women patients and men patients who had to handle fire in their occupation. The conclusion from the author's limited experience is that retraining and placement of disabled leprosy patients is possible and worthwhile. This cannot be done in the hospital. Among 494 leprosy patients investigated, 11% showed psychiatric disturbances. There was no correlation between the type of leprosy and psychiatric disorders. There appeared to be a significant correlation between the presence of deformity and the prevalence of mental illness.
Rehabilitation techniques for patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; Rehabilitation techniques for the management of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis are aimed at maintaining the patients at their optimum functional levels for as long as possible and at preventing complications secondary to disuse of muscles and immobilization. A functional staging of patients is proposed which is helpful in categorizing them in reference to the type of rehabilatative techniques required and the kinds of assistive devices needed.

Return of facial nerve function was observed in 15 out of 17 cases (87%) with follow-up of over 1 year. Personal modification of nerve suture is described. Therapeutic trial of tiapride in ENT; Tiapride was studied in 60 patients with ENT affections. The dosage was 1 to 2 ampoules IM a day for 7 to 10 days, followed by a half a tablet 3 to 4 times a day for 2 weeks to 2 months. Results were excellent or good for 16 out of 20 cases of essential headache, 6 out of 6 cases of Barré Liéou's syndrome, 7 out 8 cases of sinus pain, 6 out of 8 cases of Méniè's disease, and 6 out of 6 cases of facial paralysis "a frigore". In 7 cases of post-concussion syndrome, excellent results were observed in all the patients, on headache. Vertigo was reduced in intensity. The effects was moderate or nil on tinnitus and deafness due to Ménières syndrome, as well as in 2 casls of facial neuralgia. Tolorance was excellent as, in these 60 patients, only 2 cases of dry mouth and 1 case of vomiting in a diabetic were reported.
Facial palsy in children; During the period of 1964 to 1976, we have treated 112 children under 6 yr old affected with facial palsy, which constituted 7.5% of the total 1501 patients with facial palsies seen during the same period. Incidences of facial palsies in the infants are signficantly different from those of the adults. In the former cases, there are lower incidence of Bell's palsy and higher incidences of otogenic and congenital palsies as compared to the latter. In order to surmount the diagnostic difficulties inherent in the infant palsy, the following examinations are essential; microscopic otoscopy; temporal bone radiography; electrodiagnostic examinations including NET, S-D curve and evoke electromyography; and, virological examination of blood serum. Administration of general anesthesia was often required in order to perform these procedures. In respect to findings through the above mentioned examinations, 3 interesting cases may be specifically mentioned: one case with masked mastoiditis; one, with bilateral facial palsy of otic origin; and another, with congenital palsy caused by muscular hypogenesia. Surgical treatment was highly recommended when the prognosis of the palsy appeared to be poor due to denervation of the facial nerve.
EMG feedback and recovery of facial and speech gestures following neural anastomosis; A case report is presented of an attempt to increase muscle activity during non-speech and speech activities through surface electromyographic feedback. The subject, a 25-year-old male, had a surgical anastomosis of the seventh cranial to the twelfth cranial nerve five years prior to the initiation of this therapy. The right side of the face was immobile. Frequency analogs of muscle action potential from the right lower lip during pressing, retraction, eversion, and speech were presented to the subject. His task was to increase the frequency of the tone thereby increasing muscle activity. The subject made substantial improvement in the gestures listed above. Electrodes also were placed in various infraorbital positions for an upper lip lifting task. This gesture was unimproved. Pre- and posttherapy independence of facial gestures from conscious tongue contraction was found. Possible explanations were proposed for increases of muscle activity in the lower lip, lack of change of MAPs in the upper lip, independence of the facial muscle activity from conscious tongue contraction, and effectiveness of this feedback training.
The true nature of Bell's palsy: analysis of 1,000 consecutive patients.; In a series of 1502 patients seen in our Facial Paralysis Research Clinic 1048 were diagnosed as having Bell's palsy. Review of clinical, epidemiologic, and laboratory data, plus review of the literature, has led to the conclusion that Bell's palsy is an acute benign cranial polyneuritis probably caused by reactivation of the herpes-simplex virus, and the dysfunction of the motor cranial nerves (V, VII, X) may represent inflammation and demyelinization rather than ischemic compression. Spinal fluid analysis suggests that the disease is a phenomenon of the central nervous system with secondary peripheral neural manifestations. With our presently available information, treatment of a viral disease with an anti-inflammatory agent is rational. Prednisone treatment started within the first week of the disease can restore better function to the paralyzed face than is achieved without such therapy, and facial nerve decompression has been unnecessary.
Elevated blood pressures in infants and children.; Blood pressure should be routinely measured in all infants and children. Measurements should be performed with an appropriate size cuff and observed pressures compared to normal values for age. Elevated blood pressure is seen in one to ten percent of children, depending on the age group surveyed and the definition of hypertension selected. Thirty to fifty percent of children with elevated blood pressures are asymptomatic. The remainder have symptoms which are nonspecific, including headaches, visual disturbances, seizures, congestive heart failure, and facial palsy. Hypertension in children, unlike hypertension in the adult, usually has a definite cause which often responds to adequate medical and/or surgical treatment. For this reason, children with well-confirmed hypertension should be thoroughly evaluated. The most common causes of hypertension found in children are renal disease (pyelonephritis, vascular disease, structural malformations) and coarctation of the aorta. An approach to the child with transient or persistent hypertension is described. Diagnostic studies should be individualized and should follow clinical clues where possible. Medical management of the child with acute hypertension is discussed.
Retrolabyrinthine approach: technique and newer indications.; Excellent exposure of the cerebellopontine angle is obtained by an approach through the mastoid posterior to the labyrinth. Since the major portion of the dissection is extradural, this approach is associated with a very low morbidity. The retrolabyrinthine approach has been used for several years for selective partial section of the posterior root of the trigeminal nerve in cases of trigeminal neuralgia. Complete relief of pain has been accomplished in 25 of 28 cases, and the other 3 patients had partial relief of pain. The only complications in these patients were partial hearing impairment in 2, and 1 partial abducens nerve paralysis which subsequently recovered completely. Two patients required secondary closure of cerebrospinal fluid leaks. This approach has also been used for exploration and biopsy of cerebellopontine angle tumors and for treatment of other cranial nerve problems. We conclude that the retrolabyrinthine approach is the preferred route to the cerebellopontine angle in a variety of clinical conditions.
A critical comparison of neurosurgical and otolaryngological approaches to acoustic neuromas; Neurosurgeons have traditionally advocated the transmeatal suboccipital craniectomy as the procedure of choice in treating acoustic neuromas of all sizes. With this technique, complete tumor removal was achieved in 91% of our patients. Facial motor activity was fully preserved in 59% and it was partially deficient in an additional 29%. Conversely, recent otological reports have proposed a more flexible attitude in which the size of the tumor dictates the form of surgical therapy. In that scheme, the universally applicable and clinically proven suboccipital craniectomy is replaced by a series of procedures (translabyrinthine, middle fossa, transsigmoidal), each of which differs in its anatomical and technical requirements. This necessity for several operations seems to stem from the failure of any particular approach either to provide adequate visualization of the entire pathological process, or to afford maximum opportunity for complete tumor removal. By employing these various techniques, total capsular removal has been generally achieved in only 71% of cases. A careful comparison and analysis of these individual procedures reaffirms the superiority of the posterior fossa approach.
Problems of symptomatic therapy in multiple sclerosis; The author reviews symptoms, reversibility of symptoms, prognosis, and treatment based on the large number of MS patients in the Gottingen documentation pool. As expected, spasticity, paresis, ataxia, visual and sensory disturbances and urinary dysfunction are dominating disorders in MS. Sexual dysfunction was found in 23 percent of male and 5 percent of female patients. Visual disturbances, diplopia, facial palsy, sensory disturbances of the face and perhaps tactile sensory disturbances were found to be more reversible than other symptoms. The author points out that 30 percent of patients are still at least partially employable 20 years after the onset of MS, and that the lifespan of the MS patient has increased considerably in the last 40 to 50 years. Spasticity, ataxia and bladder and bowel disturbances remain major problems in limiting working ability. (Cook - Newark, NJ)
Extracerebral cavernous hemangioma of the middle fossa.; Two cases of extracerebral cavernous hemangioma in the middle fossa are reported. Cerebral angiography showed a large avascular mass lesion in each case, but the tumors were very vascular at operation. Recovery of vision occurred in one case postoperatively. Diagnosis and treatment of these tumors are discussed.
Contralaterally elicited electrical stimulation of paralyzed facial muscles; Functional electrical stimulation is being explored in the extremities. A major obstacle is found in programming the firing sequence. In 1976, David Zealear proposed using the activity on the normal side in axial muscle pairs that normally function symmetrically to act as a template to control the stimulator. This method was demonstrated in laryngeal muscles in dogs, and is now demonstrated in the face with future applications being proposed. The facial nerve on one side was sectioned in a series of rabbits. Implanted electrodes received electrical potentials from selected muscles on the normal side. Bursts of electrical activity on the normal side during a blink or a twitch were used to trigger a muscle stimulator, which was routed to matching muscles on the paralyzed side. This technique restored symmetric function to the hemiparalyzed face.
Correction of permanent upper facial palsy by transposition of the pedicled temporal muscle; Transposition of a temporal muscle flap according to the principles laid down by Lexer and Schmid has been suggested by the authors for the treatment of long-standing upper facial palsy. But here a lower-based pedicled flap has been used by the authors. In order to maintain innervation of the flap, it appears mandatory to separate the latter at the subperiosteal level, from above downwards, up to the perpendicular on the medial portion of the zygomatic process. Finally, emphasis is laid on the necessity to take extremely accurate landmarks prior to lateral orbitotomy, otherwise closing of the eyelids will be unsatisfactory.
Facial palsies by traumatic luxation of incus; The authors describe 4 cases of fracture of the petrous part of the temporal bone, with dislocation of the incus and facial paralysis. Necrosis in the temporal and aural area resulting infusion of hyperosmolar solutions into the right temporal artery of a premature neonate; A neonate was accidentally given an infusion of 5% sodium bicarbonate and 20% glucose solutions into the right temporal artey. Skin necrosis and facial paralysis occurred, in the distribution area of the artery. The authors suggest the following points. To avoid the risk of an accident, the pulse should first be palpated before the infusion begins. Normal saline should be given first, and a watch kept for ischaemia. If ischaemia occurs during a hyperosmolar injection, heparin and streptokinase should be given at once, and thrombolytic therapy continued for as long as necessary. Should skin necrosis occur, then skin transplantation will be required to produce satisfactory healing and a good cosmetic result.
Orbito palpetral plastic surgery; When in 1972 the French Ophthalmological Society discussed the subject of this report they were undoubtedly hoping to remind ophthalmologists that this plastic surgery was an integral part of their speciality. It was immediately apparent to the chosen reporter that besides the honor that was being done to him there was an accompanying difficult task. An ophthalmologist above all, his experience had been insufficient to carry through such an enterprise on his own. It was thus that the 'Team' which has drawn up this report came to be formed. It comprises three ophthalmologists, two plastic surgeons and a neurosurgeon. The first chapters in this book deal with the surgical anatomy of the orbit, typical ophthalmological problems, such as enucleation and evisceration, and several aspects of maxillofacial fractures. More specific abnormalities, such as exophthalmia, facial clefts, colobomas, microsomia, microphthalmia etc., are described. Typical neurosurgical problems in craniofacial surgery and some typical eyelid plastic and cosmetic surgery are also described. In the main part of the book, however, emphasis is laid on the co-operation between the three specialities--ophthalmology, neurosurgery and plastic surgery--since most abnormalities demand a multidisciplinary approach. Facial nerve surgery; In these Proceedings of the Third International Symposium on Facial Nerve Surgery (Zurich 1976) the important scientific and technical advances made during the last 6 yr by basic scientists, otorhinolaryngologists, neurologists, neurosurgeons and plastic surgeons, are reported. Recurrent Bell's palsy. Etiology, frequency, prognosis; The etiology, frequency and prognosis of recurrent Bell's palsy were studied in patients with peripheral paresis of n.facialis of various etiology. 14 (11.9%) of 117 patients with Bell's palsy had a recurrent paresis of n.facialis. 9 of these were of homolateral and 5 contralateral type. 7 recurrent facial paralyses in idiopathic Bell's palsy (i.e. 10.4% of the patients with idiopathic facial palsy), 3 facial palsies of viral origin (i.e. 8.8% of the patients with viral facial palsy), 1 in association with diabetes mellitus, 1 during pregnancy, 1 combined with positive rheumatic serological tests, and 1 in a case of Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome were found. The frequency and heterogenity of etiology of recurrent facial palsies suggest a predisposing factor or immune mechanisms. In 8 patients there was within 6 to 8 wk a good, in 2 patients a moderate and in 4 patients a poor recovery of function. The greater reduction of the compound action potential of the m.orbicularis oris in recurrent homolateral facial palsy in relation to patients with single manifestation point out the greater denervation and therefore the poorer prognosis of recurrent palsies. A prophylactic decompression to prevent a third attack of recurrent facial paresis is considered.
Arson and Moebius' syndrome: a case study of stigmatization; The ever uneasy and precarious equilibrium between psychiatry and the law is well illustrated by a recent trial, concerning a man aged 22 yr who had been born with a rare and bizarre congenital disorder. Only some 100 cases of Moebius' syndrome or congenital facial diplegia, have been described and about 10% of these have been mentally subnormal. In a typical case there is degeneration of the corpus callosum and complete bilateral paralysis of the facial nerves, so that expressive movements of the face are absent. Paralysis of the ocular nerves limits eye movements. Various associated defects are common. No treatment is described in the literature and there is no previously reported association with criminality. When the patient was 20 he took up residential catering work in a hospital, with accommodation in the nurses' home. Here he encountered teasing and ostracism more cruel and sustained than ever before. On several occasions over a period of about 17 mth he burnt and damaged clothing. At his trial for arson and criminal damage the probation report covered his physical defects and the background to the offences. Notwithstanding the fact that in another case of arson the judge thought it wise to call for a psychiatrist's report the judge sentenced him to 4 years imprisonment. This remarkable case is further discussed from a psychiatrist's viewpoint.
Selective experimental reinnervation of paralyzed facial muscles; Amelioration of facial nerve dysfunction has been variably successful and often has resulted in only gross motion. An experimental model has been developed whereby the nerve muscle pedicle technique used to reinnervate the larynx has been modified to achieve selective reinnervation of paralyzed facial muscles. A series of rabbits underwent facial denervation, following which a nerve muscle pedicle was transposed to the denervated zygomaticus muscle to achieve selective reinnervation. Subsequent follow up showed good clinical evidence of reinnervation one to four weeks postoperatively. This was confirmed by electromyographic and histologic findings. It is suggested that the nerve muscle technique that has been used to correct laryngeal paralysis also may be applied to the selective reinnervation of paralyzed facial muscles.

Tuberculous otomastoiditis in children; The authors report three cases of tuberculous otomastoiditis in children. Review of the literature, with particular emphasis on the ten other cases reported since 1960, discloses that this form of tuberculosis is most frequent in infants and young children. All too often, the diagnosis is made too late, with resulting complications such as irreversible hearing loss and facial nerve paralysis. Antituberculous medication and surgical drainage controlled the infection in all 13 cases diagnosed since 1960. Tests for tuberculosis in children with chronic ear infection should be mandatory, but periodic testing of all children is recommended.

Acupuncture in two cases of peripheral nerve paralysis; A report on a case of peripheral paralysis of the right side of the larynx in a 34 yr old male who became completely aphonic following a grippal infection. After 3 wk of conventional treatment by a well known specialist, he underwent acupuncture treatment. The second case was a 62 yr old male with facial paralysis. This patient underwent acupuncture treatment shortly after he was stricken. Clinico-enzymological correlations in trophic disorders of the buccal mucosa in patients with peripheral lesions of the facial nerve; The paper deals with trophic disorders of the buccal mucosa in 30 patients with Bell's paralysis. The character of the changes found was judged by the results of an examination of the mucosa and chemical and histochemical studies of the bioptate, obtained by aspirational biopsy. The examinations demonstrated trophic disorders in the buccal mucosa which were testified to by a slight edema and enzymatic-metabolic disorders in the form of increased activity of the acid and alkaline phosphatase as well as asparagine and alanine aminotransferase. These changes to a certain extent confirm the existence of vegetative filaments in the facial nerve, an affection of which leads to metabolic-trophic changes. Moebius syndrome. Case report with a 30-year follow-up; Moebius syndrome is uncommon, as reported in the literature. A patient with Moebius syndrome is reported, showing a 30-year follow-up after initial surgical treatment by bilateral partial transfers of the masseter muscles.
Prognostic value of electrodiagnostic methods in peripheral facial nerve palsy; The function of the facial nerve can be examined by 4 electrodiagnostic methods. In the nerve excitability test and electroneurography with determination of the distal latency the facial nerve is stimulated over the stylomastoid foramen. Chronaximetry and electromyography are performed in the muscles. Whereas chronaximetry renders an impression of the severity of the neural lesion, electromyography can also determine the onset of reinnervation activity. Early prognosis within 6 days of onset can be determined only by nerve excitability tests and electroneurography, which assess the muscle potential. If the potential amplitude decreases more than 35% within two days and the muscle potential disappears between the fourth and sixth days, total degeneration of the nerve with poor prognosis is indicated. Such data can be obtained by at least two electrodiagnostical investigations preferably on the third day after onset and one to three days later.

Acute onset of bulbar and ocular paralysis. An isolated case, with differential diagnosis; The diagnosis of botulism should be considered in all patients with the acute onset of cholinergic dysfunction and muscle weakness. The pupils are usually dilated; paralysis of ocular and bulbar muscles invariably occurs along with weakness of limb and axial muscles. This diagnosis is supported by the presence of a neuromuscular block and confirmed by the detection of toxin. Although the clinical presentation in this patient supported this diagnosis and a neuromuscular defect was present, no botulinum toxin was found. Not until Clostridium botulinum, type B organisms were cultured was the diagnosis of 'probable botulism' made in this patient. Myasthenia gravis, atypical Guillain-Barre syndrome and a brain stem vascular lesion were also considered in the differential diagnosis. The anoxic encephalopathy following the cardiorespiratory arrest was an additional complicating factor.

Value of neuronography in assessment of facial nerve paralysis; The treatment of complete facial paralyses until recently was rendered difficult by the absence of an electrodiagnostic method of examination that gives reliable prognostic pointers at an early stage. This gap has now been closed by neuronography. The sum of the action potentials (SAP) is a direct measure of the number of muscle fibers set into action by the nerves. Consequently, the lowering of the amplitude in comparison with the SAP of the healthy side corresponds to the number of degenerated nerve fibers. Now it is possible between the 7th and 10th days after the onset of the paralysis to obtain a reliable prognosis and indications for the essential treatment (further conservative treatment, or decompression of the facialis.

Bilateral facial palsy. A rare presentation of infectious mononucleosis; Infectious mononucleosis (IM) is a common systemic illness primarily involving children and young adults and due apparently to the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Although the typical case is easily recognized, unusual manifestations or serious complications occur frequently enough to pose problems in diagnosis and management. Neurologic complications are rare (1%) - these include meningoencephalitis, infectious polyneuritis (Guillain-Barre-Strohl syndrome) and mononeuritis. These complications may actually precede the full clinical picture or present as the sole manifestation of the illness, thereby causing a confusing clinical picture and delay in diagnosis. The described case illustrates how IM can present only as bilateral facial palsy without any other neurologic signs or symptoms.

Successful surgical treatment of intracranial mycotic aneurysm with brain abscess. Report of a case; A curative case of intracranial myotic aneurysm with brain abscess, which occurred as a complication of bacterial endocarditis, was reported. A 25-year old female with a congenital supravalvular aortic stenosis was admitted to another hospital because of severe headache, vomiting and convulsion on Nov. 5, 1976. Right carotid angiography revealed a dumbbell shaped aneurysmal shadow at the distal portion of middle cerebral artery. Occlusion of major branches were also seen in the middle cerebral artery. She was referred to Tohoku University Hospital on Nov. 19, 1976. On admission she was retarded in her consciousness and neurological examination disclosed nuchal rigidity and right hemiparesis with central facial palsy. Funduscopic examination revealed bilateral papilledema. On physical examination, cardiac murmur, cyanosis and clubbing of fingers were also noticed. Laboratory study showed severe normochromic anemia, elevated sedimentation rate and positive CRP. Blood culture showed beta- hemolytic streptococcus. Second right carotid angiography was performed on Nov. 19 and it showed that the aneurysm had increased in size over a period of 14 days and increased opacification of right middle cerebral artery. EMI scan revealed a high density area and a ring-like shadow. From the clinical symptoms, findings of angiogram and EMI scan, diagnosis of intracranial mycotic aneurysm and brain abscess were established. Treatment with massive antibiotics and gamma-globlin was begun and the next day she was afebrile and her general condition rapidly improved. The right frontotemporal craniotomy was performed and excision of aneurysm and total removal of abscess were carried out. Electroneurography in prognosis of intratemporal facial palsy, as compared to measurements of rheobase and chronaxy; Electroneuronography is compared to indirect chronaximetry in the prognosis of intratemporal facial palsies. In 86 patients, the 2 methods were found to be congruent and in a number of cases complementary in determining impending degeneration. Both techniques are described and their results evaluated statistically. The author's observations indicate that electroneuronography allows to some extent a quantitative evaluation by means of numeric parameters whereas the results of chronaximetry only give a qualitative account of nerve degeneration depending largely on the examiner's experience. Both methods, however, have a certain margin of failure and for more accurate diagnosis and prognosis simultaneous use of both methods is advocated.

Management of 'cold' facial paralysis; The diagnosis of 'cold' peripheral facial paralysis is done by a process of elimination; it can only be made after having formally eliminated all other causes. Once the diagnosis is made, it poses essentially the problem of the prognosis for recovery. Fortunately, in the great majority of cases the progress is spontaneously favorable, hastened, however, by medical treatment, particularly by corticotherapy. Much more rarely, this facial paralysis is serious or even grave, and its recovery will be incomplete, leaving some formidable esthetic sequelae, like paralysis, but above all hypertonia, synkinesis or even hemispasm. It is for preventing or restricting as much as possible the sequelae of these grave forms that surgical decompression of the facial nerve may be proposed.
On the meningococcal meningitis; The present work aims to the evaluation of the etiological and clinico-epidemiological aspects of the purulent meningites, observed in a Division of Infectious Diseases in the period 1968-1973, and chiefly of their neuro-psychical outcomes. As regards the etiology of the purulent meningites, in the authors' case report the meningococcal forms are prevailing and they are followed by the so-called abacterial meningites. Moreover, the authors remark some preference of the D. pneumoniae meningitis towards the elderly people, whereas the meningitis forms caused by Enterobacteriaceae appear to be rare in the neonatal period. No meaningful differences have been remarked in autumn-winter and during the spring. At the clinical level, frequent atypical onsets of the disease have been remarked and they have been characterized by a shifty and attenuated pattern. Among 393 patients affected by purulent meningitis, 359 patients recovered (i.e., 91.30% of the total, whereas 34 patients died (8.70%). As regards the meningococcal meningitis, 175 subjects out of 242 have recovered quickly, whereas 53 patients have recovered in a delayed manner. In the range of the meningococcal meningitis, 14 deaths have been also surveyed. The general lethality has been low on the whole in the authors' own experience, with the exception of the pneumococcal purulent meningitis, which have exhibited on the contrary a high lethality. In relation to the neurological complications, generalized convulsions have been mainly observed, followed by cranial nerve palsy, monoparesis and hemiparesis, which have exibited a lesser incidence. The authors report as permanent outcomes facial palsy, monoparesis, hemiparesis, hidrocephalus, hypoacusia, deafness and epilepsy. In order to evaluate the long-term neuropsychical outcomes, the authors have carried out a particularly interesting neurological, psychological and electroencephalographic investigation, which has put into evidence on the whole a slight incidence of neuropsychical steady sequelae, chiefly characterized by the so-called transitional syndrome.
Prednisone in idiopathic facial paralysis (Bell's palsy); 76 patients with severe Bell's palsy were treated for a short period with high doses of prednisone (60 mg for 4 days and from the 5th day on the dose was reduced every day by 5 mg). Preoperative facial paralysis in malignant parotid tumours; Preoperative paralysis of the facial nerve was found in 145 of 1,029 patients with malignant parotid tumours (14%) treated at nine university clinics in Scandinavia. The incidence of facial paralysis varied between the different clinics. A parallelism between the incidence of the facial paralysis and the impairment of the prognosis of the different tumour types is shown. Activities of the pain clinic of Hiroshima University Hospital from 1967 to 1977; From 1967 to 1977 a total of 2144 patients consulted a Pain Clinic. In these patients, facial spasm accounted for 344, trigeminal neuralgia 313, facial pain and headache 244, pain of the upper extremities and shoulder 198, lumbo-sacral pain 195, cancer pain 194, and facial palsy 188. Patients with facial spasm were treated with physical facial nerve block, and patients with trigeminal neuralgia were given branch block with 0.5 ml ofpure alcohol or Gasserian ganglion block. Patients with facial pain and headache were subjected to ipsilateral stellate ganglion block with 8 ml of 1% mepivacaine, single or continuous cervical epidural block with 5-8 ml of 1-2% mepivacaine, total cerebro-spinal block with 20-30 me of 1.5% mepivacaine, or EAP (electric acupuncture). Lumbo-sacral pain was managed with single or continuous lumbo-sacral epidural block with 5-8 ml of 1-2% mepivacaine. For patients with pain of the upper extremities and shoulder ipsilateral stellate ganglion block, suprascapular nerve block with 8 ml of 1% mepivacaine, single or continuous cervical epidural block, or EAP was provided. For cancer pain, continuous epidural block or intra-thecal permanent block with 0.2-0.3 ml of 10-15% phenol in glycerin was given. Patients with facial palsy were subjected to ipsilateral stellate ganglion block. Of these, 198 patients were hospitalized and subjected to nerve block.

An index for paresis and defective healing, an easily applied method for objectively determining therapeutic results in facial paresis; Residuals of facial paralysis consist of a great variety of cosmetic and functional anomalies which differ in quality and/or quantity. An internationally standardized evaluation of such defects is mandatory for the assessment of the results of different therapeutic procedures. In the present study, a system has been developed to record the results of facial paralysis following therapy. Such a system does not require specialized training, instrumentation or require significant time for completion. A clearly-defined 'Yes-No' evaluation criteria is established which creates a high interscorer reliability. The usefulness of this scoring system was tested by three examiners on 42 patients following facial nerve surgery, with an obtained interscorer reliability of 93%.

A malignant tumor of the parotid gland with metastasis into the cervical vertebra; A man, aged 66, suffered a malignant tumor of the parotid gland. Backache, pains in the arms and the elbows were the first manifestation of the symptoms and the parotid gland swelling appeared 3 months thereafter. This was followed by a facial nerve paralysis 20 days later. Tc(99m) and 67Ga-scannings were applied to the whole body. The parotid tumor was hypoactive to Tc(99m) and hyperactive towards 67Ga; these appear to be the most characteristic findings in the case of malignant tumors. There were, however, abnormal accumulations of Tc(99m) and 67Ga in the metastasis of the cervical vertebra. Histologic examination revealed the growth to be an adenocarcinoma. Possibilities of transfacial microanastomoses in the treatment of peripheral facial paralysis; Microscopic trans-facial or facio-facial anastomosis is a technique that is promising in the treatment of peripheral facial paralyses - even old ones considered as incurable by other therapeutic measures. Its principal advantage is that it is a very fine approach to the physiological function of the facial nerve. Obviously it calls for familiarity with surgery under the microscope. It must be emphasized that it is not a risky method and in no way mortgages the future, because, in case of failure, muscular transplantation or cosmetic cutaneous surgery is still possible. The author considers that its indications will become wider in the future.

Prognosis of seventh nerve palsy following removal of large acoustic tumors; The authors' experience leads them to believe that if the 7th nerve is anatomically intact after removal of a cerebellopontine angle tumor, facial motor recovery is to be expected, even in the presence of a complete facial palsy postoperatively. One may, however, have to wait as long as 12 mth for clinical signs of recovery. Recovery is likely to be better than that provided by anastomosis from another cranial nerve. The authors would recommend, therefore, that under these circumstances, at least 1 yr be allowed for spontaneous recovery. If some cosmetic procedure is required, perhaps a plastic operation rather than nerve anastomosis would be preferred.

It was at least a wk before denervation could be suspected in the latter conditions by electrodiagnostic methods. Tuberculosis of the middle ear; Two cases of tubercular otitis media are reported. These cases were treated by ordinary means for chronic purulent otitis media for a period over a year without any improvement. Case one was a woman, aged 65, who complained of impaired hearing in both ears, otorrhea, vertigo and right facial palsy. Operative procedure on the affected ear showed a tumor-like or tubercular appearance of the tympanic mucoperiosteum. Histological examination of the removed specimen revealed a typical tubercular lesion. Case two was a woman, aged 31, found to be affected with lung tuberculosis and a chronic purulent otitis media with narrowing of the right ear canal. A bacterial examination of the otorrhea revealed positive findings of tubercular bacilli. Both cases were treated by anti-tuberculosis measures by use of streptomycin, PAS and INAH, and with topical application of streptomycin in the ear. Within a month after these treatments the ear discharge was gradually reduced and became much clearer in its content.

Facial nerve dysfunction; Facial nerve dysfunction should be considered as a possible symptom of several underlying diseases which may involve the nerve from its origin near the brainstem to its periphery. Localisation of the site of facial nerve involvement can be made by careful clinical examination as well as by electrophysiological techniques. Specialised radiology is also helpful in revealing lesions within the temporal bone as well as lesions in the cerebellopontine angle. Apart from the common conditions affecting the facial nerve, the author discusses three important conditions, namely congenital cholesteatoma in the cerebellopontine angle or the petrous apex, facial nerve neuroma and meningioma. The author pleads for a careful study of the problem of facial dysfunction to enable the otolaryngologist to make the correct diagnosis and suggest appropriate therapy.

Diffuse otitis interna; In the time period from 1945 to 1974 250 patients were treated for diffuse otitis interna developing as a consequence of chronic otitis media. Para infectious cerebral nerve mononeuritis and mononeuritis multiplex: a selectively located type of para infectious, postvaccination, serogenetic neuritis; Arising from 18 of the author's own cases of parainfectious isolated, or multiple, cranial nerve neuritis, this localization type of an inflammatory reation of the peripheral nervous system is described. The causal relationship with the most varied types of infectious disease, but also with immunization or serum administration, is indicative of the pathogenetic role of an immunologic mechanism. Whether this concerns an immune complex disease, as is assumed in serogenetic polyneuritis, or a cell mediated immune response, as in the Guillain Barre syndrome, requires further investigation. Knowledge of this type of manifestation of 'cranial polyneuritis' is of clinical importance in order to avoid confusion with cranial nerve syndromes from other causes, and to avoid carrying out unnecessary diagnostic measures. Adenoidcystic carcinoma (cylindroma) of the parotid gland; Adenoidcystic carcinoma (cylindroma) of the parotid gland is a slow-growing, relentless, and often lethal disease which kills usually by local occurrence and direct extension of the disease. The reported incidence of adenoidcystic carcinoma with reference to other malignant parotid tumors varies from 5% to 37%. The incidence in this series (14 cases; 1960-1970) is 36%. The presence of facial nerve involvement adversely affects the long-term survival. Some authors regard facial nerve involvement as an indication of noncurability. The incidence of local pain is reported to be as high as 50% and is thought to be caused by perineural invasion by the tumor. This is well-documented histopathologically. There is no uniform or standard treatment for this disorder. Extensive resection of the parotid gland (including the facial nerve if there is any indication of involvement), followed by external irradiation to the parotid area and upper neck is the most rational approach to the problem. This is supported both in the review of the literature and from the present series. A radical neck dissection is not included as part of initial therapy unless there are clinically suspicious cervical nodes. Postoperative radiotherapy appears indicated in all cases of adenoidcystic carcinoma of the parotid gland. Four case histories are presented which demonstrate the hallmark characteristics of the disease, i.e., multiple cranial nerve deficits, facial pain and subsequent death by direct intracranial extension of disease. The protracted, relentless course of the disease is well-documented in 1 case in which 25 local recurrences developed over an 18 yr period.
A Bell"s palsy of long standing, and its rehabilitation. An electromyographic documentation. (author's transl); We examined a 31 year-old female patient who, since her first year of life and following a parotis operation, had suffered from left-sided Bell's palsy. The electromyographical examinations disclosed a complete loss of voluntary muscle control and of the trigemino-facial reflexes, although the direct responses of the facial nerve could be demonstrated with delayed latences. The findings indicated peripheral regeneration of the facial nerve with absence of central programming and reflex pathways. By means of rhythmic muscle stimulation, voluntary control and reflex excitability was re-established, to a limited extent, on the formerly inactive side within a short space of time.
Traumatic facial paralysis caused by a fracture of the petrous part of the temporal bone. (With reference to 47 cases observed over 4 years); Between 1971 and 1975, 47 cases of traumatic facial paralysis were observed (3.7% of the patients admitted for skull traumatism). Facial paralysis was more frequent in cases of traumatism with loss of consciousness (4.3%) than without (2.3%). In 17 cases there was no line of fracture; in 12 cases there was only a fracture of the squamous part of the temporal bone without any clear radiation towards the petrous pyramid. In only 18 cases was there a fracture of the petrous part of the temporal bone. Peroperative observations sometimes contradicted radiological data by revealing fractures which did not show up on Xray films. Of the 26 cases of immediate facial paralysis, 9 presented rapid regression within the first 15 days and 17 underwent operation. The lesion of the facial nerve observed at operation was: in 7 cases a contusion, in 7 cases compression, in 3 cases section. Of the 21 cases of secondary facial paralysis, 15 soon showed spontaneous recovery and 6 underwent operation. Observations at operation were: in 5 cases a contusion, in 1 case compression caused by a fracture which did not show up on Xray film. The results of operation were on the whole very satisfactory in the cases of simple contusion. They were regular but often incomplete in the cases of compression. As for surgical repairs of section of the facial nerve by means of microscopic procedures, this is still rather risky and the therapeutic results are often disappointing (2 failures out of every 3).
Transtympanic facial nerve paralysis; The case of transtympanic facial nerve paralysis has been presented with a review of the literature. A high index of suspicion plus a careful examination of the external auditory canal after removal of blood clots will help to make the diagnosis. Polytomography (hypocycloidal laminography) may be helpful in localizing a foreign body or temporal bone fracture. Prompt exploration, decompression, anastomosis or nerve grafting may be indicated in acute complete traumatic facial nerve paralysis. Partially delayed facial nerve paralysis should be followed by daily facial nerve conductivity studies, and most often will recover spontaneously.

Polyneuropathies as a diagnostic and therapeutic task; Despite their variety the syndromes of peripheral neuropathy are variations of just one subject. Surgical and nonsurgical management of facial paralysis following closed head injury.; The outcomes of facial nerve decompression, surgical exploration, and nonsurgical treatment for facial paralysis following closed head injury were analyzed in 30 patients with an intact facial nerve, and complete evaluation. Objective evaluation of outcome was achieved by calculation of a Facial Paralysis Recovery Profile and Recovery Index (Profile minus complications). Twelve of 15 patients with incomplete facial paralysis were treated medically. All followed patients with incomplete paralysis and bilaterally equal facial nerve excitability had a Recovery Index of + 10 (complete recovery of function, no complications). Three with partial denervation had a Recovery Profile of + 10 with mild contracture and synkinesis. The average Recovery Profiles for all patients treated by decompression, exploration, or nonsurgically were respectively 4.0, 5.7, and 5.7. The Recovery Indices were +1.8, +3, and +2.7, respectively. Where nerve excitability had become abnormal, facial nerve decompression was of no benefit in traumatic facial paralysis due to closed head injury. Nerve excitability tests of peripheral branches are of great value for prognosis and selection of patients who do not need surgical intervention. Substitution of facial nerve exploration for facial nerve decompression seems reasonable. Polytomography of the facial canal is invaluable in selection of patients for operation.

Surgical treatment of vertigo; The 5 yr follow up results obtained by the surgical treatment of 90 patients suffering from Meniere's disease are presented. Saccotomy with myo synangiosis was carried out in presence of a reversible Meniere's disease (fluctuant hearing loss with normal hearing in the intervals of the disease). The operation, which is easy to perform, relieved 50% of the patients from their symptoms and carried the risk of total deafness in 4% of the cases. Vestibular neurectomy was the operation of choice for the irreversible stage of the disease when hearing was still useful. Muscular neurotization in the field of reconstructive surgery; Attention is drawn in a short historical review to muscular neurotization, a surgical procedure described at the turn of the century. This term is applied to the reinnervation of paralyzed muscles by the proliferation of collateral neural axons arising in an adjacent muscle possessing normal function. The physiological basis for this procedure was expounded by eminent muscle physiologists following extensive research. The present experimental investigations on 20 Vietnamese pigs demonstrated that a defective anal sphincter muscle could be rectified by a muscle graft. This spindle shaped muscle graft became incorporated into the anal and rectosphincteric reflex mechanism by muscular neurotization. Complete or even parts of muscles with parallel fibres are better suited for transplantation purposes than entire spindle shaped or feather like muscles. Once the edge of the muscle has been reached by the proliferating axons all the cells can be simultaneously supplied with motor end plates in the case of muscles with parallel fibres. On the other hand, the use of spindle shaped or feather like muscles with a diagonal arrangement of the fibres entails axon proliferation over relatively large distances to achieve reinnervation of the more distal parts of the muscle with an attendant prolongation of the reinnervation procedure and, frequently, partial loss of muscle viability. In another experiment on Vietnamese pigs the total anal sphincter was excised and replaced by the denervated, but vascular semitendinosus muscle of the right hind limb. When transposed to the pelvic floor musculature the denervated muscle becomes adequately reinnervated by muscular neurotization and at the same time adopts all the properties typical of a sphincteric muscle. The newly formed sphincter displays changes in its enzyme pattern and becomes capable of continuous tonus; the spinal reflex arc is set up and the transplanted muscle develops characteristic metabolic and contractile properties. In another experimental series the reinnervation of paralyzed extraocular muscles by muscular neurotization was investigated in 10 rabbits. The denervated but still vascular inferior oblique muscle was successfully grafted onto the inferior rectus muscle, with obvious clinical application in future. The clinical application of muscular neurotization in surgical reconstruction is demonstrated in 4 cases, the first being one of facial palsy and the second one of blepharoptosis, whilst muscular neurotization was used in the two last cases to treat anal incontinence due to partial destruction and absence of the sphincter, respectively. In the one case a muscle graft was taken to reconstruct the anal sphincter and in the other case a new sphincter was reconstructed by transposing the denervated gracilis muscle onto the pelvic floor muscle. Both cases were eminently successful with restoration of anal continence and the rectosphincteric reflex mechanisms.
