Its relationship with the syndrome of the auriculo temporal nerve; On the one hand, the authors report a case of traumatic peripheral facial paralysis complicated by a paroxysmal homolateral weeping (syndrome of crocodile tears), and, on the other hand, the observation of a syndrome of the auriculo temporal nerve resulting from an operated purulent parotitis. The etiological conditions of the appearance of these two syndromes are in accordance with their usual description.
The Melkersson Rosenthal syndrome: clinical features, nosology and treatment; The term 'Melkersson Rosenthal syndrome' was coined by the Basel otologist Erich Luscher in 1949. This syndrome bears the names of the Swedish neurologist Ernst Melkersson of Goteborg and of the German neurologist Curt Rosenthal of Breslau. Melkersson (1898-1932) died at the outset of his life work 4 weeks after his promotion to the position of lecturer, the cause of his death being a septic infection. Melkersson regarded the syndrome of periodic paralyses of the facial muscles in connection with 'angioneurotic' oedema attacks in the lips as a peculiar combination of symptoms. Rosenthal (1892-1937) a Schleswigean doctor, was the victim in Paris of a traffic accident while on his way to London for the 'Emergency Association of German Scientists Abroad'. He described this syndrome in more detail and pointed out the arthritic symptoms, the varying nervous manifestations and the lingua plicata (which now has lost its diagnostic value). This review article not too lengthy, but factual, as far as is possible in this still uncomprehended syndrome, describes the formerly confusing nomenclature, its signs and symptoms, the manifestations or the skin and its neurologic aspects (cranial nerves, peripheral nerves and central nervous system). The differential diagnosis is discussed in brief as are the changes in the EEG and the psychopathologic phenomena. As regards the neuropathology, only one case has been described which included an autopsy of the brain. The neurovegetative pathophysiology of the M.R. syndrome is given much attention to, while the treatment is discussed as well. This is a useful review; 35 references are cited. d
Prognosis in Bell's palsy; This is a concluding report of a study in which only patients with Bell's palsy initially seen within ten days of onset are included. The purposes are to observe the natural course of the disorder and to illustrate electromyographic (EMG) criteria by which early forecast of recovery is possible. Appraisals of facial muscle strength, nerve stimulation responses and electromyographic needle electrode examinations correlated with the time required for recovery and the relative degree of recovery of patients with Bell's palsy. Three categories of recovery are evident. Of 90 patients, 79% recovered completely within two months (class I), 7% recovered adequately within two to six months (class II) and 14% required longer than six months (class III). Using clinical and electromyographic methods it should be possible to forecast recovery within three days after onset in order to preselect patients in need of any proposed curative treatment program designed to salvage the facial nerve. For prognosis in patients without clinically detectable facial muscle function, the data suggest that they be evaluated on a daily basis from onset until day 4 (past 72 hours). Finding that residual motor unit potentials are sustained in four to five muscles during that period strongly indicates a favorable outcome. Finding activity in two to three muscles could be less favorable and finding zero to one muscle with activity is clearly unfavorable. During this period of time there is a tendency for progressive loss of EMG activity in the facial muscles, both in patients with favorable and with less favorable outcomes.
Massive acquired cholesteatoma of the temporal bone; Nine patients with massive acquired cholesteatoma of the temporal bone were treated by radical mastoidectomy, facial nerve decompression, and excision of the inner ear. The commonest presenting symptoms were otorrhoea and deafness but otalgia, vertigo, external swelling and facial nerve palsies were also seen. Polytomography was helpful in assessing the degree of bone erosion preoperatively. The large cavity present following cholesteatoma excision was partially obliterated by a superiorly based temporalis muscle pedicle which helped to seal the internal auditory meatus and prevented the development of a cerebral hernia. Those patients with preoperative facial nerve palsies showed evidence of nerve degeneration and had incomplete recovery at a one year follow up.
Trigeminal zoster producing facial paralysis and postural hypotension; Postural hypotension is seen in endocrine and electrolyte disturbances such as adrenal insufficiency, hypopituitarism, diabetic ketosis, and salt depletion syndromes. The authors describe a case of facial paralysis and severe disabling postural hypotension following zoster infection of trigeminal ganglion.
Temporal bone histopathology of osteopetrosis; The temporal bone of an 8.5 yr old girl with osteopetrosis (Albers Schonberg disease) was studied to evaluate the pathogenesis of its frequent complications in hearing and facial nerve function. The patient was blind and had acute otitis media, but facial paralysis was not noted. Although the size of the temporal bone pyramid was markedly increased due to an enormously thickened periosteal layer, changes in the endosteal and endochondral layers were less marked. Exostotic growth of periosteal bone was seen in the middle ear wall, and the tympanic cavity appeared to be narrowed. At the oval window region, the facial nerve was pushed down towards the stapes due to extreme overgrowth of periosteal bone of the epitympanum, and the superstructure of the stapes was imbedded deeply into the dislocated facial nerve and had strongly compressed it. Although the footplate was free from ankylosis, the crus of the stapes appeared to be immobilized because it was lodged in the facial nerve. Such changes appeared to be the pathogenesis of one form of facial nerve paralysis and conductive hearing loss associated with osteopetrosis.
Ultrasound treatment of Meniere's disease: Long term follow up of 356 advanced cases; 12 yr experience of ultrasound treatment of 356 patients is presented. For evaluating the results a new multifacetted scoring system was developed, where each individual patient was evaluated on the basis of 4 parameters. According to this evaluation 71% of the patients improved after the operation, while 29% remained unchanged or deteriorated. Because of lack of improvement, 42 patients underwent reoperation by different methods; in half of them ultrasonic irradiation was again used. The hearing deteriorated in about 40% of the patients, to which result the long observation times also contributed. The caloric response became reduced in 70% of the patients. Marked depression of the caloric response characterized the patients who were relieved of vertigo. Transient facial paralysis in 4 patients was the only complication.
Intracranial extradural liposarcoma in the posterior fossa. A case report (Japanese); A liposarcoma, which originated in the left intraauricular area and infiltrated the posterior fossa, was seen in a 25 yr old housewife, who was admitted because of symptoms of intracranial hypertension. She showed left facial palsy and deviation of the tongue to the left without any cerebellar signs. Neurologic examinations suggested a mass lesion in the posterior fossa. Suboccipital craniectomy was performed and the tumor (4x4x3 cm) in the extradural space was partially removed. Microscopically the tumor consisted of lipoblasts and diagnosed as liposarcoma. Intracranial liposarcoma, whether primary or secondary are very rare tumors.
CSF findings in unilateral, bilateral and alternating facial nerve paresis; Etiology of idiopathic facial paralysis remains mostly unknown. Differentiated evaluation of CSF however for cytological or proteinic abnormalities should be performed with serological examinations. In 9 patients treated within 8 months in hospital diagnosis could be made by these procedures. Inflammation, if it is the cause of facial paralysis, can only reveal pleocytosis, if localised within or next to the leptomeninges; protein of CSF perhaps will increase, if local inflammation of the nerve is further from the subarachnoid space. 'Idiopathic facial paralysis' however will not exclude focal inflammation far from the subarachnoid space. Surgical decompression should not be performed without a previous examination of CSF because of its uncertain success.
Recurrent multiple cranial nerve palsy; The authors present seven cases of proven recurrent nerve palsy of the cranial nerves. The duration of the disease is between one and thirteen yr. The number of recurrencies is four per patient. The recurrencies are characterized by headache (in general retrocular) or hemicranial pain, several types of ophthalmoparesis, fifth nerve involvement, facial nerve paresis and, more seldom, eighth nerve and optic nerve paresis. It is interesting to point out than when the third cranial nerve is involved there is a dissociated paresis. All together, the data tend to show a lesion of the cavernous sinus. Many of the symptoms could be mistaken with painful ophthalmoplegia. The painful ophthalmoplegia and the multiple nerve cranial palsy could be part of the same clinical entity. The first one could represent a local form, the second one a multifocal form or an extension of the primary process behind the cavernous sinus.
The clinical features of sclerosteosis. A review of the manifestations in twenty five affected individuals; Sclerosteosis is a unique autosomal recessive condition in which skeletal overgrowth is associated with syndactyly, digital malformation and nail dysplasia. Analysis of the course and clinical features in 25 affected individuals showed that the condition is progressive and potentially lethal. Facial palsy and deafness are common complications and raised intracranial pressure may develop. The clinical and radiographic stigmata of sclerosteosis permit differentiation from the other disorders of the 'osteopetrosis' or 'Albers Schonberg disease' group, in which bony thickening and cranial nerve palsy occur.
Linear scleroderma, beginning with peripheric facial paralysis (Hungarian); A rare case of linear scleroderma beginning with peripheral facial paralysis is reported. The authors' observations point to both immuno allergic origin and origin in the nervous system. This rare disease with neural symptoms necessitated surgical exposure of the facial nerve and the performance of fractional PEG; and initially caused difficulties in diagnosis. However, these experiences are valuable contributions to medical knowledge of the causes leading to peripheric facial paresis.
Otitis and meningitis, associated with the cerebral metastases of a patient with breast cancer (Hungarian); The cerebral metastases of primary tumors often cause diagnostic difficulties. The frequency and the symptoms of the malignant tumors leading to cerebral metastases as well as the difficulties of their diagnosis are analysed. 6 months after surgical intervention, performed because of carcinoma of the mamma, facial paralysis on the right side, and 2 months later seropurulent otitis on the same side and meningitis developed, necessitating a surgical approach. Neurosurgical consultation could not unequivocally clear the presence of cerebral abscess or cerebral metastasis. The latter was verified only during the post mortem examination.
Rheumatic facial paralysis, as misleading diagnosis (Hungarian); The most frequent cause of peripheral facial paralysis is rheumatic (Bell's) paralysis. However, the diagnosis of this paralysis may be misleading, since in the background of the facial paralysis, sometimes not ischemia, but other morphological change may be hidden. Over 10 years the author has collected data revealing intratemporal involvement of the facial nerve in 18 patients, who were previously treated for 'Bell's palsy'. As the cause of the facial paralysis neurinoma of the facial nerve, in 5 patients, in 1 patient meningeoma psammomatosum of the facial nerve, and in 2 patients late metastasis of malignant mammary or salivary gland tumor, have been observed. In 6 cases intrapyramidal cholesteatoma, in 2, granulation of unknown origin, in 1 case diffuse hemangiomatosis and in 1 patient ectopic parotid tissue were found. Besides more perfect diagnostical possibilities, the importance of detailed and careful anamnesis is pointed out, since in the majority of cases, intact tympanic membrane was present. The justification of explorative decompression and if necessary its use on a broader scale, and with more courage, is advocated.
Transposition of the lips for correction of facial paralysis; The authors present a simple operation to correct the marked asymmetry of the lips and lower face resulting from facial paralysis caused by a wide variety of conditions.
Malignant external otitis in children; Malignant external otitis is a very serious variant of external ear infection. It is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, affects elderly diabetic patients, and bears high mortality. The disease may occur in children in whom malnutrition and anemia create suitable conditions for P aeruginosa infection. The disease differs in children, it invades the middle ear and facial nerve in its intratemporal course. The treatment should consist of large doses of carbenicillin sodium and gentamicin sulfate, together with the thorough surgical debridement of all infected tissues.
Tolosa Hunt syndrome: one cause of painful ophthalmoplegia; The author reports 12 cases of Tolosa Hunt syndrome, a benign steroid resistant cryptogenic granuloma that presents as painful ophthalmoplegia. This syndrome is differentiated from other causes of painful ophthalmoplegia including tumors, aneurysms, collagen disease, specific infections, mucoceles, and benign granulomas of unknown etiology. These other conditions should be excluded by appropriate tests. Surgical exploration is not necessary if there is a prompt remission on steroid therapy.
A cured case of hypertensive intracerebellar hematoma (Japanese); A case of hypertensive intracerebellar hematoma which was surgically treated and cured, is reported. A 41 year old male had two cerebrovascular attacks with headaches and vomiting followed by left hemiparesis. Drowsiness and dysarthria appeared the next day. The patient was admitted to a hospital, where right facial palsy, loss of right gag reflex and paralytic hemiplegia on the left side were noted. On the 7 th day, the patient's consciousness became clear but the other neurological symptoms remained. On the 14th day, bradycardia and central hyperventilation appeared: the patient became drowsy again and was transferred to the authors' clinic. When the patient was admitted, he showed typical cerebellar signs such as nystagmus, ataxia, and slurring speech with pyramidal sign on the left side and cranial nerve paralysis on the right side, and also showed changes of vital signs as in a medullary syndrome in its late stages. Vertebral angiogram revealed an invasive process in the right cerebellar hemisphere. The old blood (30 g) was removed by suboccipital craniectomy. The hematoma cavity communicated with the IVth ventricle through a small perforation in the medial wall of the hematoma. Spontaneous intracerebellar hematoma, including of hypertensive origin, is not rare in autopsy reports but surgically treated cases have only rarely been reported. The main reason for the few survivals probably lies in the fulgurant course of this disease.
Corticosteroids in neurology (Dutch); A discussion is presented of the indications of treatment with preparations with corticoid effects in neurology, and the complications to which they may give rise.
The treatment of mixed parotid tumours by enucleation and radiotherapy; A series of mixed parotid tumours treated by simple enucleation and radiotherapy between 1962 and 1968 is discussed. There were 73 primary and 8 recurrent cases. Only 2 small recurrences occurred in the 73 primary cases, although 4 other patients were lost to follow up after 7 years or more. In the 8 recurrent cases, 7 had been treated elsewhere by enucleation alone, thus confirming the opinion that this operation is frequently unsuccessful. Treatment was by further local excision and radiotherapy and no recurrences have occurred. The view is therefore expressed that simple enucleation and radiotherapy is the treatment of choice in all primary mixed parotid tumours.
Suboccipital removal of acoustic neuromas. Results of 125 operations; The surgical results obtained in 125 patients with acoustic neuromas, using the suboccipital approach, are reported. These reults do not differ from those obtained in other neurosurgical materials, with the same distribution of tumor size, and the same surgical approach. The material consists of 20 medium size tumors, and 105 large. However, the results, regarding both mortality, postoperative facial paralysis as well as postoperative condition in general are unsatisfactory. A historical review of the development of the surgical treatment of acoustic neuromas is given, and the necessity of a closer neurosurgical otologic cooperation is stressed, both with regard to diagnosis of the neuromas as well as the surgical treatment.
Experiences in medicamentous dysphagia prophylaxis in geriatrics; In geriatric practice oropharyngeal dysphagia of neuromuscular origin is not rare. In its background, mostly cerebrovascular changes, bulbar paralysis, pseudobulbar paralysis or other such organic damage to the brain play a role. Realizing the geriatric significance of neuromuscular dysphagia, the authors, pondering over the clinical pharmacological data available to them, began using an anti cholinergic agent, Stigmosan. In old patients with dysphagia the effect of 1/2 to 1 tablet of Stigmosan half an hour before meals was very good in the majority of the cases; the 'swallowing' dysphagic patients, who not infrequently were also aspirating patients as well, became free of all complaints.
Peripheral facial paralysis: diagnosis; Peripheral facial paralysis is a diagnostic challenge. Every effort must be made to determine etiology since often a treatable cause can be found. Patients with peripheral facial paralysis are often labeled as having Bell's palsy without any adequate evaluation. Bell's is an exclusive term reserved for patients in whom all known causes of acute acquired isolated peripheral facial paralysis have been ruled out. This point is stressed since 17 percent of the last 160 consecutive patients referred to us with a diagnosis of Bell's palsy were found to have an underlying cause.
Bilateral malignant external otitis in a 10 year old girl; Malignant external otitis which has a very severe prognosis has been described as being related to diabetes in old age. The authors present a case with malignant external otitis which occurred in a 10 yr old girl. The external otitis which appeared at first on the left side was accompanied on this side by a facial paralysis; 6 mth later, on the right, a malignant external otitis was found without facial palsy. Furthermore, this girl was affected by a diabetes insipidus for which no hypophysial or renal cause was found. After reviewing the literature, the authors discuss the clinical aspects and treatment of this case.
Human peripheral neurolymphomatosis (reticuloendothelial polyradiculoneuritis); This is the clinical and pathologic report of a case (woman of 53) of reticulo endotheliosis of the nervous system. She had a history of transient facial palsy followed 6 mth later by progressive weakness, paresthesiae and severe pain in both lower limbs. Clinical examination revealed signs of sensory and motor polyradiculoneuritis with involvement of the oculomotor, facial and trigeminal cranial nerves. She died 10 mth after the onset because of bronchopneumonia. Pathologic findings in the nervous system were limited to the cranial and spinal roots and ganglia. Histopathologic examination showed intense infiltration by lymphocytes, histiocytes, plasmocytes and macrophages and a large amount of reticulin. The left oculomotor nerve, both Gasserian ganglia, the right trigeminal nerve and the lumbosacral nerves and ganglia were particularly involved. The literature on human peripheral neurolymphomatosis is reviewed and the differential diagnosis of this condition from Marek's disease, sarcomas, leukemic polyradiculoneuritis, sarcoidosis and Hodgkin's disease of the nervous system is discussed. The importance of recognizing this variety of polyradiculoneuritis, and methods of treating it are emphasized.
Melkersson Rosenthal syndrome: report of a case; The authors have made a review of the Melkersson Rosenthal syndrome and a new case is reported. The diagnosis of our patient was based on the recurrent facial nerve palsy, furrowed tongue, and the history of episodic lip and facial swelling accompanied by hemicranial pain. This is a syndrome without evident etiology. It is chronic and has not responded to treatment. Although it is futile to draw conclusions from one case, perhaps this syndrome is due to an autonomous nervous system defect.
Clinical features of salivary gland tumours; This paper reports on epithelial tumors arising primarily in the major and minor salivary glands. The purpose of this presentation is to summarize the experience with salivary gland tumors on the basis of approx. 3000 salivary gland tumors as well as a review of the literature to date. The tumors are classified according to the classification recommended by the WHO in 1972. The incidence, location, symptomatology, grade of malignancy and treatment of the different tumor types in this classification are reviewed. Diagnostic procedures are discussed and a scheme for surgical treatment and radiotherapy of the different types of salivary gland tumors is proposed.
The use of neuromuscular free autografts with microneural anastomosis to restore elevation to the paralysed angle of the mouth in cases of unilateral facial paralysis. With an analysis of late results of muscle grafts in the treatment of 103 cases of facial hemiparesis; A new method is described for the correction of paralysis of the elevator muscles of the angle of the mouth in cases of unilateral facial paresis, by transplanting skeletal muscle as a free graft together with its motor nerve of supply, the latter being anastomosed to normal filaments of the facial nerve on the uninvolved side of the face, using microsurgical techniques. The results in twelve patients treated over a period of one year, are encouraging and are being given continuing trial. The late results of free autogenous skeletal muscle grafts in restoring movement to the eyelids and mouth regions in 103 cases of unilateral facial paralysis, involving 157 grafts, are presented.

Wegener granulomatosis: the Iowa experience; During the eight years (1967-1975) the diagnosis of Wegener's Granulomatosis (WG) was established in 12 patients hospitalized at the University of Iowa and VA Hospital, Iowa City. Eight were male, 4 female with an age range 6-69. Two patients, initially diagnosed as midline granuloma, subsequently evolved to a diagnosis of WG with the development of renal involvement after an interval of 3 and 4 years. Simultaneous sinus, pulmonary and renal involvement was seen in 4/12 patients; sinus and renal in 4/12; sinus and lung in 2/12; lung and renal in 1/12; and lung only in one patient whose tissue biopsy was interpreted as lymphomatoid Granulomatosis (LG). Other clinical findings included ophthalmic involvement (2/12), facial palsy (1/12), arthralgias (3/12), skin rash (3/12) and diabetes insipidus (1/12). Ten of 12 patients presented with a hemoglobin < 11.5 Gm; 7/12 with leukocytosis > 11,000; 7/12 with thrombocytosis > 500,000; and 11/12 with an elevated sedimentation rate. No consistent diagnostic pattern of serum immunoglobins (IgA, IgM, IgG) was observed. One patient was treated with prednisone alone for 2 years and subsequently lost to followup. Three of 12 patients have died: 1 patient received no therapy; 2 patients, who presented with thrombocytopenia, azotemia and renal failure, developed bone marrow suppression and were intolerant of cytotoxic therapy. Eight of 12 patients are alive: 6/12 are continuing on therapy with cytotoxic agents (cyclophosphamide) with satisfactory clinical responses; 2 patients are clinically in remission: 1 patient with LG treated 6 months with prednisone, and 1 patient with WG treated 17 months with azathioprine. Remission on these patients now dates 42 months and 21 months, respectively. One patient developed a unique complication of therapy consisting of extensive 'shelling out' of multiple large nodular lesions with the subsequent development of obstructive airways disease. This review supports the concept that prompt institution of cytotoxic therapy prior to the onset of renal deterioration has definite value in the management of this illness.
The transcochlear approach to the skull base; A new approach to tumors of the skull base is described. This approach is accomplished by forward extension of the translabyrinthine opening into the cerebellopontine angle. The facial nerve is mobilized in the temporal bone from the stylomastoid foramen to its entrance into the internal auditory canal. Having removed the barrier of the facial nerve, additional bone removal can be carried forward to the internal carotid artery, which now becomes the forward limit for temporal bone resection. The access attained through this exposure allows removal of tumors arising from the petrous tip, as well as tumors arising directly from the clivus. The authors provide the case histories of four patients in whom this approach was successfully used in removal of skull base tumors.
A unilateral congenital facial palsy (Japanese); 4 Cases of congenital facial palsy, without any other physical anomaly are reported. The patients' history revealed normal births without any birth trauma. The facial palsy was noted in all cases within 10 days after birth. There was no history of having any disease except for an attack of otitis media in 1 case. There was a partial paresis in 1 case, a boy 2 yr and 8 mth old; a total paresis in 2 cases, boys, 2 yr and 6 mth and 1 yr and 2 mth old; and a paresis affecting only the oral angle in a girl, aged 3 yr and 6 mth. Following a thorough physiological examination of topology, the course of the facial nerve in the temporal bone was examined surgically. In 1 case, the facial nerve was found to be situated in an anomalous position; while in 2 cases, there were anomalous stapes and the long foot of the incus. In the last case, the facial nerve was found to be normal, but it was considered that the paresis was due to hypoplasia of the depressor anguli oris muscle. Congenital facial palsy may be manifested as a result of a middle ear anomaly, especially of the 2nd branchial arch without any pathological factors involving the facial nerve per se.

Contributions to the surgical treatment of facial paralysis (with reference to 386 facial decompressions) (Roumanian); Ischemia plays an etiopathogenic role not only in idiopathic paralysis but also in a remarkable number of traumatic, otic and viral facial paralysis. The common traits in the pathogenesis of these paralyses are: an inextensible facial bone canal, the absence of drainage orifices, and oedema. Decompression of the nerve must be obtained by cutting a fine, narrow gap in the bone canal, without broad denudation of the nerve. Total facial paralysis in which the gustatory disturbances do not disappear within 2 wk, or which in the course of 8 wk do not give signs of clinical recovery, must be operated.
Surgical treatment of facial nerve involvement caused by leprosy; Complete and partial facial nerve paralysis can result from leprosy. The latter is more prevalent and results in lagophthalmos and corneal hypoesthesia. The former is characterized by loss of facial expression, deviation of the face to the nonparalyzed side, difficulty in chewing, and drooling, in addition to lagophthalmos and corneal hypoesthesia. Affected patients are at risk to develop blindness, as well as suffering social and economic deprivation because of the effects of facial nerve paralysis. Prevention of blindness and amelioration of the latter were successfully achieved by muscle transfer procedures, temporalis transfer to the eyelid, and masseter transfer to the mouth and nasolabial fold in small, minimally equipped hospitals in Africa.
Intrameatal acoustic neurinomas (Hungarian); Four cases with intrameatal acoustic neurinoma observed between 1969 and 1974 are reported. The first tumor was removed from combined translabyrinthic suboccipital approach, and the three other tumors from approach through the scala media. In the first case, the tumor appeared from sudden cochleovestibular loss and facial paralysis. Two tumors resembled Meniere's disease (in one case the caloric vestibular irritability was normal, in the other case absent). The fourth tumor lead to important neural impaired hearing, (with residual hearing only in the sphere of high voices), to vestibular anesthesia and facial tic. Out of the three latter tumors, in two distinct facial fatigability was observed and demonstrated by the author's method. However, the patients did not suffer from clinically manifest facial paralysis. The findings of the positive contrast material by meatocysternography were identical with the operative findings in all four cases. After the operation, the hearing remained in one case (in the case of the smallest tumor) unchanged; in the other cases, loss of hearing occurred. In all four cases vestibular anesthesia persisted. In the first case, after the operation, improvement of the facial paralysis was observed. In two other cases, total paralysis developed, which, however, improved later. In the fourth case the facial function remained intact, but the distinct fatigability, observed before the operation, and the tic ceased. The favorable possibility of the removal offered from 'middle fossa approach' makes profitable all effort to detect the acoustic neurinomas in the intrameatal stage.

Study of the functional outcome of 47 cases of viral facial peripheral paralysis and Bell's palsies; 47 cases of Bell's palsy and viral facial nerve paralysis have been lengthily studied on an analytical and functional basis. An important number of these cases corresponded to serious forms seen right away or lately. The importance of analytical evaluation and electric and functional explorations is underlined. Relationship of phytohaemagglutinin induced lymphocyte transformation to disease activity in systemic lupus erythematosus; Phytohaemagglutinated induced lymphocyte transformation was studied in 19 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in relation to disease activity, peripheral blood lymphocyte count, serum iron and folate levels, and corticosteroid treatment. Similar studies were performed on a group of 28 age and sex matched controls and on 10 patients with facial palsy who were examined before and after 7 days of high dose corticosteroid treatment. The patients with SLE were found to have impairment of lymphocyte transformation which was most marked in active stages of the disease and associated with a lymphopenia. This depressed transformation, which improved with the development of a remission, could not be attributed to the effects of corticosteroid treatment, inhibitory serum factors, iron deficiency, or any numerical reduction in blood lymphocytes, thus indicating along with evidence from other sources that SLE patients have a defect of cell mediated immunity. The aetiological implications of these findings are discussed.
A peculiar case of panencephalopathy with widespread distribution of plaques, status spongiosus and demyelination (Japanese); In a 56 yr old Japanese male whose father and one sister had died of the same disease, the onset of the illness was at the age of 46 yr with complaints of gait disturbances and sharp pains in the lower extremities. Subsequently, dysarthria and marked ataxia in the trunk and extremities developed. Six years later, apathy, urinary incontinence, atactic eye movements, bulbar palsy, fasciculation of the muscles and convulsions became manifest. The EEG showed no periodic synchronous discharge, while irregular theta and delta waves were extremely abundant. The CSF was normal except for an occasionally positive Wassermann reaction. The patient died from a subarachnoid hemorrhage at the age of 56, when the decerebrated state had lasted for about 3 yr. The total duration of the illness was about 11 yr. The brain weighed 930 g., showing atrophy of the cerebrum, especially in the frontal region. The cerebellum, midbrain, pons and spinal cord also showed atrophy. On the cut surface, the atrophy of the white matter, caudate nucleus and thalamus was severe, while that of the putamen and globus pallidus was less so. Atheromatous changes of the arteries were scarce. Histologic examination revealed that numerous plaques and status spongiosus associated with neuron loss, degeneration and astrocytosis were present throughout the cerebral cortex. A number of plaques, many of which were reminiscent of the kuruplaque, were also observed in both the molecular and granular layers of the cerebellum. Small to moderate numbers of plaques were found in the striatum, midbrain, pons and subcortical white matter of the cerebrum and cerebellum. A moderate to severe degree of neuronal loss and degeneration accompanying astrocytosis was observed in the basal ganglia, brainstem and cerebellum. In the spinal cord, loss of nerve cells was generally mild. Moreover, another finding in this case was the severe demyelination which was distributed, more or less, throughout the entire CNS. Comparing the degree of demyelination with the presence of protoplasmic astrocytes and fat laden macrophages, fibrous gliosis in these demyelinated areas was definitely mild. Changes of the cortex (status spongiosus, neuronal loss and degeneration, and presence of the numerous plaques) might indicate Creutzfeldt Jakob disease and kuru. However, the combination of these changes with widespread demyelination in this case is unique and has not been reported in the literature, before.
Malignant external otitis. A severe form of otitis in diabetic patients; Two cases of malignant external otitis are presented and the literature is reviewed. The disease seems to occur exclusively in elderly diabetic patients. Diagnosis is mostly a clinical one, and requires a high index of suspicion. The characteristic clinical manifestations are pain and severe tenderness of the tissues around the ear and mastoid, persistent drainage and the presence of granulation tissue at the junction of the osseus and cartilagenous portions of the external ear. Roentgenographic findings are not helpful in the early stages. The pathogenesis of this disease depends on the presence of clefts in the cartilage forming the floor of the external auditory canal at its junction with the osseous portion through which infection can spread from the external ear to the deep soft tissues. Serious and often fatal complications may ensue. The most common and earliest symptom to appear is facial nerve palsy. Pseudomonas aeruginosa has been isolated uniformly, in pure or mixed cultures. This entity, therefore, should be borne in mind whenever an elderly diabetic patient presents with external otitis not amenable to the usual methods of therapy. Ps. aeruginosa should be strongly suspected, and its isolation should prompt vigorous systemic treatment with gentamicin and carbenicillin before extensive necrosis of cartilage and bone takes place. Any delay in diagnosis and management will lead to serious and often fatal complications.
Multifocal sclerosis in children; A case of multiple sclerosis is described in a 6 yr old girl. During 5 yr, she had 7 relapses with the same typical clinical and biological findings. After a review of the literature 64 cases in children are summarized. The onset symptoms are comparable with those shown in the adults but abnormal gait, facial palsy, headache, tremors, dysarthries are much more common. In 37.5% of the cases, death appears after an acute course of less than 2 yr. The others are regressive cases, with minor neurological sequelae. Etiopathogeny and therapy are the same as in adults.
Occult tumors of the infratemporal fossa. Report of seven cases appearing as preauricular facial pain; Seven patients had occult malignant neoplasms either originating in or extending to the infratemporal fossa. Common symptoms were facial pain centered over the temporomandibular joint and facial numbness. These symptoms were sometimes associated with middle ear effusion and trismus. Multiple biopsies are often necessary to establish the diagnosis. The average delay in diagnosis from first symptom was 14 mth. Infratemporal fossa neoplasia belongs in the differential diagnosis of facial pain.
Bone sarcoidosis; Sarcoidosis of the bone has been observed in 24 patients for up to 43 yr. It was always present in hands and/or feet and also elsewhere in 4 other patients. Soft tissue swelling preceded the radiological abnormality for up to 4 yr in 9 patients, accompanied it once, followed it once, and was absent in 13 (55%). Bone involvement was usually an incidental finding when sarcoidosis presented elsewhere, including lupus pernio (50%) and other chronic skin lesions (41%), lungs (75%), eyes (51%), lymph nodes (21%), liver (17%), spleen (13%), parotids (13%), facial palsy in 2 patients and erythema nodosum in 1. Pulmonary infiltration, with or without lymphadenopathy, was evident in three fifths of the patients and hilar adenopathy alone in one fifth. Sarcoid tissue was observed in the bone, but not in the surrounding soft tissue swelling of 2 amputated fingers. There were 3 types of bone lesions: a) lytic in 20 patients; minute 1 mm cortical defects or larger, usually rounded defects that on healing become corticated leading to punched out 'cysts'; b) permeative in 8 patients; these showed progressive cortical tunnelling with remodelling of trabecular and cortical architecture; c) destructive in 3 patients, with secondary joint surface involvement and in one a periosteal reaction.
The transmeatal approach to the geniculate ganglion; With the transmeatal approach to the geniculate ganglion a decompression of the facial nerve is possible in cases of Bell's palsy and herpes zoster oticus when cochlear and vestibular function are intact. In the 10 patients whom we operated on since 1971 and who had a follow up period of more than 6 months, a recovery of facial function in all 3 branches of the nerve was found.
The treatment of peripheral facial paralysis by spinal or hypoglosso facial anastomosis; The authors report a series of 18 patients with peripheral facial palsy resulting from removal of acoustic neuroma (16) or petrous bone fracture (2) and treated by spinal accessory or hypoglossal facial anastomosis. After a review of the literature concerning this operation, the authors report their own experiences based on 12 spinal accessory facial anastomoses and 6 hypoglossal facial anastomoses. Anastomosis is suitable in patients whose VIIth nerve was obviously destroyed during removal of a neuroma, and operation should be performed as early as possible. EMG data influences the choice of nerve more than as an indication itself. When VIIth nerve is presumed to be preserved, anastomosis should be performed only if no recovery of the facial palsy has appeared after the third month. The authors describe the operative procedure for spinal accessory and hypoglossal facial anastomosis. Magnification helps in accuracy of nerve suture. The authors report their results and emphasize the necessity of early surgery, using the microscope and the contribution of the patient.
Steps for the diagnosis and treatment of peripheric facial palsy; The Pitanguy technique for the correction of deformities produced by peripheric facial palsy are presented. A dermovascularized flap beginning at the nasolabial sulcus and a flap for correction of the lagophthalmus are described. Anatomic, etiologic and diagnosis aspects are also demonstrated.
Cheilitis granulomatosa (Melkersson Rosenthal syndrome); A spontaneous, recurrent, and finally permanent swelling of one or both lips, without an evident cause, is the characteristic feature of a disease with which the name Miescher (1945) is connected. Initially Miescher's cheilitis granulomatosa was considered as a separate entity. Today it is the nearly general opinion that the disease is part of the Melkersson Rosenthal syndrome. The characteristic signs of this syndrome are: facial swelling, facial nerve paresis, and plicated or fissured tongue. An oligosymptomatic manifestation of the Melkersson Rosenthal syndrome in a healthy woman of 24 is described. Excision of the lower lip was performed. The microscopic features were identical in 7 blocks prepared. In and beneath the epithelium were scattered formations of mononuclear inflammatory cells. The connective tissue under the epithelium was edematous, less so in the deeper layers. Near the basis some muscle tissue was found. Cell infiltrates existed, partially as perivascular cuffs. The inflammatory cells were mainly lymphocytes, but plasma cells, histiocytes and epithelioid cells were also encountered. Most infiltrates contained Langhans type giant cells. These cells were partially surrounded by epithelioid cells. The picture was consistent with the diagnosis of cheilitis granulomatosa. The importance of serial sections of the tissue specimen is emphasized. Satisfactory postoperative results were obtained.
Birth trauma and related obstetrical factors. Analysis of 73 cases (Japanese); The subjects of this study were 73 traumatized new born babies among a total of 4163 vaginal deliveries at Tokyo Metropolitan Police Hospital over a 6 year period, from January 1969 to February 1975. Incidence, etiological factors, prognosis of these traumas and the preventive treatments of delivery are discussed in detail. On these 73 cases, various kinds of trauma were observed, such as cephalohematoma (46 cases, 1.11%), skeletal fracture (the clavicula, the humerus, and the temporal os) (11 cases, 0.26%), torticollis (10 cases, 0.24%), dislocation of the articulatio (sternoclavicular and humeroscapular) (2 cases, 0.05%), intracranial hemorrhage (2 cases, 0.05%), and facial palsy (2 cases, 0.05%). The various obstetrical factors were suggested to contribute to the cause of these traumas. The incidence of trauma was significantly increased as compared to the controls when the babies were either too big or premature and also as a result of obstetrical management such as breech extraction, vacuum or forceps deliveries. The result of this investigation suggested that adequate obstetrical management was essential in order to prevent the birth trauma especially when the causing factors were prospected.
Surgical treatment of facial nerve pareses after temporal pyramid fractures (Polish); The technique of exposure, control inspection of continuity and decompression of the paralysed facial nerve in its intracranial course from middle cranial fossa approach is described. The method of nerve exposure in its petrous and tympanic parts and in the area of geniculate ganglion is discussed in detail. Certain personal modifications of this method are presented including particularly the epidural approach from superior tympanotomy (from the mastoid and tympanic tegmentum to reach the tympanic part and proximal portion of the mastoid part). Two cases of traumatic facial nerve palsy in the geniculate area are described in which trauma resulted in fracture of the cranial basis involving the pyramid. In both cases a satisfactory result was obtained with complete or considerable return of movements of the facial muscles. Cases of facial nerve function improvement after partial removal of pyramid or after resection of acoustic nerve tumors are described briefly.
Melkersson Rosenthal syndrome in childhood; A case of cheilitis granulomatosa in an 11 yr old boy is presented. The frequency of Melkersson Rosenthal syndrome in childhood is compiled from data in the literature. The Melkersson Rosenthal syndrome does not differ in children in its clinical and histological picture known from adults. In childhood, females are more often affected than males. The etiology of the syndrome is still unknown. Symptomatic and temporal improvement could be achieved following local injections of triamcinolone acetonide suspension.
The influence of facial nerve sacrifice in surgery of malignant parotid tumors; Malignant parotid tumors in 224 patients were dealt with surgically at the Mayo Clinic between 1940 and 1969. The clinical histories, including follow up of 5 years or more in every case, were reviewed with particular attention to sacrifice of the facial nerve in conjunction with the excision of tumor. This was done in 65 cases. High grade malignancy necessitated nerve sacrifice; other frequent indications were preoperative facial nerve paralysis, pain, and rapid growth of the tumor. Over the 30 year review period, the trend was toward more radical surgery, often including nerve sacrifice, and away from local excision and radiotherapy. Nerve grafting or anastomosis of a sacrified nerve was seldom performed in an attempt to lessen the cosmetic defect of facial paralysis. Later reconstructive procedures are favored.
Masked otological diseases under the clinical picture of the ischaemic facial palsy; Peripheral facial palsy is one of the most frequent diseases of the brain nerves. On account of its localisation there are many different possibilities for its impairment. Despite detailed diagnostics the causes of a peripheral facial palsy are only discovered by operation. The references of cases in the literature and of seven personal observations show that by unsatisfactory functional restitution the conservative treatment of ischaemic facial palsies (Bell's palsy) should be taken into consideration.
Electrophysiologic test results after neurotomy of the chorda tympani in facial nerve paresis; The results of chorda tympani neurotomy in the treatment of ischemic pareses of the facial nerve are reported. A relatively simple operative method for the treatment of pareses of the facial nerve, described and performed by Chouard and Blatt, was used in 55 cases since 1971. The presuppositions for this special treatment are the knowledge of the transmeatal ear surgery, a microsurgical instrumentarium and the consequent observance of the indication criteria for the treatment of ischemic pareses of the facial nerve. On average hospitalization lasts 8 days. Of the 55 patients 46 had a highly restricted function of the facial nerve before treatment, in 5 patients the function was deficient. In the after examination the condition was to be regarded as normal in 35 cases, in 11 patients the function was essentially improved and only in 9 patients this intervention had no success.
Animation of facial palsy in Moebius syndrome by means of a circumoral sling. Case report; The case of a 3-year-old female is reported whose condition was diagnosed as congenital, complete paralysis of the right facial nerve in 1962; and a short time later more specifically described as Moebius syndrome. In 1971, a circumoral fascial sling was inserted. Voluntary movement on the right side of her mouth was noted and continued to improve, making facial actions more symmetrical. This function has remained stable during a five year follow-up.
The Wallenberg syndrome with myocardial aneurysm: An autopsy case (Japanese); A postmortem examination in a 69 yr old man revealed a thrombus in the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and a marked softening in the lateral area of the medulla oblongata the blood supply of which is dependent on this artery. These pathologic findings coincided with the clinical findings. Furthermore, an aneurysm caused by a posterior myocardial infarction was found projected against the interventricular septum. In this aneurysm, numerous mural thrombi were found. Arteriosclerotic changes were found in the vertebro basilar artery, aorta, and renal arteries. Seen in the PICA and lenticulo striatal artery as well as in the bilateral renal artery, were thromboembolisms which might have originated from the mural thrombi of the aneurysm. The cause of death was bulbar palsy due to arteriosclerotic and thromboembolic changes in the arteries resulting in irreversible brain damage. The findings are compared with those reported in the literature, and the incidence and clinical pictures of the Wallenberg syndrome are also discussed.
Rehabilitation in peripheral facial paralysis; The psychologic impact of facial paralysis must be at the center of the concerns of the therapist. The social, cultural and occupational context and the symbolic identification of the deformed face must be taken into account in the esthetic prejudice; in this respect one should never underestimate the reactions of discouragement and latent depression in coming to grips with a condition the rehabilitation of which is still too often neglected.
Lid magnets for facial paralysis; The author presents his experience in the use of lid magnets. The positioning is delicate but tolerance is good and the aesthetic and functional result satisfactory. The essential indication is the development of corneal problems overnight from defective occlusion.
The Bausch and Lomb 'T' lens in the treatment of corneal disease; This study was not designed to make a comparison with other soft lenses, and enthusiasm over the success rate must be tempered by remembering that the criteria for success, symptomatic relief and re epithelialization, are somewhat limited. The Plano 'T' lens did, however, perform well in achieving these specified objectives. The ease of fitting, regardless of corneal shape or size, or the presence of corneal or conjunctival irregularities, offers a distinct advantage over many other soft lenses. The tolerance was extremely good. Occasional lenses were lost, especially in patients with facial palsy, but only one serious complication arose in the whole study.
Peripheral facial paralysis in children; Causes, clinical picture, diagnosis, treatment and outcome of this condition were studied in 13 boys and 8 girls aged 5 mths to 12 yrs. Causes were Bell's palsy (5 children); otitis, mastoiditis or both (9 children); malignant tumours (2 children); congenital abnormalities (2 children); trauma, herpes zoster and rheumatic fever (1 case each). Treatment was mainly surgical (14 cases) or medicinal (5 cases). Decompression is recommended when these patients fail to improve after 4 to 6 wks of conservative treatment.
Facial paralysis, topodiagnosis, clinical orientation and treatment; The anatomical diagnosis in these patients is reached through clinical history; physical examination (including neurological, otological and ophthalmological examination); Schirmer's test; assessment of taste in the anterior 2/3 of the tongue; tests for submaxillary and sublingual saliva. Clinical diagnosis is completed with Hilger's test; electromyography; electronystamography; audiometry; radiograms and blood sugar concentrations. Medicinal treatment includes dexamethasone, nicotinyl alcohol, diazepam and cyproheptadine. Decompression surgery is considered after the second wk of conservative treatment depending on progress.
Use of sympathetic block in facial paralysis; The author reexamines the physiopathological basis of peripheric facial paralysis. He presents several cases managed with cervical sympathetic gland anesthetic blockage and concludes by stating that it is the treatment of choice for those conditions.
Preliminary experience with lid magnets for paralytic lagophthalmos; 43 Patients with paralytic facial palsy were operated upon with lid magnets, according to a method first devised by Muhlbauer and others (1973). When 37 patients were re examined 3 months to 2 years postoperatively, 27 had both magnets in situ functioning well. In nine patients one or both magnets had been removed because of return of 7th nerve function. Including our information about those patients not available for re examination, the method has definitely failed in only four. Cosmetically and functionally the results are subjectively as well as objectively encouraging and appear superior to a lateral tarsorrhaphy.
Our technique of hetero lateral facio facial anastomosis by means of nerve autografting in the treatment of permanent peripheral facial paralysis; The authors describe the technique used in 12 surgical cases of heterolateral facio-facial anastomosis by nerve autograft in the treatment of permanent peripheral facial paralyses. Their main contention is that section of 50% of the neurones of the peripheral branches of the facial nerve on the unaffected side does not impair motricity to any extent and that it therefore is possible to anastomose the proximal portion of some healthy branches to the corresponding distal portion of the affected side by placing between them a graft from the external saphenous nerve. The principles for fascicular suture as defined by Seddon and later by Millesi are followed. The technique differs from that made popular by Smith and later by Samii inasmuch as: - the bilateral hidden face-lift incision makes possible a final passive musculotegumentary suspension of the paralysed side immediately improving the patient's appearance while the nerve re-establishes itself; - retrograde interfascicular dissection on the paralysed side allows precious centimetres to be gained; - pinpointing of the nerve suture area is possible by the placing of a silicone-coated ring with a clip some distance away.
Data processing and otospongiosis (2 part). Statistics from 15 years of stapedectomies; The authors conclude that the problem of the operative replacements in the stapedian surgery of otospongiosis constitutes a very special aspect of the operative techniques and a significant aggravating factor. The more a technique is developed the less it provokes failures calling for a replacement, but it also renders dangerous from the cochlear aspect the replacement necessitated by its failure. In practice, unanimity is now assured on the need for closing the oval window with a tissue graft, which combines the functional flexibility of an elastic graft with the protective role of a resistant and viable closing membrane for the oval window.
Ramsay Hunt syndrome (5 cases); The authors present five cases of Ramsay Hunt syndrome treated with different drugs and the results obtained are reported.
Acute sinusitis and otitis: Their complications and surgical treatment Infectious diseases of the head and neck; The major complications associated with acute suppurative disease in the ear and paranasal sinuses are discussed as well as their medical management and the indications for surgical intervention. Both rhinocerebral phycomycosis (mucormycosis) and malignant external otitis are life threatening acute infections in which surgical intervention often must accompany the medical management. The specific details of surgical treatment, which are discussed in standard textbooks, are not to be described in detail.
Automatic recording and evaluation of neuronography; Neuronography and evoked myography provide earlier a more precise prognosis of facial palsy than nerve excitability test (NET). The authors developed an electronic device for the maximal stimulation test (MST) of May, M., that is automatic. The device counts the spikes of the evoked myogram. A time window is related to the stimulus to exclude stimulus noise and background muscle noise from the counter. Only spikes seen in this window are processed. The number of spikes generated per stimulus is the measurement of the live axons in a stimulated nerve.
Traumatic palsies of the facial nerve; The authors analyze 50 cases of traumatic lesions of the facial nerve, from whom 31 were examined clinically and electromyographically in an interval of 6 mth to 22 yr after the trauma. Operative revision was performed in 14 injured. Better prognosis of traumatic palsies was presented with comparison of ischemic palsies.
Level diagnostics in facial nerve injuries; After a brief survey on the anatomical peculiarities of the course followed by the facial nerve and of the structures it innervates, the authors share their experience with the methods employed in establishing the level of its injury. To this end the Schirmer's test of tear production, taste determination through electrogustometry, investigation of the secretion of saliva and audiometry are used. On the ground of the obtained data eight levels of facial nerve lesion are determined in accordance with Jepssen's scheme. A total of 32 patients with different levels of facial nerve injury were studied. Most of them were subjected to operation, and thus the results of the functional nervus facialis investigation were verified. Level diagnostics is of utmost importance in the treatment and prognosis of facial nerve injuries.
Facial palsy (F.B. ear); A case of complete unilateral facial-palsy of lower motor neurone type, of two months duration, following removal of foreign body from the same ear under general anaesthesia is reported. Exploration revealed a bony spicule, as a result of fissure (fracture in the anterior wall of the bony facial canal), pressing on the facial nerve. Progressive clinical improvement as confirmed by electrical tests has followed removal of the bony spicule together with decompression of the nerve.
The use of steroids in Bell's palsy: a prospective controlled study.; A prospective, controlled, double-blind study was designed to evaluate the effect of steroid treatment on the natural history of Bell's palsy. Fifty-one patients were included in the study between 1972 and 1974. The patients were evaluated and started on treatment within two days of onset of Bell's palsy and followed for six months. Treatment was given in randomized double-blind fashion and consisted of either vitamins or a total of 410 mg of prednisone plus vitamins in descending doses over 10 days. The recovery of facial motor function was determined by three physicians who had no knowledge of the treatment received by the patients. They examined photographs of the patients taken six months after onset of paralysis in eight positions of facial function and categorized them as to complete fair, or poor recovery of facial function. These results of this evaluation were submitted to the biostatistician who broke the treatment code. The results of this study demonstrate no statistically significant beneficial effect of steroid therapy upon recovery from Bell's palsy. Factors considered included the patients' age, sex, the presence of pain, ageusia, hyperacusis, diabetes, hypertension, the progression and degree of palsy, the results of nerve excitability and salivary flow tests, and the time at which recovery was first noted or became complete. Bell's palsy remains without a proven efficacious treatment.
A critical analysis of current trends in the management of Bell's palsy.; The treatment of Bell's palsy has been a controversial subject for many years. During the past 10 years 152 papers pertaining to this affection of the facial nerve have apperaed in the American literature. Ninety-seven of these were general discussions of the etiology, pathology, prognosis and treatment of this condition: 20 were concerned with ascertaining the status of the facial nerve by electrical tests and four with the activity of the chorda tympani nerve in patients with Bell's palsy. The remaining 31 articles specifically discussed the treatment of Bell's palsy. As a result of this obvious interest in Bell's palsy, one would expect that the treatment of this affection of the facial nerve would be more or less uniform at this time. This is not the case, however, for the literature demonstrates it to be in a state of flux. Although steroid therapy has replaced other regimens of medical therapy to a large extent, surgical intervention still has its proponents. It is interesting to note that at the time of this review of the literature, no report of a controlled, double-blind study of the efficacy of steroid therapy for Bell's palsy has appeared in the American literature.
Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome; The Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome consists of recurrent facial edema, mainly localized to the lips, recurrent facial paralysis and plicated tongue. The edema eventually becomes permanent, and in combination with residues of facial paralysis, may bring about considerable disfigurement, thus necessitating medical or surgical intervention. The different elements of the triad often do not occur simultaneously, and two positive findings are often considered sufficient for the diagnosis. A case report of a 52 year old woman with lip edema and partial facial paralysis is presented. Antihistamines and corticosteroids systemically were found to have no influence on the edema, and ultimately plastic correction was resorted to, without any striking improvement of her condition.
Natural history of bell's palsy: the salivary flow test and other prognostic indicators.; Fifty-one patients with Bell's palsy were evaluated within two days of onset and followed for six months without surgical intervention or effective medical treatment in order to observe the natural history of the disease. Sixty-three percent had a complete return while 37 percent had incomplete return. Age, the presence of pain, and taste alterations had no prognostic value. The progression of the palsy, response to maximal stimulation and salivary flow testing were approximately 80 percent accurate in predicting outcome. The salivary flow test was the most useful prognostic indicator since salivary flow became reduced within two days of onset in the patients likely to develop denervation while the other tests did not become altered until 3 to 14 days after onset. In patients with Bell's palsy, the salivation test seems to be the only method capable of predicting denervation before it begins; therefore, it should be ideal for selecting patients for appropriate treatment.
Malignant bilateral external otitis in a 10-year-old girl; Malignant external otitis in which the prognosis is very severe has been recently described, as related to diabetes in old age. We present a case with malignant external otitis which occurred in a 10 year old girl, with a very peculiar development. Indeed, the external otitis which appeared at first on the left side was accompanied on this side by a facial paralysis, and six months later in the right, a malignant external otitis was also found without facial palsy. Furthermore, this young girl has been affected by an insipid diabetes, for which no hypophysial or renal pathology has been found. After reviewing the literature on that subject, the authors discuss the clinical aspect of that case and its treatment.
Prosthetic support for unilateral facial paralysis.; Removable prostheses were used to determine that esthetics and speech could be improved for patients with permanent unilateral facial paralysis. Esthetics had to be compromised somewhat to obtain the maximum benefit for intelligible speech. This procedure can be beneficial in helping patients who are high surgical risks or for whom surgery, for various reasons, is unacceptable.
Recommendations for treatment of traumatic lesions of the facial nerve; The electroneuronographic registration of the summating potentials of the face muscles has been used to assess the prognosis in 72 traumatic facial nerve lesions. The following guide lines have evolved from the experience gained: a conservative attitude is indicated if the degeneration of the motor fibres is less than 90% 6 days following the onset of the palsy and a surgical revision of the facial nerve is indicated if the degeneration of the motor fibres reaches more than 90% during the first 6 days following onset of the palsy. The clinical differentiation in early and delayed traumatic facial palsy cannot be used as a prognostic sign. The amount and rapidity of degeneration of the motor fibres has more prognostic value than the latency between trauma and onset of the palsy. The importance of electroneuronography for the prognosis of iatrogenic facial nerve lesions as well as the value of a careful follow up of regeneration in facial nerve lesions with preserved continuity of the nerve are discussed.
